div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

IN going the round of his customers a short time ago a wholesale grocer's traveller chanced"to leave his order-book at the shop of one of them. The shopkeeper, being of an inquisitive nature, glanced over the contents, and his astonishment can be imagined when lie read at the foot of the order he had just given, "No weighing machine kept here." Needless to add, the order was cancelled. PASSENGER : "Why, guard, how's this ! There's no room in this train !'' Guard : "There'a room enough, but there are too many passengers." IN a cemetery adjoining a small town in the State of Vermont there is a tombstone bearing this remarkable legend: "Sacred to the memory of three twilit." SIIE : "I never saw such a man! He never has any money but lie fritters it away." He: "Aren't you then afraid of marrying hiM ?" She : " Oh, dear, no. After he has married me he'll never have any money." REVERSRD PRECEDENCE. —" Are they husband and wife?" "No ; wife and husband." Tire malfeability of gold is so great that a sheet of foil, it is said, can be beaten as thin as the slice of ham in a railway sandwich. " PRISONER, you have been convicted several times before." "Yes, your honour; but only in the provinces." VAN ARNDT : "And do you really think you could support us in the style to which i I have been accustomed?" Her Father : "I really think so." Vi Arndt: "Then you may become my fathe-in- law."

A WOMAN who started to jump into the river and drown herself suddenly remembered that she had left the cat in the pantry, and hurried hack home. She afterwards said :--" The idea of my struggling in the water, and thinking that that cat was a- licking the cream off my milk in the pantry at that very minute, was more than I could bear I" TIIE FIRST DAY OGT.—Steward : "Did you ring, sir?" Traveller " Yes, steward, I-I rang " Steward: "Anything I can bring you, sir?" Traveller : "Y -yes, st-steward. Bob-bring me a continent, if you have one, or an island—anything, steward, so 1-lullong as it's solid. If you can't, sus-sink the ship." "1 um:. awful hard luck," said a forger to his warder at Portland. "I spent a month learning the signature of a reputed millionaire, and just when I had the cheque ready the fool went bank.

Lpromt (at 11.10 p.m.) : "o—er—bliss Josdick, won't you sing something?" Miss Fos- dick: "Certainly, Mr. Linger. Let's see, what song is it I heard you say the other day always carries you away?" AUNT: "Johnny, you should never leave the table without asking leave first." Johnny: " Well, from the look you gave me over the third helping of pie, I thought you'd be glad to see me go. FRIEND: "What under the sun is that?" M`Fadd ; "That? That, my dear sir, is the greatest art treasure I've found in years—a genuine old master. Picked it up at an auction." "I can't see anything but a piece of dirty canvas in a frame." "Great Angelo? Where are your eyes? There in the corner is the artist's name as plain as day.'

_ _ IN THE WP.ONG Box.—Mrs. Briggson : "Harold, mother called in at your office yesterday, and seeing some bronchial troches on your desk, took several. To-day she is suffering dreadfully, and thinks you meant to poison her. Mr. Briggson (the archi- tect) : "Bronchial troches Great Scott ! that was a box of samples of our little mosaic tilings for hotal and office corridors ! " A REASONABLE REQUEST. —Husband : " My dear, I want to ask you one favour before you go off on that long visit," Wife: "A thousand, my love. What is it?" "Don't try to put the house in order before you leave." "It isn't hard work." "Perhaps not ; but think of the expense of telegraphing to you every time I Want to find anything. ' BLESSINGS OF BRAINS.—.9IIO (complainingly) : "Before we were married you used to bring me flowers almost every day; but now you never think of buying me even a uuch of violets." He (gallantly) : The pretty flower girls don't attract my attention so much as they used to." She : "Oh, you darling ! Never mind; I don't really care for flowers, i.nywy." TAKING' : " Hear about that burglary at Smith's? They must have been a desperate set of fellows." Mrs. Brown: " What did they do?" Brown: "Made their way into the kitchen, and ate some of Miss Smith's home- made cake." TOMMY (discontentedly) : "My presents were jtuv. what I wanted ; but " Aunt Mary : But what, child?" Tommy (more discontentedly) : "Oh, they were just what I expected ! " THE VITAL POINT. —Kitty: "What do you sup- pose her age is?" Tom: "I don't know. Bat a woman's age doesn't matter so much as how long she bad been that age." DOUBLING THE NUMEER.—Lady : "This house would suit me, but there are not enough closets." Landlord : "The number can easily be doubled." "Lady : "Very well, then, I'll sign the lease." Landlord (half an hour later) : "George, send a carpenter to that house to divide each of those ' closets into two." A-NSWEILEU.—" Turn back," pleaded the maiden, "0 Time, in thy flight, and make me young again, just for to-night." " Certainly," rejoined Time, affably. "About bow far must I turn back?" "None of your business." LADY: "Is Mrs. pinks at home?" Servant "No'm." Lady: "Can you tell me when she will be at home?" Servant: "As soon as she gets the parlour dusted, mum, an' she's almost finished now." A SOCIAL SuccEss.—Carper : "My dear fellow, I am surprised that a man of your tastes has one of those autotflUic self-playing pianos in his parlour." Upperton "Greatest thing in the world, my boy Starts to play, puts people at their ease, everybody talks, and no piano-player to be insulted by inattention." Mr. Nibbler: "No; I found it didn't pay. "I sold a story to an editor for a sovereign five years age, and then spent three pounds buying the paper before it was published." The Marchioness of Salisbury gives a certain number of dinners and receptions daring the sea- son, but these little festivities are generally voted very stiff, the Tory politicians have complained again and again of the cold exclusion of their leader, even when he has the grace (or the humour) to invite them to his own house. Lord Salisbury is always discovered to be most objection- able in this respect when he is in offica. Then he becomes utterly impatient of crowded and noisy assemblies, and, if not better advised, would Lave nothing to do with them.

There is a chance of one of the newly-made millionaires to acquire an ancient county seat. Earl Carrington has announced his desire to sell Wy- combe Abbey, the family seat in Bucks, either with three hundred acres of Park or with three thou- sand acres. His freehold property in the town of Wycombe his lordship proposes to keep. lis lord- ship is selling Wycombe because he has just pur- chased from the Earl of Ancaster, Gwydr Castle, I.lanwrst, North Wales, which he will add to his already large estates in \Vales.

There has been much heart-burning in the Guards Corps at the 2nd Grenadiers being alone selected to send men to the Gold Coast, and such vigorous pro- test has been made that the whole arrangement has now been reconsidered by Lord Methuen, and steps have been taken to keep the different battalions in good humour. Lord Methuen has now got the Commander-in-Chief to let the Scots and Cold- streams send men, as well as the Grenadiers. There are to be also representatives of the Ist Lifeguards and the 4th Hussars, now in the home district. The officers selected to take charge of this contingent of the special force are Lieutenant the Hon. G. loud and Captain L. G. Drummond, A.D.C. to Lord Nletimen. The doctor is Surgeon-Captain D. M. O'Callaghan. The Guards are very jealous of each other, but now they are pacified.

Many longing looks are being turned towards Montrose by the large shoal of Liberal fish left out of the water b 3 the adverse tide of the general elec- tion. The general admission that should the Mont- rose Liberals and Mr. John Morley agree together, Mr. Morley has the first claim, makes all the more pronsunced the chorus of disfavour which has greeted the assertion of a gentleman with local con- nections that he has a prior claim, which he cer- tainly should not waive in favour of Mr. Morley. A division among the Liberals means the loss of the seat, but as the election cannot be held until after Parliament has met, there is plenty of time for a good many thing to happen. Among the numerous outs is Mr. Alpheus Morton, the outcast of Peter- borough, to whom Mr. Campell-Bannerman once openly offered as a gift an ancient castle, either in the constituency or not far away from it. and Mr. Nlorton believes he would hare got it but that the War Office declined to sanction a transaction which may after all have been one of Mr. Campbell-Ban- nerman's pleasantries.

We always have among us men who are in ad- vance of their age, and practical people have to bear with their soaring visions with all the patient tolerance they can muster. Dr. Parker has a soul above material considerations. On Monday he eli- cited the cheers of the unemployed, whom he in- vited to the City Temple to listen to his remedy for their present distresses, by propounding a solu- tion which can. only be called in the slang of the day, "A large order." This is no less than pulling down and rebuilding London, and all our large cities, and as if this were not enough, the visionary divine would throw in a picturesque addition in the shape of a waterway between London and Brigh- ton. At whose expense and with what prospects of recoupment the demolition and reconstruction of our cities is to be accomplished is a mere detail, as to which we are not informed. It has been stated and not denied that the wife of an American preacher on whose model Dr. Parker largely founds himself has shown great business aptitude in mak- ing a fortune out oi dealings in real estate. The re- builaing of London would provide new worlds for such a speculator to conquer.

I am officially informed that the plan of action in ,tree is to rush Coomassie—not to lnnd troops and keep them waiting, but to have 6 000 levies to cut a road and go straight ahead with the troops. The coolies will be able to cut a road at the rate of about eight miles a day, anti therefore Coomassie should be reached in tour weeks from the time of St a rti g. The doctors going out are twenty in number, and noted more for knowledge of malarial fever than wounds. This speaks volumes upon what is dreaded.

In another quarter of the world, when we have had a difficulty on our own account similar to that now trouoling the whole of Europe in regard to Armenia, the Foreign Office dealt with the matter with a very strong hand. It will be remembered that quite recently the British Government de- manded the condign punishment of the Viceroy of zectiuen for neglecting to protect the missionaries ttacke.ti by the mob at Cheng-tu, the capital of the province, in May last. There was some hesitation and delay at Pekin, and Admiral Buller ascended the Yangtze, calling on the way on Chang Chih- Tung, the Viceroy of Nankin. I suggested at the time that this was no mere friendly call by the Admiral on the tire-eating, foreign-hating Viceroy. I am now able to say that if the Chinese Govern- ment had not issued a satisfactory decree punish. log the inculpated Viceroy the Admiral had orders to seize and hold Nankin and Wuchang, the capital of Hunan province, which is higher up the river, and near hankow. Hunan is notorious as the centre ot the anti-foreign literature which has led to more than one outbreak of violence against Europeans.

The " Trilhy "boom continues. The book itself is selling at the rate of 5,000 a week, one of the heaviest sales ever known in the book trade. Mr. On Maurier has in hand another novel. but its sub- ject is not yet indicated even. That he or his agent is fully aware ef the height of the tide of prosperity which the artist-uovelist has reached is shown by the prieP asked for the new book. It is no less than £l5OOO for the book rights alone—a most unpre- cedented price His serial rights should be worth quite as much, if not more.

The ardent advocates of the enfranchisement of the fair sex are very angry with the First Lord of the Treasury. They assert that at Glasgow Nfr.Bal- four displayed great cowardice in declining to say whether women ought or ought not to have votes. He has repeatedly, in a position of greater freedom and less respoip.ibility, professed himself a strong advocate of women's suffrage. But there is now a disposition to suspect his sincerity.and I have often heard it sugwested that, in deference to Mr Cham- hellain and the Duke of Devonshire, who affix ms frankly that women ought not to have votes, he has either changed his convictions or agreed to conceal them.

To whatever cause it is to be assigned. there has been lin extraordinary decline in the number of law student called to the bar at the present examina-1 t ion. The total is little more than half what it WOA twelve months ego. For some Years the groans of the ever growing army of briefless ones have been ascending to the sky, and the cry of an overstocked profession may have something to do with the de- cline. On the other hand it may be a m«re passing flueruntion, and it is certainly toe soon to speak of a check having been given to that host of young lawyers who lounge day after day about the law courts without fingering a single fee.

I hear it stated that the House of Commons is to be asked to provide a new residence for the Duke end finches,' of York, and that the settlement made by Mr. Gladstone in respect of the family of the Prince of Wales is to he reopened. The report pro- bably means that Parliament is to be called noon to make proper provision for the Duke of York as heir presumptive. The heirs in the direct line of suc- cession have, under Mr. Gladstone's arrangement, certain claims which have not been exercised by the Prince of Wales in regard to the Duke of York. 4r
At Poona on Monday a Sikh Sepoy shot tvso native soldiers and Lieutenant Riddell, of the 4th Rifles, dead, end then blew his own brains out.

div.head: 'I'HE 14XAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 23, 1895.
div.p: 'I'HE 14XAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 23, 1895.
Weaving was practised in China, according to tradi- tion, B.C. 3000. . .

The ancient Mexicans bad a year of eighteen months, of twenty days each. The first thimbles were made in Holland. They were brought to England in 1695. The British isles comprie no fewer than 1,000 separate islands and islets, without counting the jutting rocks or isolated pinnacles. _ .

In the famous Garden of Olives at Jerusalem there are eight fburishing olive trees that are known to be over one thousand years old. Spiders are met with in the forests of Java, whose webs are so strong that it requires a knife to cut through them. A spider weighing four pounds, w tich has taken up her residence in a catedral at Munick, re- gales herself with a large supply of lamp oil. According to the Eleveur, one of the pike of the Aquarium of St. Petersburg is considered by a com- petent zoologist to have been hatched towarns the end of the fifteenth century. Despite its 400 years of cap- tivity and its age, it seems to be in excellent health. An American, having failed to persuade his wife to discard bloomers, arrayed his hens in that style of gar- ment. When she saw the fowls thus attired, she solemnly vowed never to wear bloomers again. A white tongue denotes a febrile disturbance ; a brown, moist tongue, indigestion ; a browmdry tongue, depression, blood poisoning, typhoid fever ; a red, moist tongue, inflammatory fever ; a red, glazed tongue, general fever, loss of digestion ; a tremulous, rnoist, and flabby tongue, feebleness, nervousness. Male elephants are employed as well as female elep• hants in the Indian army, although the latter are pre- ferred. When the former are captured they cannot be liberated again, for in that case the chances of impri- soning other elephants in the same district would be at an end, as they would warn others away. The little economies that have made Japan so rich may be noticed everywhere. The dust of charcoal is gathered up and mixed witb chaff of wheat, barley and other grains, and with chopped straw. It is then mois- tened into paste, rolled into balls about as big as a bil- liard tall, and makes excellent fuel. New bread and hot morning rolls have been condemned as injurious and difficult oh digestion. However true 'this charge may be, the use of nJw bread appears even from the hygienic point of view, to have some com- pensating advantages. Dr. Troitzki ssates that he has found the new and uncut bread contains no micro or- ganisms, as the heat necessary to bake the bread neces- sarily d:stroys them, while soon after exposure many microbes,not infrequently pathogenic are to be found On the loaves.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER. MY DEAREST NELLIE,
div.p: LADIES' LETTER. MY DEAREST NELLIE,

You will be delighted when you see all th( lovely new materials that we fortunate girls that be able to choose from this winter. All of them are nice, and some of them are—well—are alto- gether beyond description; anyhow, I can't describe them. It is chiffons that I refer to parti- cularly, and one of the very nicest is a charming crinkled gauze, absolutely uncrushable, and dyed in the daintiest tints imaginable. This is twenty inches wide, and cost Is. 10d. the yard, Chen 6 gauze, in delicate colours, is still in vogue, and a novelty is found in pearl embroidered chiffon or net, which is dotted all over with pearl beads about half the size of a pea. I have already seen a natty little evening bodice of this chiffon in palest blue. It was made over a satin or sateen founda- tion in the same shade, and tied with a satin ribbon to match, caught in the centre with a paste ornament. The skirt was of blue satin, embroi- dered with a Louis Seize design of ribbon, garlands, and bows in silver. Painted dresses are extremely chic, and this would look well in pick or cream satin, painted with Watteau blue, while the skirt would be quite pretty, perfectly plain, especially if it is made of the satin soie I have mentioned before.

There are some very nice crepons seen just now, and a lovely dress is made in fancy material of this kind of wintry thickness, in blue and black. The dress boasts a most charming bodice. It has effective

lines of trimming in sable, and handsome collar. like shoulder lapels of green velvet bordered with sable. A suitable hat is one of the latest importa- tions from Paris—of brown velvet, the brim united to a crown of turquoise blue velvet, between which comes a great ruche of black gauze ribbon, and a spreading bow of Paisley ribbon, the most fashion- able trimming of the moment. Some becoming frocks are being made for little girls. Those which are intended for the morning are quite simple with gathered waistband bodices and short plain skirts; the latter are cut with bias seams, so that they have a considerable amount of fulness round the base. Velveteen makes up into dressy little frocks for the afternoon. A new model has a fitting bodice and plain skirt; the former is cut square back and front, like an evening bodice. This space is filled in with a gathered silk chemisette. Full bishop sleeves and a band collar are also made on the same silk. A smart little frock for home wear is composed of bright blue Amazon cloth. The bodice has a rounded yoke ; the lower part of it is arranged to set full and droop over the waistband. Three strips of white satin ribbon are laid from the base of the yoke to the waist, after the fashion of pleats, another piece of ribbon outlines the base of the yoke and the collar-band, as wells as the cuffs and waistband, the ribbon being overlaid with a coarse cotton lace in a string tinting. For girls a little older a suitable costume can be made in plain or fancy

Still the battle goes on between toques and bonnets, and bonnets and hats. lam not a fanatic for any particular style of headgear, beyond the broad idea °that hats are suitable for young and bonnets for older ladies. Toques can be worn by either or by both, but in my opinion nothing suits a young and pretty face 'better than a stylish toque. And some of those one sees in velvet are all one could wish in this way. div.head: How to Avoid Colds.
div.p: How to Avoid Colds.

There is one simply way of avoiding colds—keep your meuth shut when out ot doors. The man or woman who comes out of a close room, especially late at night, and breathes through the mou:h will either catch a bid cold or irritate the lungs sufficient to cause annoyance and unpleasantness. If people would just keep their mouths shut and breath through their noses, this difficulty and danger would be avoided. Chills are often the result of people talking freely while out of doors just after leaving a poorly-ventilated room. It is during youth that the orator number of mankind cot- tract habits of inflammatien which make their whole lives a tissue of disorders.
. Walking_Backwards7N Cure for Headache

An apostle of physical culture says that an excellent and never-failing cure for nervous headache is the simple act of walking backwards. Ten minutes is as long as is usually necessary to promenade. It sometime., how- ever, requires more than ten minutes to walk at all, if one is very " nervous." But it is not understood that it is necessary to walk a chalkline. Any kind of walk- ing will do, provided it is backwards. It is well to get in a long, narrow room, where the windows are high, and walk very slowly, placing first the ball of the foot on the floor, and Wen the heel. Besides curing the headache, we are told that this exercise promotes a graceful carriage and that half-an-hour's walk back- wards every day will do wonders towars producing a graceful gait.—" Science Siftings."

div.head: Mechaniral Horror.
div.p: A Mechaniral Horror.

Perhaps the stramgest'of all clocks Is to be found in India, being one in possession of a Hindu prince. According to a description, published in " Machinery " (South Africa), near the dial of an ordinary-looking clock is a large gong hung on poles, while underneath, scattered on the ground is a pile of artificial human skulls, ribs, legs and arms, the whole number of bones in the pile beirg equal to the number of holies in twelve human skeletons. When the hands of the clock indicate the hour of one, the number of bones needed to form a complete human skeleton come together with a snap by some mechanical contrivance the skeleton springs up, seizes a mallet, and, walking up to the gong, strikes one blow. This finished, it returns to the pile and again falls to piecrs. When two o'clock arrives, two skeletons get up, and strike, while at the hour of noon and mid- night the entire heap springs up in the shape of twelve skeletons, and strikes, each one after the other, a blow on the gong, and then fall to pieces, as before.

div.head: Woman's Progress in 1895.
div.p: Woman's Progress in 1895.

A compilation entitled "The Progress of Women in ! 1895" has been made by Mrs. Louise C. Purington, ! M.D., of Dorchester, in co-operation with Miss Frances E Werird. Under the heading "Religious," it is noted that half of the Board of Deacons in a new church in New York are women,that the Episcopal Diocesan Convention , of Southern California gave women the right to vote for vestrymen and trustees, that Dr. Jennie M. Taylor has gone to Africa as the first dental missionary among women, and that Dr. Hee King Eng is the first Chinese woman graduate of an American college to practise in China, and the second woman graduate of her race to take an Occidental medicine degree. In the political field it is noted, for the first time in the history of Germany, a woman, Dr. Granck-Kuhne, of Berlin, took , part, by invitation, in a public discussion at the Evange- heal Secial Congress, that the Belgian Parliament had for the first time been asked to consider a Bill for woman's municipal enfranchisement,that various we mei have taken prominent official positions in public .if and that nearly four hundred Englishwomen were elected on the Poor Law boards, and forty women on the parish councils. In litera- ture it. is pointed out that women have accomplished much coca, especially in the higher branches of science, and in art that an English painter has been asked to send her portrait painted by herself to the Uffizzi Gallery at Florence, that a New York painter has received honourable mention for her picture in the Paris Salon this year. Women are rapidly coming to the front in all kinds of industry. Among new departures may be noted a superintendent of weddings; the first undert3ker at Chicago ; an auctioneer in London ; a room clerk at a large hotel in Colorado Springs ; many census enumerators, ten in Boston alone ; a stable fore- man ; a professional marketer ; a blacksmith ; and two sheriffs. In New York City Sixteen women make a liv- ing by designing new styles of hats. In Japan many women achieve financial independence by amusing other women. In Chicago a woman has opened a shoedressing and boot-blacking parlour. One hundred or more women are in barbers' shops in Chicago alone. They are sought for their steady nerves and light touch unimpaired by nicotine or liquor. In Philadelphia women are running the elevators in large public buildings.

div.head: PECULIAR RAILWAY.
div.p: A PECULIAR RAILWAY.

One of the most .peculiar railways in America is the elevated railway across the Isthmus of Panama. The only steam used on this remarkable railway is supplied by the brawny arms of halt-naked Indians, who,turning a handle, work the machine like It rude velocipede. The car is something tho shape of the small hand-3riven machine used by navvies on our railways, and holds about three passengers, not includimy, the native pro. Petters, who have to walk while working. The posi.ion in which the passengers are placed, is scarcely so com- fortable as a seat in a Pullman car, but affords at least a capital opportunity of studying the peculiarities of the beautiful tropical scenery below, of hearing the morn- ing call of the whistling grasshopper, the screeching of green parotpiets, and all the minstrelsy of the woods, with, it nosy he, the howl of an occasional baboon. A collision on this line, however, and an abrupt descent into the mass of foliage beneath, might lead to a closer acquaintance than desirable with spiders, centipedes,and snakes, which abound in the vicinity of the railway.

div.head: HIDDEN HAND;
div.p: THE HIDDEN HAND;
CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BIC Illus. E. D. E. N. SOLITHWOETIL
CHAPTEIt IX. MARAII ROCK. " There sits upon her matron face A tender and a thoughtful grace Though very still,—for great distress - I.lath left this patient mournfulness." -

Beside an old, rocky road, leading from the town of Staunton, out to the forest-crowned hills beyond, stood alone, a little, grey stone cottage, in the midst of a garden enclosed by a low, mouldering s one wall. A few gnarled and twisted fruit trees, long past bearing, stood around the house, that their leafless branches could not be said to shade. A little wooden gate, led up an old paved walk to the front door, on each side of which were large win,. cloys.

4ln this poor cottage, remote from other neigh- bours, dwelt the friends of Herbert Greyson, the widow Rocke and her son Traverse. No one knew who she was, or whence, or why she came. Some fifteen years before she had appeared in the town, clothed in rusty mourning and accom- panied by a boy of about two years of age. She had rented that cottage, furnished it poorly, and had settled there, supporting herself and child by needle-work.

At the time that Doctor Greyson died and his widow and son were left perfectly destitute, and it became necessary for Mrs. Greyson to look out for an humble lodging where she could find the united advantages of cheapness, cleanliness, and pure air, she was providentially led to inquire at the cottage of the widow Rocke, whom she found only too glad to increase her meagre income by letting half her little house to such unexceptionable tenants as the widow Greyson and her son. And thus commenced between the two poor young women and the two boys an acquaintance that ripened into friendship, and thence into that devoted love so seldom seen in this world. Their households became united. One fire, one candle and one table served the little family, and thus considerable expense was saved as well as much social comfort gained. And when the lads grew too old to sleep with their mothers, one bed held the two boys and the other accommodated the two women. And despite toil, want, care—the sorrow for the dead and the neglect of the living, this was a loving, contented and cheerful little household. How much of their private history these women might have confided to each other, was not known, but it was certain that they con- tinued fast friends up to the time of the death of Mrs. Greyson. After which the widow Rocke assumed a double burthen, and became a second mother to the orphan boy, until Herbert himself, ashamed of taxing her small means, ran away, as he had said, and went to sea.

Every year had Herbert written to his kind foster-mother, and his dear brother, as he called Traverse. And at the end of every prosperous voy- age, when he had a little money he had sent them funds; but not always did these letters or remit- tances reach the widow's cottage, and long seasons of intense anxiety would be suffered by her, for the fate of her sailor boy, as she always called Herbert. Only three times in all these years had Herbert found time and means to come down and see them —and that was long ago. It was many months over two years since they had even received a letter from him. And now the poor widow and her son were almost tempted to think that their sailor boy had quite forsaken them. It is near the close of a late autumnal evening that I shall introduce you, reader, into the interior of the widow's cottage. . _

You enter by the little wooden gate, pass up the mouldering, paved walk between the old, leafless lilac bushes, and pass through the front door, right into a large, but poor-looking, sitting-room and kitchen.

Everything was old, though neatly and comfort- ably arranged about the room; a faded home-made carpet covered the floor, a threadbare crimson curtain hung before the window, a rioketty walnut table, dark with age, sat under the window against the wall; old walnut chairs were placed each side of it; old plated candlesticks, with the silver all worn off, graced the mantel-piece; a good fire—a cheap comfort in that well-wooded country—blazed upon the hearth; on the right side of the fire-place a few shelves contained some well-worn books, a flute, a few mi lerAls and other little treasures belonging to Traverse; on the left hand there was a dresser containing the little delf ware, tea-service and plates and dishes of the small family. Before the fire, with her knitting in her hand, sat Marah Rocke, watching the kettle as it hung swing- ing over the blez, and the oven of biscuits that sat baking upon the hearth. Marah Rocke was at this time about thirty-five years of age, and of a singularly refined and delicate aspect for one of her supposed rank; her little form, sli ht and flexible as that of a young girl, was clothed in a poor, but neat, black dress, relieved by a pure white collar around her throat; her jet black hair was parted plainly over her "low, sweet brow," brought down each side her thin cheeks, and gathered into a bunch at the back of her shapely little head ; her face was oval, with regular features and pale olive complexion • serieus lips, closed in pensive thought, and soft, ark-brown eyes, full of tender affections and sorrowful memories, and too often cast down in meditation beneath the heavy shadows of their long, thick eyelashes, completed the melancholy beauty of a countenance not often seen among the h rd-working children of toiL Marah Roche was a very hard-working woman, sewing all day long and knitting through the twilight, and then again resuming her needle by candle-light, and sewing until midnight, and yet Marah Rocke made but a poor and precarious living for herself and son—needlework, so ill-paid In large cities, is even worse paid in the country towns, and though the cottage hearth was never cold, the widow's meals were often scant. Lately her son, Traverse, who occasionally earned a trifle of money by doing, "with all his might, whatever his hand could find to do," had been engaged by a grocer in the town to deliver his goods to his customers during the illness of the regular porter; for which, as he was only a substitute, he received the very moderate sum of twenty-five cents, a day. This occupation took Traverse from home at day- break in the morning, and kept him absent until eight o'clock at night. Nevertheless, the widow always gave him a hot breakfast before he went out in the merning, and kept a comfortable sapper waiting for him at nif,dit. It was during the last social meal that the yot would. tell hiS mother all that had occurred in his woria outside the home that day, and all that he expected to come to pass the next, for Traverse was wonderfully hopeful and sanguine. And after supper the evening was generally spent by Traverse in hard study, beside his mother's sew- ing-stand. Upon this evening, when the widow sat waiting for her son, he seemed to be detained lonzer than usual. he almost feared that the biscuits would be burned, or, if taken from the oven, be cold, be- fore he would come to enjoy them; but just as she had looked for the twentieth time at the little black walnut clock that stood between those old plated candlesticks on the mantel-piece, the sound of quick, light, joyous footsteps was heard resounding along the stony street, the gate was opened, a hand laid upon the door-latch, and the next instant entered a youth some seventeen years of age, clad In a homespun suit, whose coarse material and clumsy make could not disguise his noble form or graceful air. _

He was like his mother, with the same oval face, regular features, and pale olive complexion, with the same full, serious lips, the same dark tender brown eyes, shaded by long black lashes, and the same wavy, jet t lack hair—but there was a differ- ence in the character of their faces; where hers showed refinement and melancholy, his exhibited strength and cheerfulness—his loving brown eyes, Instead of drooping Faily under the shadow of their lashes, looked up brightly and confidently full in the face—and lastly, his black hair curled crisply around a broad, high forehead, royal with iatellect. Such was the boy that entered the room and came joyously forward to his mother, clasping his arm around her neck, saluting her on both cheeks, and then laughingly claiming his childish privilege of kissing "the pretty little black mole on her throat."

"Will you never have outgrown your babyhood, Traverse i" asked his mother, smiling at his affec- tionate ardour. "Yes, dear little mother! in everything but the privilege of fondling you that feature of baby- hood I never ahall outgrow !" claimed tite youtit, kissing her again with all the ardour of his true and affectionate heart, and starting up to help her set the table. He dragged the table out from under the window, spread the cloth, and placed the cups and saucers upon it, while his mother took the biscuits from the oven and made the tea; so that in ten minutes from the moment in which he entered the room, mother aad son were seated at their frugal wanner.
" ridiDpose, to-morrow being- SatuicTay, you will have to get up earlier than usual to go to the store 7" said his mothei. _

"No, ma am " replied the boy, looking up brightly, as if he were telling a piece of good news. "I am not wanted any longer! Mr. Spicer's own man has got well again and returned to work." "So you are discharged 7" said Mrs. Rocke, sadly. "Yes, ma'am! but just think how fortunate that is I for I shall have a chance to-morrow of mending the fence, and nailing up the gate, and sawing wood enough to last you a week, besides doing all the other little odd jobs that have been waiting for me so long; and then Monday I shall get more work!" "I wish I were sure of It!" said the widow, whose hopes had long since been too deeply crushed to permit her ever to be sanguine. When their supper was over, and the humble ser- vice cleared away, the youth took his books and applied himself to study on the opposite side of the table at which his mother sat busied with her needle-work. And there fell a perfect silence between them. The widow's mind was anxious and her heart heavy; many cares never communiceted to cloud the bright sunshine of her boy's soul, oppressed her. The rent had fallen f&arfully behind hand, and the landlord threatened, unless the money could be raised to pay him, to seize their furniture and eject them from the premises. And how this money was to be raised she could not see at all! True, this meek Christian had often in her sad experience proved God's special providence at her utmost need, and now she belitved in His ultimate interference, but in what manner He would now interpose she could not imagine, and her faith grew dim, and her hope dark, and her love cold. While she was revolving these sad thoughts in her mind, Traverse suddenly thrust aside his books, and with a deep sigh, turned to his mother, and said:
"Mother, what do you think has ever become of Herbert 7" _ _

"Id; not know. I dread to conjecture. It has now been nearly three years since we heard from him I" exclaimed the widow, with the tears welling up to her brown eyes. "You think he has been lost at sea, mother, but I don't! I simply think his letters have been lost! And somehow to-night I can't fix my mind on my lessons, or keep it off Hertert! He is running in my head all the time! If I were fanciful now, I should believe that Herbert was dead and his spirit was about me (—Good heavens, mother! whose step is that ?" suddenly exclaimed the youth, start- ing up and assuming an attitude of intense listen- ing, as a firm and ringing step, attended by a peculiar whistling approached up the street and entered the gate. "It is Herbert it is Herbert !" cried Traverse, starting across the room and tearing open the door with a suddenness that threw the entering guest forward upon his own bosom, but his arms were soon around the new-comer, clasping him closely there, while he breathlessly exclaimed: "Oh, Herbert I am so glad to see you! Oh, Herbert why didn't you come or write all this long time? Oh, Herbert I how long have you been ashore? I was just talking about you I" . . _ .

"Dear fellow—dear fellow I i have come to make you glad at last, and repay all your great kininess ; but now let me speak to my second mother," said Herbert, returning Traverse's embrace, and then gently extricating himself and going to where Mrs. Hooke stood up, pale, trembling and in- credulous; she had not yet recovered the great shock of his unexpected appearance. "Dear mother, won't you welcome me?" asked Herbert, going to her. His words dissolved the spell that bound her; throwing her arms around his neck and bursting into tears, she exclaimed:

"Oh, my son! my son I my sailor boy! my other child! how glad I am to have you back once more! Welcome?—to be sure you are welcome I—is my own circulating blood welcome back to my heart I—but sit you down and rest by the fire! I will get your supper directly I" "Sweet mother, do not take the trouble I supped twenty miles back where the stage. stopped." . .

"And will you take nothing at all 7"'' "Nothing, dear mother, but your kind hand to kiss again and again l" said the youth, pressing that hand to his lips, and then allowing the widow to pat him into a chair right in front of the fire. Traverse sat on one side of bim and his mother on the other, each holding a hand of his, and gazing on him with mingled incredulity, surprise and delight, as if, indeed, they could not realise his presence except by devouring him with their eyes. And for the next half-hour all their talk was as wild and incoherent as the conversation of long- parted fri,ands suddenly brought together, is apt to be. It was all made up of hasty questions, hurried one upon another, so as to leave but little chance to have any of them answered, and wild exclamations and disjointed sketches of travel, interrupted by frequent ejaculations; yet through all the widow and her son, perhaps through the quickness of their love as well as of their intellect, managed to get some knowledre of the past three years of their "sailor boy's" life and adventures, and they entirely vindicated his constancy when they learned bow frequently and regularly he had written, though they had never received his letters. " And now," said Herbert, looking from side to side, from mother to son, "I have told you all ray adventures, I am dying to tell you something that concerns yourselves." " That concerns us 1" exclaimed mother and son in a breath. "Yes, ma'am I yes, sir! that concerns you both eminently; bat first of all, let me ask how you are getting on at this present time 7" "Oh, as usual," said the widow, smiling, for she did not wish to damp the spirits of her sailor boy; "as usual, of course. Traverse has not been able to accomplish his darling purpose of entering the Seminary yet; but—" "But I'm getting on quite well with my education for all that," interrupted Traverse; "for I belong to Dr. Day's Bible class in the Sablsath school, which is a class of young men, you know I and the doctor is so good as to think that I have some mental gifts worth cultivating,, so he does not confine his Instructions tp me to the Bible class aloft, bt permits me to come to him in his library, at Willow. Heights for an hour, twice a week, when he examines me in Latin and Algebra, and sets me new exercises, which I study and write out at night; so that you see I am doing very well." "Indeed, the doctor, who is a great scholar, and one of the trustees and examiners of the Seminary, Bays that he does not know any young man there, with all the advantages of the institution around him, who is getting along so fast as Traverse is, with all the difficulties he has to encounter. The doctor says it is all because Traverse is profoundly in earnest, and that one of these days he will be

-- "There, mother! don't repeat all the doctor's kind speeches I He only says such things to encourage a poor boy in the pursuit of knowledge under difficulties," said Traverse, blushing and laughing,

iugb —" Will be an honour to his kindred, country and race," said Herbert, finishing the widow's incomplete quotation. "It was something like that, indeed," she said, nodding and smiling. " You do me proud!" said Traverse, touching his forelock with comic gravity. "But," inquired he, suddenly changing his tone and becoming serious, " was it not—is it not—noble in the doctor to give up an hour of his precious time twice a week, for no other cause than to help a poor, struggling fellow like me op the ladder of learning 7 " "I should think it was; but he is not the first noble heart I ever heard of," said Herbert, with an affectionate glance that directed the compliment, "nor is his the last that you will meet with. I must tell you the good news "Oh, tell it! tell it 1 have you got a ship of your own, Herbert?"

"No, nor is it about myself that I am anxious to tell you. Mrs. "(mite, you may have heard that I had a rich uncle, whom I had never seen, because, from the time of my dear mother's marriage to that of her death, she and her brother, this very uncle, had been estranged 7 " "Yes," k aid the widow, speaking in a very low tone, and bending her head over her work; "yes, I have heard so; but your mother and inyself seldom alluded to the subject." "Exactly! mother never was fond of talking of him I Well, when I came on shore, and went, as usual, up to the old Washington House, who should I meet with, all of a sudden, but this rich uncle. He had come to New York to claim a little girl whom I happened to know, and who happened to recognise roe, and name me to him. Well, I knew him only by his name; but he knew me both by my name at,d by my likeness to his sister, and received me with wonderful kindness, offered me a home under his roof, and promised to get for me an appointment to West Point. Are you not glad ? say, are you not glad 7" he exclaimed, jocosely clapping his hand upon Traverse's knee, and then turning around and looking at his mother. "Oh, yes, indeed I am very glad, Herbert I° exclaimed Traverse, heartily grasping and squeezing his isiead's head.

"Yea, yes, I am indeed sincerely glad or your good fortune, dear boy," said the widow; but her voice was very faint, and her head bent still lower over her work. "Ha I ha! ha! I knees you'd be glad for me ; but now I require you to be glad for yourselves. Now list,en: When I told my honest old uncle—for he is honest, with all his eccentricities—when I told him of what friends you had been to me—" Oh no ! you did not! You did not mention US TO HIM I" cried the widow, suddenly starting UP and clasping her hands together, while she gazed in an agony of entreaty into the face of the speaker. "Why not 7—why in the world not 7 Was there anything improper in doing so 2" inquired Herbert, in astonishment, while Traverse himself gazed in amazement at the excessive and unaccountable agitation of his mother. "'Why, mother? Why shouldn't he have men- tioned us? Was there anything strange or wrong In that ?" inquired Traverse. "No, oh, no; certainly not fcrgot, it was se sudden," said the widow sinking back in her claair and struggling for self-control. "Why, mother, what in the world is the meaning of this I" asked her son. "Nothing, nothing, boy; only we are poor folks, and should not be forced upon the attention of a wealthy gentleman," she said, with a cold, un- natural smile, putting her hand to her brow and striving to gain composure. Then, as Herbert con- tinued silent and amazed, she said to hiva : "Go on—go on—you were saying something about my—about Major Warfield's kindness to yon —go on!" And she took up her work and triea to sew, but she was as pale as death, and trembling' all over at the same time, while every nerve was acute with attention to catch every word that might fall from the lips of Herbert. " Well," recommenced the young sailor, " I WaS just saying that when I mentioned you and Tra- verse to my uncle, and told him how kiml and dis- interested you had been to me—you being like mother, and Traverse like a brother,—he was really moved almost to tears! Yes, I declare I 55. W the rain-droi.s glittering in his tempestuous old orbs, as he walked the floor mutteling to himself, poor woman—good, excellent woman.'" While Herbert spoke, the widow drop Pea 11,edr work without seeming to know that she had to he' both bands clasped together, and her eyes were fixed in intense anxiety upon the face of the youtes as she repe,ted "Go on—oh, go on 1 What more did he say When you talked of us I" "He said everything that was kind and good. Ile said that he could not do too much to compenests you for the past." "Oh I did he say that ?" exclaimed the widoW' breathlessly. "Yes—and a great deal more I—that all that be could do for you or your son was but a sacred 001:1 he owed you." "Oh, he acknowledged it he acknowledged it I thank heaven I oh, thank heaven I Go on, Herbert Go on I" "Ho said that he would in future take the whel6 charge of the boy's advancement in life, and tho he would place you above want for ever ; that be would, in fact, compensate for the past by Ileiug you and yours full justice." "Thank heAven I Oh, thank heaven !" exclaimea the widow, no longer concealing her agitation, het throwing down her work, and starting up and Pac- ing the floor in excess of joy. "Mother," said Traverse, uneasily, going to her and taking her hand, "mother, what is the mess- ing of all this? Do come and sit down !" She immediately turned and walked back to the fire, and resting her bands upon the back of the chair, bent upon them a face radiant with youthful beauty. Her cheeks were brightly flushed, her eyes were sparkling with light, her whole countenanee resplendent with joy—she scarcely seemed twentir years of age. "Mother, tell us what it is," pleaded Traverse. who feared for her sanity. "Oh, boys, lam so happy at last at last! after eighteen years of patient 'hoping against bePer , shall go.mad with_joy 1" - _

"Mother," said Herbert, softly. " Cuildren, lam not crazy! I know what I all saying, though I did not intend to say it I Aria you shall know, too But first I must ask Herbert another question : Herbert, are you very sure thaal he—Major Wartield—inew who we wero 7" "Yes, indeed. Didn't I tell him all about youll Your troubles, your struggles, your disinterested:, ness, and all your history since ever I knew you! answered Herbert, who was totally unconscious that he had left Major Warfield in ignorance of one vert important fact—her surname. "Then you are sure he knew who he was talking, about 2" "Of course, he did l" "He could not have failed to do so, indeed! Butt Herbert, did he mention any other important fact, that you have not yet communicated to us?"

"No, ma'am." - e with " he allude to any previous acquaintanc us 2" "No, ma'am, unless it might have been in theo words I repeated to you—there was nothing else I —except that he bade me hurry to you and make' you glad with his message, and return as soon eel possible to let him know whether you aceePt offers." "Accept them! accept them of course I do! t have waited for them for years I—oh I childrenh yolj gaze on me as if you thought me mad! I am not so I not' nor can I now explain myself! for since he has chosen to be confidential with Herbert, I can net be so prematurely bat you will know all. wh."2 Herbert shall have borne back my message to Maim Warfield." It was, indeed, a mad evening in the cottagt And even when the little family had separated tolu' retired to bed, the two youths lying together, as! formerly, could not sleep for talking, while tllO4 widow, on her lonely conch, lay awake for joy. (To be continued.)

div.head: INTERESTING AFFAIR NEAR YORK.
div.p: INTERESTING AFFAIR NEAR YORK.

The strange case of a young lady at Gate Helmsley, near York, has been exciting the attention of the York- shire newspapers, and one of them has done a smart piece of work in the interview from which th 3 follow- ing particulars are gleaned. Miss Alice Hood, the lady in question, was visited by a " Yorkshire Gazette " re- porter, and her mother told a remarkable story of her child's escape from death. It commenced with the story of a slight illness. Five years ago the girl, never robust, was overtaken by de- bility of an alarming character,and her condition caused her mother terrible fear. It was conjectured that she might have outg,rown her strength,and have thus fallen into a decline. Miss Hood was languid, indifferent, and depressed, and the distressing symptoms grew upon her. & skilful and well-reputed doctor of medicine was called in, said Mrs. Hood, and attended the girl some time.

" She took medicine, of course ?" " Many bottles, but she was not benefited by it, se far as I could see. She had to take permanently to her bed, and I was obliged to feed her like a baby. We had to call in a second doctor."
Did he say what ailed her ?'' asked the reprter.

" I thought Alice was in a consumption. She was brought down to nothing,and was like a skeleton. When she was in bed I could scarcely sec that there was any- one between the sheets at all. I never thought she would get better, and many others who knew her thought the same. She was pale and thin,and appeared to be suffering from artemia. The doctor said she might recover at, perhaps, 21 years of age."
" She must have had a change for the better long be- fore comitg of age, I think ?"

" Oh. yes, a twelvemonth before. P was in this way ; I read in a newspaper about Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. It was the case of a young woman who was affected exactly as my daughter was, and they had cured her when nothing else had a..y effect. They are not like ordinary medicine. I therefore purchased a box of the Pills." And what is your experience of them ,Mrs. Hood ?" " Well, before Alice had taken the contents of the first box she found herself much better. The poor girl seemed as if a load had been removed from her. Her strength returned ; she could go out and come back re- freshed. ' I feel much better, mother.' she was wont to lay. Her appetite gradually returned,and she was soon able to work a little in the house. She took eight boxes in all, giving up the Pills only when she was entirely her self again, thanks to their effect. I can safely say that Dr. Williams' Pink Pills are very wonderful things, and not like any other medicine I ever heard of." Mrs. Hood was very pleased to tell the reporter all about the sarp rising cure of her daughter, desiring that others similarly affected would be led to try the same means ; for Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People are a wonderful specific for pale, sallow, and antemic girls, en riching the blood aad fortifying the nerves in both s exes, and thus curing diseases of the blood, such as crofula, chronic erysipelas, and restoring pale and sal- low complexions to the glow of health. div.head: ASHANTI EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE ASHANTI EXPEDITION.
DEPARTURE OF TROOPS FROM LIVERPOOL.

On Saturday, at noon, Messrs. Elder, Dempster, and Co.'s steamer Angela sailed from Liverpool for the West Coast of Africa, having on board the advanced detach- ment of the military expedition to Coomassie and about 7,000 packages ot military stores, including canned pro- visions, camp equipments, and a large supply of cart- ridges and other ammunition The special service officers of the detachment include Captain C. W. King (in command of the Army Service Corps in place of Lieutenant-Colonel F. F. Johnson), Captain E. E. Bernard, Lieutenant and ‘Quartermaster T. Challoner, Lieutenant and Quartermaster J. Edwards (Army Ser- vice Corps), Major and Paymaster S. S. C. Dolby (Army Pay Corps), and Captain C. Matthew (Ordnance Store Corps). There are also in the detachment four warrant officers and eight non-commissioned officers of the Army Service Corps, a staff quartermaster-sergeant and a ser- geant of the Army Pay Corps, and a sergeant, corporal, and private of the Ordnance Store Corps. The above- mentioned staff proceeds to Cape Coast Castle for the purpose of carrying out the necessary hospital, commis- sariat, and sanitary arrangements pending the arrival of the troops of the expedition. Sir Francis Scott again spent a considerable time on Saturday with the chiefs of the War Office, and after- wards called at the Colonial Office, where he interviewed the heads of that department. The Portsmouth contin- gent of the Army Medical Staff Corps which have volun- teered for Ashanti left on Saturday for Aldershot. 1 Instructions were received at Aldershot on Saturday for Lieutenant Lines and Surgeon-Majors Wolseley and Callaghan, of the Army Medical Staff, and a number of ' non-commissioned officers and privates, to be in readi- ness to sail at the end of the week. The Royal Engineers ' of the Telegraph and Bridging Battalions who have been warned for active service are away on furlough, but their leave will expire on Wednesday, and they will leave for Liverpool on Friday for embarkation on Sun- day.

Arrangements have been made bythe War Department with Messrs. Elder, Dempster, and Co., for troops leav- ing Liverpool for Ashanti to embark on Saturday. In order to provide the extra accommodation required Messrs. Elder Dempster, and Co., have substituted the Bathurst for the Loanda. which it was originally intended should sail on that day. Altogether the troops will num- ber 125 men and 25 officers. A further consignment of stores and ammunition will also be pent out by the Bath- urst. Another supply of ordnance, stores, and supplies is being prepared at Woolwich Arsenal for conveyance in the mail steamer Loarida. The ordnance stores will include 60 tons of carbine ammunition, ambulance stretchers, medical stores, hospital comforts, flags and lamps for signalling purposes, butchers' and bakers' im- plements, and similar stores for use in campaign. The food likely to keep longest good, such as biscuits,tianed meats, &c., will be reserved to the last, and the country thrcugh which the expedition will have to pass will be utilized for yielding all the food which can be procured en route. This will lessen the number of carriers, and enable the troops to be supplied with fresh meat and newly-baked bread. The director of supplies will pay for all food, even in the enemy's country.

Among the special service Officers who reported them- selves at headquarters on Monday was Prince Christian Victor,who arrived from Windsor, and is busily engaged in preparing for the campaign. With regard to the de- cision of the Admiralty to send a hospital ship to Accra, the base of operations, the department has caused sur- veys to be made of the Peninsular and Oriental steamer Coromandel,and the result has been favouranly reported upon. Should it happen that this vessel is finally se- lected, she will proceed shortly to Accra under the Com- mand of Captain W. A. Wheeler. The steamer Angola which left the Mersey on Satur- day with the first contingent of the Ashantee expadition had to shelter all night in Moelira Bay on account of the severe weather. The telegram received bp Messrs. Elder, Dempster, and Co., on Monday, from the pilot,said that the Angola left the shelter at daylight on Sunday all well, with a moderato westerly wind. African mail advices at Liverpool state that two clays before the steamer left-Bathurst,Captain Donald Stewart arrived from Coomassie at Accra. It was said that he and his comnanions bad been well received by the Ashantis. There was a curious report current that the Ashanti had offered to clear all the woods leading from Cape Coast Castle to Coomassie for the British.

The annual meeting ot tne Warrington Bands Association was held at the Town Hall, on Friday night,lllr.T.J.Down occupying the chair. The balance sheet for the past year showed that the income in- cluding £5O from the Warrington Corporation amounted to £54 Is., which left a ba!ance in hand o! £7 Os. 3d. Among other items of expenditure there is a sum of £44 14s. Gd, the amount paid to bands for playing in the Park.—Mr. Down apolo- gised for his few attendances during the past year, which he said was not due to lack of interest,but to unavoidable causes. Hisliuterest in the Association was as great as ever. He thought a great amount of credit was due to the committee and the secretary, Mr. Taylor, for the satisfactory work of the past season. There had been 55 per- formances during the year and the attendances had been very large indeed. He thought that if they averaged them at something like 4,000, thay would not he much wide of the mark, and therefore they had given pleasure to upwards of 200,000 people during the season, many of them comparatively poor people, who could not probably afford to pay to go to a concert. The cost of the 55 performances had also been small, being only £44 14s. 6d. He did not think that there was any town in the kingdom which could supply the same quantity, and same quality of music at the same price. (Applause) He was glad that by the grant of £5O by the Corporation to the association, the wretched begging business was done away with. (Applause.) —Mr. Taylor said that the season commenced on Sunday, April 14, when the Mayor's chaplin, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton declared the season open. Since then, there had been 55 performances, and the season closed wii,h a massed band of 200 instru- mentalists. There had been 15 different bands which had taken part, all of which were composed of Warrington bands. lie was glad that f, he Cor- poration had made the approaches to the bandstand very much better, lie was sorry that the bands had not occupied the open spaces in the town,. but they did not wish to compete with merry-go-rounds and barrel organs which occupied the open spaces in Orford, and Howley Mr. Mullins proposed the re-election of Mr. Down at president for the succeeding year. He said that Mr. Down's name went a great way with being at the head of affairs.—Mr. J. Skelton seconded and the motion wat carried unanimously.—Mr. Down thanked the members and said that he would do his best for the association.—The whole of the vice- presidents of last year were re-elected, with the ad- dition of the Mayor, members of the Town Hall, Park. and Baths Committee, and Mr. Gibson. Mr. J. Fairhurst was re-appointed treasurer, and Mr. Joseph Taylor the secretary.

div.head: IHE FX A MINER, SATURDAY, NOV EMBER 23 1895.
div.p: IHE FX A MINER, SATURDAY, NOV EMBER 23 1895.
PRESENTATION TO MR. S. HUNT, CHIEF
CONSTABLE.

On Friday at the Parade room of the police station, a presentation which had been subscribed for by members of the police force, was made to Mr. S. Hunt, the retir- ing chief constable. The presentation took the form of a handsome walnut timepiece, and the effioies of Lord Nelson and the,Duke of Wellington, which had been supplied by Mr. A. Woods, jeweller, Sankey-st. The inscription on the timepiece was as follows: " Presented to Samuel Hunt, Esq., Chief Constable of Warrirag- ton for 29 years, on his retirement, by the members of the police torce, 1895." A little after one o'clock,the members of the police force were paraded in the police station,P.C.Phillips being the drill master. All the police were present with the ex• ception of Detective InspectorSpinks,Detective Sergeant Monaghan, and P.C. Newey, who were at the Liverpool Assiz-s, and two constables who were out on duty. After asking whether there were any complaints to inake,and receiving no reply, Mr. Hunt said that he had asked that question for a large number of times during the period which he was chief constable, and he had very rarely to hear of any complaints. He was now leaving them,but he would be pleased at any time in the future to be of any service to any of them, as he had been in the past. The presentation was then made to Mr. Hunt by In- spector James who said that being the senior officer of the force under Mr. Hunt and the oldest in years it bad naturally devolved upon bins to make this presentation. Some of them had served under Mr. Hunt for nearly a lifetime, whilst others had been with him a great num- ber of years, only one having served a less term than 12 months. He cbuld say for those who had gone and those who still remained that they bad all received at the Chief Conatable's hands a large amount of kindness, consideration and justice, which had endeared him to them all. With regard to the presentation they con- sidered it scarcely worthy of him but they hoped he would appreciate it as coming from those who had served under him so long, amicably,and he hoped, satis- factorily. They had all great pleasure in giving him that testimonial of their goodwill, and hoped be would live long to enjoy his well-earned retirement and pen- sion. . .

Inspector Cox endorsed all that had been said by Inspector James. Mr. HUNT in reply said it gave him very great pleasure to accept that noble gift. Not that he felt that he deserved it hut from the simple fact that he had always done his duty honestly and fairly, night and day. There might have been times when he had been somewhat morose and abrupt, and he was afraid that had become I partly his nature, but what policeman was there who I was not sometimes morose and abrupt? He was happy to read them a complimentary extract from the police report to the Home Office for December last which said that in the strength of the force, 54 men, there had been no vacancies. The only variations were one resigned to improve hi a position and one dismissed. Tne force had also been well-conducted and there had been less reports against the men than in any previous year. He thought they might all feel proud of that official statement. When he first made acquaintance with the good old town of Warrington in December, 1863, the police force con- sisted of 14 officers all told, and they had to present's the peace in a population of 26,000 persons. Since that time including the men of those years and the present day there had been no fewer than 287 individuals who had acted as peace officers for the borough—a nice little army of brave men, ever ready to discharge their duties at constant personal risk. He was thank- ful to beable to bear his testimony to the character of the force, whose members had invariably been staunch and reliable. The speaker said he learnt to depend upon the zeal and fidelity of the force to the utmost and that had materially assisted to lighten his own labour and sense of responsibility. On Monday their new Chief Con- stable would take charge of the force and he believed Mr. Talbot was a first class officer and they would receive every consideration at his hands. The men afterwards dispersed and returned to their duty.
