div.head: EXTRAORDIN ARY LOCAL P ROPE RTY
div.p: EXTRAORDIN ARY LOCAL P ROPE RTY
CASE. A DISPUTED INHERITANCE.

An interesting and peculiar local property case, " Harrison v. Davies "was heard at Liverpool Assizes on Monday. It was an action for the recovery of a house and shop valued at £9OO, and situated in Warrington. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Greer, and the defendant by Mr. Shee,Q.C., and Mr. Horridge. It was stated by Mr. Greer that the plaintiff and defendant were brothers, being the sons of John Harrison, of St. Helens, who. in May, 1881, died intestate, leaving the property which was now in dispute. The defendant, Edward James Davies, or Harrison, had been brought up as the eldest son, and plaintiff as the second son and the former, as the supposed heir-at-law, succeeded to the property. Inquiries made recently, however, had enabled the plaini,iff. Alfred J. A. Harrison. to discover, he believed, that Edward James was born before his parents were married, and that, as a consequence, plain- I tiff was entitled to the property. The plaintiff's conten- tion was, therefore, that defendant was born a few I months before the marriage, notwithstanding that the I date on the register of births was subsequent to that of I the marriage. For 14 years the defendant had been in possession of the property, and he submitted that the I Statute of Limitation barred the claim ; but against that the plaintiff pleaded that there had been concealed fraud in the case, and that the statute commenced to run only from the discovery of the fraud, or from the time it might have been discovered with reasonable diligence.— Sarah Mlaughlin deposed that she was 62 years of age, and was sister of Mary Harrison' who was the mother of plaintiff and defendant. Mary Harrison died in 1889. Witness's sister, who in 1855 was Mary Davies,managed a shop in Bridge-street, St. Helens, and in the same house there lived her brother John Davies (now dead), and John Harrison, a lodger, who subsequently married her. In the summer of that year Mary Davies gave birth to the defendant,witness being present at the time. She remembered Harrison coming home from Man- chester, on the day the baby was born, with a piece of silk, which he said was for the wedding dress. The mother remarked that if she had kept well she was to have been married in a week or 80. Three weeks afterwards witness heard that John Harri- son and Mary Davies had been married, but very little stir had been made. The doctor who was present at the birth of the child was also dead.—Mr. Greer put in the three certificates—the one showing, the date Of the mar- riage being dated the 17th June,lBss ; the second indica- ting the date of the defendant's birth to be the 10th July, 1855 ; and the third showing the date of the plain- tiff's birth to be the 4th April, 1864.—Elizabeth Florton,a relative of Mrs. Harrison,gave evidence of having nursed defendant when he was born, and stated that at that time the mother was not married.—Alfred John Albert Harrison, the plaintiff, said that it was after the death of his mother that he heard from an uncle, John Davies, that his brother was not born in wedlock.—Cross- examined : Witness said that he did not know much about his uncle's character, but he had heard something about his having been convicted of burglary, and hav- ing had some drmk at times. Witness did not know I that his uncle was not very friendly with witness's father' and brother. Witness knew that certificates did not I help him in the case. The entry in the family Bible (produced) showed " Edward James Harrison, horn 10th July," which was the date on the certificate. The name and date were written with different inks, and the year was not entered.—ln reply to his lordship, plaintiff said that he believed that the entry of defendant's birth in the Bible was in defendant's own writing, and that the entry of the marriage was in his father's writing.— Thomas Renshaw, a farmer, deposed that he had busi- ness transactions with the father of plaintiff and defen- dant, and some seven or eight years ago he said to witness, "Ted is not my son."—Joseph Flarrison,younger brother of the parties, said that when his mother once spoke about the rent of the property she remarked that defendant had no right to the rents if she had a mind to speak.—Cross-examined : Witness said that there was another Edward James Davies, the son of witness's aunt and that man also, witness understood was born out of wedlock—This closed the case for the plaintiff. Mr. Shee, Q.C., in opening the case for the defence, said that defendant never knew and never heard a sug- gestion that he was not the legitimate son of Mr. and Mrs. Harrison until 1889. This action, if plaintiff succeeded, would not only injure defendant's social posi- tion but would make him forfeit property which he poseessed, and which he had fairly dealt with, for he gave his mother the benefit of it until she died. This was a stale claim, for on the evidence now adduced it could have been brought in 1881, and not in 1894. It had been started on a statement made years ago by Uncle John Davies, who was now dead, but whose evi- dence the jury were not likely to act upon. Again, this action could not succeed unless fraud was proved. The defendant's case was that his parents were married after the benne had been published, and not secretly, and that the marriage took place b fore he was born. He would call the midwife who attended his mother in July, 1855, and she would state that Mrs. Harrison at that time was weoring her wedding ring, and that Mrs. M'Laughin was not there, but at the time was living at Much Wootton. The certificates bore all this out, and they I were people who were in no way interested in the matter. The plaintiff's case was also that the doctor who was present at defendant's birth was dead, but the jury would hear from the midwife who attended Mrs. Harrison that there was no doctor present at all.— Edward James Harrison, the defendant, said that he had never been known by the 'name of Davies. The family Bible referred to was in the same condition now as it was when he received it. He thought the entries were in his own handwriting, but they were not made after he had heard of the suggestion that he was not his father's lawful son. Never in his life had he heard his father say that he was not his son, and his mother never said if she liked to speak witness would have no right to the property. Witness and his uncle, John Davies, were on friendly terms.— Cross-examined : Witness said that if the writing in the Bible was in his handwriting it was done at his fat4er's dictation. It was incidentally mentioned that the Knly surviving witness (Lydia Davies) to the marriage of de- fendant's parents had been subpcenaed by both sides but had not come. She was living at Penketh.—Evidence was given to the effect that after the death of Mr. John Harrison the widow went to see Mr. R. Davies, solicitor, and there spoke of the defendant as her eldest son, and that when she went to Mr. Forahaw, solicitor, to make a will, she again referred to the defendant as her eldest son.—Mr. Lewis. midwife, 74 years of age, living in St. Helens, deposed that she was called to attend on Mrs. Harrison 40 years ago last July. There was no doctor present when the baby was born. Mrs. Harrison was wearing a thick gold ring at the time, and she spoke of Mr. Harrison as her husband.—Mrs. Longton said that she knew Mrs. Harrison for 30 years. On the 9111 of July, 1889. they were talking about their families, and Mrs. Harrison remarked "I was married on the 17th of June. and Ted was born on the lOtt. July of the same year."—Other evidence of a similar character having been given, William Naylor and Thomas Thompson de- posed to Mr. Harrison having told them that he had been, married about a month when his e,dest son, the defend- ant, was born.—Couneel on both sides having addressed the court, the jury—before his lordship summed un— said that they were satisfied that there was no case for the plaintiff.—A verdict in favour of the defendant having haen formally given, judgment was entered I accordingly.

div.head: PARISH CFIIIRCH BAZAAR SATURDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. _
div.p: THE PARISH CFIIIRCH BAZAAR SATURDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. _

The openin—g—olthe l'a—rish Church Bazaar which had been continued from Wednesday to Saturday was per- formed on Saturday by the Mayor and Mayoress (Coon - cillor and Mrs. JAM'S Fairclough), there being a fairly large gathering of ladies and gentlemen present. The RacToa,remarked that on the previous day he had alluded to the deputations which were waiting upon the Government. The Romsn Catholics had just been given R hearing, and had pressed two very important points ; it had he.n stated that a large and influential deputa- tion would go next from the Church of England. (Ap- plause.) It was supposed that the outcome of these exertions would be that the Government would grant an additional sa. per head for scholars. This was very important indeed ; and it was said that the Government would press for a fuller representation upon the manage- merit committees and a more complete audit of the ac- counts. For their own committees (Church of England) they would be thankful to have as full a representation as possible,and they always looked out for the best men. (Applause). So far as the local committee was concerned. he would say that the members were always most anxious and earnest to deliberate in the hest way possible, and they were assisted by three as good treasurers as it was possible to find. (Applause.) to to the previous night the bazaar had realized £1,040. They had just received a cheque from Lord Newton for £2o—(applause)—which, with £soo;the sum they were anxious to raise that day, would make a very satisfac- tory total. Ile then asked the Mayor and Mayoress to open the bazaar. (Applause.) The MAYOR, after having congratulated the committee stallholders, and other promoters of the bazaar for hav- ing so handsomely done their work, said he had the greatest pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause.).

The Rev. A. A. MARKHAM proposed. and Councillor Wool:A seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to the Mayor and Mayore.,s for their services in opening the bazaar, and as a souvenir of the occasion the seconder of the proposition presented to the Mayor and Mayoress a hound copy of the official guide and programme of the bazaar.

The vnte having been unanimously accorded, The MAycnc. on behalf of the Mayoress end himself, exnressed thanks for thP kindness that had been shown to them, and hoped the concluding day of the hazier would be euccessful.
The sales on Saturday realized £255 us. 101., Mak- fnr the, four days, the handsome total of 1,298 53. 611.

It is stated that at Arcola, 111., a singular case o; poisoning occurred a few days ago. Daniel Miller.aged CO years, was eating supper, and accidentally swallowed a fly that had been on a fly-paper. He lived about three hours afterwards.

div.head: LOCAL MISSIONARY MEETINGS.
div.p: LOCAL MISSIONARY MEETINGS.
SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CgURCH.

The foreign missionary sermons were preached at the above church on Sunday by the Rev. J. Gunnell, who preached sermons suitable to the occasion, and in the evening an anthem was given by the choir. A public meeting was held on Momlay evening, the chair being occupied by Mr. R. G. Henshall. There was a good con- gregation, and there were present the Revs. G.D.Mason, W. G. Triggs, H.Walmsley (formerly of Warrington,and returned nassio..ary from Honduras), and J. Cooling (returned missionary from Madras). After singing and prayer, an encouraging report was given by the Rev. G. D. Mason, who said that during the past year £248 03.1 d. had been received from the Warrington circuit,of which public meetings had realised £122 19s. H., total subscriptions, £95 23. 4d. ; juvenile associations. £I.B 43. 6d. ; and Christmas cards, £ll 133. 6J. Sankey Bridges had contributed £0 03. 6,1.( °wards this amount. The Chairman expressed his pleasure at being present at the meeting, and hoped that they would break the re- cord so far as the result financial and otherwise was concerned.—The Rev.H.Walmsley then gave an interest- ing account of the mission in British Honduras. He said that this was one of the smallest missions, and was apt to be overshadowed by the larger missions of China, India, and South Central Africa. The population of B itish Honduras was composed chiefly of a race which had descended from Spanish and Indians,who had inter- mixed, and who were Roman Catholics,and predisposed to Roman Catholicism ; and also Creoles, who were des- cended from run-away slaves, and were black, or partly black. It was among this people that the missions were chiefly held,and most encouraging results were obtained. It was 70 years since the first missionary was sent to British Honduras, and now the circuit of Belize was entirely self-supporting„and also contributed upwards of a£loo towards the other circuits of the colony, and also the neighbouring Republic of Hoeduras. In one circuit there was a distinct tribe known as Carribs, whose ancestors were terrible cannibals, and the people are still very degraded. Notwithstanding these adverse conditions, this circuit contributed £9O a year towards th. 3 carrying on of the work, and thus assisted the missionary fund. Mr. Walmsley next pro- ceeded to describe the degradation of the republics of Mexico, Guatemale, Nicaragua San Salvador, Panama, and the South American republics,and said that this half continent was almost the most morally degraded portion of the world. The only missions in theme countries were in British Honduras, the republic of Honduras. and British Guiana. He said that this vast district would almost enter into competition with China and yet there was very little notice taken at it by the English people. He was not perhaps able to rouse public enthusiasm tor that country but here was a large field for mission , labour. Mr. J. Cooling afterwards gave a very racy account of the missions in India. The Rev. W. G. 'friggs then addressed the meeting, and after the usual vote of thanks, the meeting terminated. Collec- tions were taken during the meeting on behalf of the I missionary fund. PADGATE WESLEYAN CHURCH.

The foreign missionary anniversary in connection with the above church was held on Sunday, when the Rev. J. Cooling was the preacher morning and even- ing. A public meeting was held in the church on Tues- day evening, when the chair was occupied by Dr. T. Starkey Smith, J.P., and there was a good congregation. The deputation consisted of the Rev.T. S. Cooling,B. A.; for a great number of years missionary at Madras, and the Rev. H. Walmsley,formerly of Warrington, and later missionary to the colony and republic of Honduras in Central America. There were also present the Rev. J. Gunnell, Rev. G. D. Mason, and the Rev. W. G. Triggs, and Mr. William Bennett. After singing, and prayer by the Rev. W. G. Triggs, the Rev. G. D. Mason gave the annual report of the Wesleyan missionaries in vari- ous parts of the year. Referring to the financial aspect, he said that the amount which had been contributed by Padgate was £25 183. 11d. The Chairman said that he thought that after the interesting and in- spiring report they had just listened to, it would be very leasy to put their shoulder to the wheel to help on that great cause. It was always a pleasure to be on the winning side,and he was certain that the missionary cause was the winning side. He had always great pleasure in coming to Padgate as nearly all present were his personal friends. He would not however detain them that night,but would call upon two missionaries, who weremot exactly returned missionaries,but were here on I furlough, and would return shortly to their felds of ' labour.—The Rev. H. Walmsley then gave an account of his labours in Honduras which he said was an out of the way place,without a mile of railway,or telegraph wires, and with scarcely any comfort according to English Ideas. Mr. Walmsley then gave many illustrations of the difficulties he had to meet during his residence in the country. The difficulties of travel were however only initial difficulties, the real work being arrived at when the missionary mixed among the people who were in a very &graded condition.—The Rev. J. Cooling after- wards addressed the meeting, and lie gave a most en- couraging account of the work of Christianity in India, and said it had made great strides in that great country. Ele gave numerous racy and interesting instances which proved his assertions. A collection was afterwards taken on behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society, and the meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks and the pronouncing of the benediction.

div.head: VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS AND THE
div.p: VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS AND THE
STATE.
THE ARCHBISHOPS' DEMANDS.

The text of the memorial which was presented to Lord Salisbury by the Archbishot. of Canterbury on Wed- nesday, on the subject of voluntary schools, was pub- lished in the " Times "on Saturday. The document, which is signed by both the Archbishops, sets forth the principles by which they consider that all legislation affecting elementary schools should be governed. They insist upon the maintenance of the religious character of education, and the right of parents to determine the kind of religious instruction given to their children, and set forth the following outline of measures recom- mended :- 1. The abolition of the 17s. 63. limit, and of the other limitation on the grant in Article 107, as entailing undeserved hardships on schools least able to bear them. 2. The exemption from rates of all elementary school buildings. 3. The increase of contributions from public sources sufficient to meet the general increased cost of education throughout the country, to be administered in such a manner as will prevent what is harmful in the competi- tion between voluntary and board schools. While on the whole we think it better that the re- quired contributions should come from the Imperial Exchequer rather than from the local rates, we recog- nise the difficulties which surround the question,and we desire to express our readiness, speaking generally, to support other definite proposals which may he formu- lated by her Majesty's Government and which would give the necessary relief. 4. The rearrangement of .all Government grants so that poorer schools may share equitably with richer schools in those grants. 5. The revision of school board precepts by some superior public authority, 6. Increased facilities for federation of voluntary

schools. 7. That classes, scholarships, and other educational advantages provided by school boards at the cost of the public shall be open to the teachers or scholars of board or voluntary schools on the same terms. 8. Provision that all reasonable facilities shall be afforded for the separate religious instruction of children in board sr voluntary schools, whose spareuts may desire it, in the spirit of the Industrial Schools Act of 1866. 9. Liberty to provide is any district "annual grant" schools where the Department is satisfied that no satis- factory provision exists for the children for whom the school is intended, regard being had to the religious be. lief of the parents. 10. The embodiment of the proposed changes in an Act sf Parliament.
THE LATEST SALVATIONIST SCHEME.

Commissioner Booth-Tucker is leaving for India this week, in order to start there a work somewhat related to the " Darkest England " scheme. The number of people in India who live in a chronic state of want is of course very great. In many parts the population is con- gested to a degree which we can hardly conceive here, while on the other hand there is a huge area of waste lands. The Salvation Army scheme is to found peasant settlements on these waste lands, and Commissioner Booth-Tucker's mission is the initiation of this scheme. The undertaking is in some measure the result of an ap- peal issued last year by the Madras Government,but the Salvation Army has been feeling its way in the matter for some time. If the settlements are to be successfully started, the countenance,if not the active assistance, of the Indian Governments will necessarily count for a good deal. Moreover several well-known Indian authorities, like Sir William Hunter and Sir William Wedderburn, have expressed their general approval of the Salvation- ists scheme,and it has also come under the notice of the Indian Office. The operations of the scheme will be fourfold—peasant settlements., and land agency to fa tate generally the acquisition of lands for the natives, a village loan scheme to combat the great curse of India, the usurious money-lender,and agricultural schools. No difficulties are likely to be experienced in getting waste lands—tracts have already been promised—and it is esti- mated that after the initial outlay the settlements will be fully self-supporting. In the first place it is proposed to raise a loan of £5,000 for the purpose of starting a settlement of 5,000 acres, which would support 500 families.

The latest discovery of a portion of the stolen silver ingots was made at a private house at Dalston, of a remal of £5O or £6O, the tenant of which is said to be a man in a good position in the City, who has been missing for about a week. The ingots were dug up in the garden in the presence of the other occupants of the house. Twenty-eight of the missing ingots stolen are now ac- counted for.
CHRISTMAS CARDS, NEW BOOKS, ETC.

RAPHAEL TUCK AND SOM.—The majority of the British public know and respect the name of Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons, standing as it does at the " hall-mark" of everything in connection with art and illustration. For years now have they been the chief suppliers to the Christmas card trade and always with far-reaching success, and in addi- tion, the output each winter has been increased in extent and value. No exception to this rule char- acterises the season 1895-6 and the motto adopted —one truly representative of th 3 firm—is " One Better." They certainly have gone " one better," so much so that the demand has necessitated a con- siderable increase in the premises of Coleman-street. The varied assortment ot Christmas and New Year cards, booklets, calenders, art novelties, etc., which we have just received, gives a good idea of the elegance and novelty in design which the publishers have this year produced on their cards, etc., many of which are perfect gems of beauty. A series which for the last two years has attracted so much favour is the Black and White Series, limited this season to platinotype, photogravite and collotype. This series now forms an important branch of the trade and perhaps the most tasteful. A portfolio of four classic figures entitled "Grecian Maids," is a sample worthy ot special note. Herbert Horwitz is the artist and the fonr pictures represent " Blossom Time," " Far Away," " The Flower Festival," and the " Laurel Wreath." Each is 131 inches by 9 and the type of work is superb for beauty and delicacy. We have never seen anything to excel these pictures, which are individually worth not only a frame but an ex- alted position. A new idea in the same lino is the mounting on one card two or three designs of much smaller size thus making a chaste finish to a series which we think could not be improved upon. There are also single, double, and trifold cards having mounted upon them exquisite etchings of hunting iscenes, landscapes, and other classic figures similar to the "Grecian Maids." To attempt to enumerate the remaining artistic dainties would be an almost endless task,still a brief mention of the more impnr- Itant ventures may be given. The success which was accorded the calendars of last year has encour- aged the publishers to introduce no less than 100 new designs, each in calendar form. Shape, of course, varies exceedingly, but not so the artistic excellence,which throughout is of the highest order. Illustrated books and booklets make a choice col- lection of pictorial and poetic treasures, carefully edited and most tastefully printed. Cards there are in all shapes, sizes, and colours, some warm and glowing in tint and conveying a Michaelmas hearti- ness,others more devoted to gradation of colour and effect, others humorous, but all first class in their way and calculated to achieve exceptional popularity. Ths juvenile section of the community also has its demands well attended to, and the num- ber of booklets, mechanical novelties, &c., is largely in excess of all expectations. Considerable attention is paid to the construction of these novelties with a view to educational value, so that while being amused and interested by the coloured prints, the rising generation is also receiving knowledge of a generally useful nature. Moderate prices in all de- partments are fixed, so that many homes will be brighter at the expense of but little outlay.

CASSELL IND Co.—What is truly styled a treasury for little ones is "80-pep" a strongly and prettily bound book of almost 200 pages. It is full of simple but interesting little stories on topics interesting [to youngsters of every age from 4to 10, and pro- fusely illustrated. There are several gorgeously coloured plates of a humorous character, and which cannot fail to greatly interest the little ones. All the type is exceptionally large and readable thus rendering it possible for youthful pairs of eyes to study absorbedly these interesting pages, without any ill effect. From all points of view "80-peep" is the best book for little children which has yet come under our notice; it is a thorough nursery book and should command, we think, a universal sale.— " Cassell's "Christmas Annual " Yule Tide " comes cut in a brilliant red and gold cover, strikingly suggestive of the firesideover which so many copies [ of it will be held. The literary and pictorial con- ,1 tents commend themselves to all, from youth to I old age. "Q "contributes a lengthy love story, entitled " la." and Mr. W L. Alden is the author of I a story entitled " King Arthur," a tale of Hama Ghosts. A farce in one act comes from the pen of Mr. Max Pemberton, while another con- tribution is from Mr. George Grossmith, who pro- vides the readers of the magazine with one of his characteristic humorous duets, which is entitled " Strephon and Lubin," or the cheerful tenor and the disagreeable has. The music accompanies the words, and all admirers of the popular humor- ist will be anxious to emulate him by singing this pleasingly ridiculous duet. Among the full-page coloured pictures are "A Willing Captive," by Gor- don Browne, "That Yule Log" (humorons),by H.R. Millar, "As Good as a Fay,— by J. C. Dolman,R.l. "At the Holly Tree Inn" (for children), by Miss Florence Hardy, "Fancy Land," by Miss Gertrude Bradley, " Too Hot," by W. H. Trood, "Vaulting Ambition," (a comedy in six scenes) by Claude A. Shepperson. The last of all represents a cheerful- looking boy, invalid in bed, and possesses the sug- gestive title of "PH be well by Christmas." "Yule [ Tide," for 1895 is undoubtedly a first-class produc- tion from all standpoints, and the public who invest in it will certainly not think it a poor shil- ling's worth. Presented with the number is a large coloured plate entitled "Prisoners of War," a capital representation of the curiosity excited by two doleful British midshipmen held as prisoners in a French port in the time of Napoleon. THE "LID!" ANNITAL.—From tie office of the "Lady" we have received "Snowflakes," the popu- lar annual of that magazine. It is in every respect the number par excellence of all its predecessors, lembodying as it does short, stories by Grant Allen, I Adeline Sergeant, Robert Barr, S. Baring Gould, Florence Marryat, Joseph Hocking, &c. Each and every story in it is representative of the best style of the authors named, and many of them are of a striking character. A comedietta well adapted for home representation is presented under the head- ing of "Twixt you and Me." There is a "Snow- flakes" minuet 1377:Meyer Lutz of an attractive nature,while for those who love verse there are two short poems. Each of the stories is illustrated in a manner which does great credit to both printer and the artist, and among those who come under the latter category are Hal Ludlow, Frank Nudd, George Hasler, and George Gatcombe. "Snow- flakes," with its wisely selected contents, size, and literary and artistic finish, ranks high among the almost, innumerable shilling magazines which herald the annual approach of Christmas. This year's plate is from an original painting by W. Oliver, and is entitled "A Fateful Moment.' The colours blend very harmoniously and the signi- ficance of the " Fatefut I.oment" is readily under- stood,

div.head: Will SOLDIERS DIE.
div.p: Will SOLDIERS DIE.

We have not yet heard the last of theterrible mortality that has attended the, military operations of the French in Madagascar. It is soug.ht by the authorities to attri- bute a portion of the deaths to homesickness,or nostalgia, as it is called in medical terminology. It is certainly a well-defined malady in every army and carries away a great many soldiers from apparently unknown causes. A great many brave warriors waste away with hopeless longing for their wives and children. The records show that thousands of German soldiers who were compelled to fight in Napoleon's army succumbed to " heimweh.” It was more pronounced in that army because the Germans are very fond of their home and dear ones,and were fighting under the colours of their conqueror, in some cases against their own countrymen. But it is a tangible quantity in every army, and no doubt was a factor in the death rate of the recent French campaign.

div.head: NEGRO LYNCHING IN MARYLAND.
div.p: NEGRO LYNCHING IN MARYLAND.
REMARBAgLE PLUCK OF A SALVATION LASS.

The New York correspondent of the "Daily Chronicle" telenraphs as follows :—Another case of negro lynching occurred twa days ago at Frederick,Mariland. A negro, James Goings, had committed a criminal aseault on a helpless servant at a farmhouse near the town. The girl died of her injuries. Goings was arrested, only,however„ ta be drag,ged from gaol soon afterwards and hanged by a determined mob. An affecting scene took place before the man was ex-cuted. A Salvation Army lass who had tramped beside him all the way from gaol implored per- mission to pray for the doomed wretch. The mob con- sented, and the eves of many of the lynching party were dimmed as the plucky girl knelt near the trembling negro and offered a petition for his soul. When prayer was over Goings was strug up to a tree, and a merciful shot by a bystander, soon ended his sufferings.

div.head: NEW YORKER;; AND THE DUKE.
div.p: THE NEW YORKER;; AND THE DUKE.

The people of New York were determined to give the poor Duke of Marlborough no rest. The following des- cription of an incident after the wedding shows the in- terest the Americans take in the Duke. A reporter says —" After the breakfast the Duke and Duchess left by special train for Idle Hour, Mr. Vanderbilt's house on Long Island. Unfortunately,when the train reached its destination there was no carriage to meet them. The Duke and Duchess, after waiting a few moments,started out resolutely to tramp to the act lodge, half a mile away, though it was getting dark and very foggy, and the road was soft and muddy. They were followed by a curicus crowd. One bold-faced woman in red, en a bicycle,aude up to within a foot or so of the Duchess,and said, in a tone audible enough to be heard by all. Why, she's aller than he.' At that the Duke turned round,and, addressipff the woman,said, `We will let you pass.' Here the belated carriage, a brougham. appeared, and the Duke and Duchess climbed hastily into it and were soon within the private grounds."

div.head: TAX MURDER. OF MR. STOKES.
div.p: TAX MURDER. OF MR. STOKES.
INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENCE.

On Saturday the Foreign Office issued the correspond- ence whieh has passed between tne Marquis of Salisbury and Sir F. Plunkett respecting the murder of Mr. Stokes. In a despatch dated Brussels, November 3rd, Sir F. Plunkett stated that M. Van Eetvelde expressed, on behalf of the Congo State Government, the regret of the latter that the Conseil de querre which condemned Mr. Stokes had not been constituted legally,and that Captain Llthaire had not allowed him to appeal to the court at Boma. The Congo St ite promised to arraign Captain Lothaire before a tribunal, and to inflict punishment proportionate to the gravity of the offence in case his guilt was proved. Moreover,it offered to pay an indern. nity of 150.000 francs. Lord Salisbury, in reply, wrote recognizing with satisfaction the desire of the Congo Government to make reparation, and accepting the engagement undertaken by that Government that Captain Lothaire should be brought before a tribunal competent to thoroughly investigate the whole ques' to adjudicate on the accusations made against Captain Lothaire, and to inflict punishment proportionate to this gravity of the offence in the event of his guilt being' established. The despatch added that her Maje tyl Government awaited further information as to the char- acter and composition of the tribunal. 'Phis was duly forwarded to M. Van Eetveld€ by Sir F. Plunkett, who received an acknowledgment in which was enclosed an order on the Banque Nationale for the sum of 150,000 francs. Sir F. Plunkett forwarded these to Lord Salis- bury, who in a despatch dated Novena her 13th wrote "I have to request you to inform M. Van Eetvelde that I have received the copy enclosed by you in your des- patch of the 10th November of his note on the 9'h, and that while taking note of the renewed assurances r,spec- tiag the trial of Captain Lthaire, and the restitution of the whole of the property of Mr. Szokes, I acknowledge on behalf of her Majesty's Government the receipt of the BUM of 150,000 francs forwarded through you as repara- tion on the part of the Government of the Independent State of the Congo for the execution of Mr. Stokes In virtue of a trial the irregularity of which is admitted."

div.head: W ORTH LIVING
div.p: W ORTH LIVING
p HELL

Such was the subject of a celebrated sermon preached in Manshester,but the more practical problem of the day is how to make life worth living on earth. One of the important tri- butaries of the river of happiness is the possession of a com- fortable home. A home made bright and cheerful not only by the kind and loving dispositions of those living there. but made attractive by the good taste displayed in the furnishing. Furnishing lea very important factor in he matter of con- tinued self-fatisfactioo. 8o much jerry new London furniture Is being now retailed by drapers that one needs to pause be- fore rushing impetuously into the first draper's because of a cheats rid ticket. High-class makers, such as Lamb,Gillows, and Garnett,still exist, to whom the wealthy can still go with a long purse but to most people this would be a too expensive experiment. Again the average man nowadays has a strong liking for a bargain ; anything obtainable at about half or quarter the cost has a strong fascination f r him. Is it possi- ble to obtain such an advantage in furnishing ? Yes, and more than possible, it is an absolute fact. We cannot do better than recommend a visit to MR. WORSLRY'S FUR- NISHING PANTHISON, GAYTHORN, MANCHESTRR.

'FHB Successful Establishment of any of the large ware- houses of Manchester is always of interest to the citizens. One of the most brilliant example* of the vaine of perseverance, enterptise, and tact is the now busy hive of industry so well known a. The Pantheon, which occupies such a prominent position in Gay thorn, near the C ntral Station, Manche:ter. The building is a massive pile of modern design, 150 feet long, six storeys high, with show- room accommodation covering an area of over one million square feet. The plate-glass windows are each 12 feet square, each sqoare if broken costing nearly £3O to replace. '1 en of these immense show windows lot ma portion of the frontage. This will give a faint idea of "The Pantheon" in outward appearance, but ah i—herepen fails alt-get her in attempting to I o justice to anything like an adequate description of the interior. "The Pantheon" was sped Ily built to give the largest and most convenient floor space for showrooms, and cost £21,C00, the floors specially constructed to carry ehormous weight. To-day it stands as one Gf the smartest furnishing houses in England, containing by far the largest and most. comprehensive stock of any two houses in this large city. Prom basement to roof. from fl •ortoceillng, "The Pantheon" Is filled to overflowing with thousands ot well bought, care- fully selected bargains, to attempt description of which would be as futile as Liverpool attempting to crush

The destinies of' The-Pa-dth—;;n'7-;;:e eTn-ir—olle'd and pre- sided over by its sole absolute proprietor, Mr. W. H. Worsley, whose sole study is an ever increasing desire to satisfy and please the thousands of customers who daily patronise and support his efforts. We invite the reader to accompany us in an imaginary visit to " The Pantheon ' to see what it con- tains and how it is managed. On arr,val we are at once streak with the magnificent

div.head: STARTLING APPEARANCE
div.p: STARTLING APPEARANCE

of " The Great Pattheon," the immense long line of stupen• dons show windows dkplaying for sala capital specimens of high-class Second-hand Furniture ny high-class makers, the sale of which has made "The Pantheon ' famous.

div.head: UPON ENTERING THE BUILDING
div.p: UPON ENTERING THE BUILDING

Iwe tee at —once that as far as stock is concerned there is sufficient furniture for nearly the whole of Manchester. We see at once visitors walking round inspecting from Oloham, Bolton. Bury, Bur ley, ElFckburn,Bacup. Rochdale, Preston. Wariington and alt parts of Lanca,hire and Yorkshire, Cheshire, the Potteries, Wales, ac. It is the cardinal rule of " The Pantheon " to give the fullest facilities for inspec- tion without feeling compelled to buy. The ground floor is filled with the large specimens of bedroom furniture suitable for large rooms ; we are told the smaller suites are on the top floor, to which we can travel by means of the hoist, or walk. Bedroom suites on the ground floor we notice by Lamb, original cost £l5O, price £35 ; by Goodall. cost ! £l6O, for £5O ; by Henry Ogden. cost £2OO, tor £6.5. These , ! are among the best suites, but one that strikes us with special attention is a fine handsome Bedroom Suite hy Behan in solid American walnut, heavily carved In bas relief, with large wardrobe fitted with brilliant crystal bevel mirrors ; dressing table unique with neatly fitted jewel drawers, sur- mounted by large swing dressing glass ; washstand fitted' with statuary marble and shaving mirror. thr..• chairs. pedestal table de nuit, and towel horse ; what originally cost £6O you can otnain for £25. Over 2114 droom Suites are in stuk, on show, from 355. to £lOO, forming a display so impressive that wears almost STRUCK DUMB WITH AMAZEMENT.

We now go up stairs to the Dining-room Showroom. Vi'llat a sight, long avenues of Sideboards Is the first impression ; huncirrds of Sideboards, with hundreds of Suites. also Dining Tables, Overmantels, splendid collmion of 13roimes, Ormolu Clocks. Vases. &C. In this department we tiro magnificent Sideboards original cost from £lOO to £2OO. at prices simply astounding. LW to £2.0. The next So r above is the Drawing- room Furniture Showroom, which is simply a show of

DAZZLING BEAUTY dissolving one's sensitive aporeciation into impressive loveli- ness. No deprrrtmeut is so interesting to la tea as the draw- ing-room eh rwroom; a keen delight is experienced In selecting weird and fantastic furniture for the drawing-room /13,thetic, Moorish, and Egyptian Cabinets, peculiar Green and i ronzrrd Tables, Occasional Chairs of charming variety. Cosy Corners, Comfortable Lounging settees and chairs equal to the highest class firms in the Kingdom al quarter the price The largest showroom for Drawing-room Furniture in Manch, ster, containing over 100 Suites, 100 Cabinets, 200 Overmaritels, 500 Tables. Suites from £3 10s. tie. to £5O. Cabinets from 3./s. to £45. Marvellous value, worth in most cases three or tour times the money charged. The next depa, torrent adjoining is cases three or four times the money changed. The next de- partment is the Be-Weed end Bedding Department. which contains an enoranous stock of Beesteads. The brill•ant- r burnished brass displayed here is 30 immense as to present almcut a

SBA OF GOLD. Magnificent specimens of the bressworkers art is here dis played to perfection. Brass Bedsteads may be purchased solid and complele for as low a price as 355. to the best at £35. A clear sath)g of 50 per cent. Is effected in bedsteads and bedding Brass and Iron Bedsteads, strong and durable, mty he secured from 61. fd. to 30s. The bedding is all new, mmufactured on the premises; everything is new in this department, the work here giving employment to over 50 hands. Nothing Is allowed to be used here except it has pre- viously been washed and purified. All bedding sold at Wor- slry's may be guaranteed as of SPOTLESS PURITY.

Wool Beds complete. guaranteed all wool, trim N. fie., Hair Mattre,ses from 18s. 6d., Feather Beds from 225. 6d. The next place of interest to Visit is the Bedroom t. arrant., 4)epartment, which is displayed In a showroom, 63 yards by 15 yards, larger than most of the combined showrooms of most furnishing establishments. Otte is bound to admit that The Panthesit is certainly far ahead of nny t Ival establish- ' ments In point of else and convenience. The shown om visited so far are lofty, well lighted, and of immense area. The Bedroom P-rniture Showroom is magnificent ; 300 Bedroom Suites are eisplayed in avenues, the finest collec this extant, at prices simply incredible, astonishing every one, pulverising and exterminating all competition. Com- plete Bedroom Suites, solidthroughout, at .3 10.. up to £3O, magnificent la style stud finlatt. Enarnelle I Suites from 30s. to £7. The next departme.A is for Kitchen Furniture, the varied steak of which is quite sufficient, to satisfy the most exacting. Thousands of chairs, hundreds of tables sad dressers, every requisite for the kitchen at half the usual prices charged. A department is also provided for Iron- mongery. One of those modern monstre establishments, whose re- sources are so boundless, and whose stocks are so comprehen- sive, that it can, with equal care and despatch, furnish throughout a cottage or a mansion, is to be found in the famous house of J.,. GERSHON, furnishing contractor of 44, Olslham-street, Manche-der. This colossal business was commenced in 1870, and being condueted with remarkable ability, energy, and foresight, anti on sound commercial principles, it rapidly grew in public favour and patronage until at the presets!, time it is the largest and most represen- tative house of its kind in fdanchester. Mr. Gershon at- tends to every customer psrsonally. and does not leave cus- tomers in the hands of salesmen. Operations are carried on in a magnificent block of four-storey buildings. occupying a prominent and attractive position, and having a splendid frontage. They comprise shops, offices, and capacious show- rooms on the ground floor, and further suites of extensive showrooms on the first, second, and third floors, together with showrooms at the rear of vast capacity, and filled to re- pletion with an immense collection of valuable goods. Mr. Gershon is a thorough exponent of the general house furnishing, ana stocks held are unrivalled In 'Manchester eitherin msgnitude, variety, or worth; if wide experience, and far-sesing policy are absolutely requisite in proper selecting and getting together such a stupendous conglomer- ation of mi cellane ins goods, it is equally true that a great amount of ability of no common order is necessary to arrange and group them with such admirable effect, and to maintain at the same time sush regard for the comfort and convenience Of visitors. Where eversthingthat can possibly be considered to belong to this branch of business is fully represented, it is an endless task to attempt anything like an enumeration in detail, it will be sufficient to indicate the leading lines with whieh the house is ocetipled. Superb and comprehen- sive stocks are held in Drawing, Dining, and Breakfast Room Suites, made of all the best woods, artistically elegant in design, and magnificently and gorgeously upholstered in .11 materials of various colours, shades, and tints. Bedroom Suites made of the most dainty materials, and of the choicest, patterns. And substantial, solid-looking Library, StuAy, and Hall Furniture, together with inex- haustible. supplies of splendid couches, ottomans, and so as, duchesee stands. sidebo rds, book-cases,cheffoniers, cabinets, Davenports, easy, occasional, and other chairs, dining tables, dressing, work, card 100, a d occa,ional tables, whatnots, overrnantels, chests of drawers, as well as a large assortment of bedsteads of every deseription, p ttern, size and price ; bedding, mattresses, cur ts ins, fenders, firelrons and carpets, rugs, And mats of every pattsrn and design, from all the most celebrated makers. Briefly, the stock embraces every article of whatever kind that can possibly be required in furnishing any or every kind of residence, from the cottage to the mansion of the noble; and not only is each in- dividusl article to be found in these marvellous stores, but each article is represented by a large collection, often unique In its kind. ensl including a wide selection in style, quality, and prices This enterprising firm have also manufacturing premises of considersble extent, and thoroughly equipped with plant and machinery of the newest and beet kind and a large number of skilled workmen are constantly employed in the ma utacture of cabinet work of all descriptions. Repairs, too, are executed on the premises, a little army of assistants is employed in the control of this stupendous establishment, and competent men are sent all over the kingdom to fit up private residences, hotels, offices, publio buildings, and mansions, in conjunction wi is their business. The connection of Usis representative house is tar-reaching and most valuabie. its goods hive acquired the highest repu- tation In Lancashire and the neighbouring counties, and the name of •• Gershon "In an ample guarantee for everything DIA is super or to his line of business. The proprietor is a man of extensive experience and ot great and varied know- ledge in the va,ious branches of the business in which he is engaged. His able and energetic supervision is given to the whole of the concern, and the utmost vigilance is used that nothing shall emanate from his estab ishment which shall tend o detract firm the high and well-merited reputation the firm has achieved. Mr. Gershon is held in great esteem in private life hr his abiLty, public spirit, and commercial integrity. We strongly advise those about fornishing to call at Mr. GERSHON'S Universal • urnishing Arcade, 44, OLDHAM - STREET. M ANCII HST hit. (Next door to the Adelphi Bank).

THE end of the first stage of the The Liberator Trial. Liberator trials was reached on Wednesday night when three of the defendants, BALFOUR, THEOBALD and BROCK, were found guilty of charges made against them. The fourth defendant, DIEM'', whose con- nection with the unfortunate companies was a comparatively short one, was not found guilty as the jury disagreed in his case. The convicted prisoners have not yet been sentenced as there are still other charges to be gone into. At one time it was alleged that the prejtidice against the prisoners, and against Bsf.roua in particular, was so strong that they would nt receive a fair trial at the hands of a British jury, but, we should suppose, there are fow who , are still of that opinion, now that the trial has been held and the verdict given. In BA.LFOUR'S case it was his own action in hastily leaving this country and proceed- ing to Argentina, and there using ev3ry possible method of evading extradition, which did a great deal towards raisiag a strong feeling against him- self and to some extent against his colleagues. Now, at all events, neither BALFOUR nor his two con- victed co-directors can complain that they have not had a fair and exhaustive trial. The trial has lasted seventeen days, they have had the benefit of able and eloquent counsel, an impartial judge, and no one can say that the Attorney-General, who has prosecuted, has unduly pressed any of the charges. The result is that they have been found guilty of fraudulent action in presenting a false state of things to their shareholders with view to deceive them and defraud the persons whose money it was sought to obtain by cooked balance sheets and ,an array of fictitious profits. The Lands Allotment Company paid a dividend of five per cent., besides a bonus of three per cent. to its ordinary shareholders from 1875 to 1892, dividend for the most part being paid out of capital, secured on the strength of glowing reports. The directors themselves in the meantime benefited to the extent of £31,500 in fees and pro- fits.

It now seems possible that there may be no Ashantee war after all. There are in England at the present time certain natives of Ashantee who profess to be envoys for King Prempeh of that country, and they appear to be willing to agree to any Conditions which the English Government may impose. Some doubts are entertained as to whether these envoys are fully authorised to act on behalf ot the black potentate of Coomassie. It would be rather awkward if all the terms of the settlement were agreed upon and it was then found that King Prempeh repudiated his so-called representatives, for as soon as the wet season sets in the expedition will not be able to proceed. All the preparations for the expedition are, therefore, being proceeded with as though no negotiations were taking place, but if Prempeh duly " climbs down " there may be no " little war "after all.

It used to be said when the Shahzada so per- sistently stuck to his London house that he was really afraid to go back to Afgitahistan without first having brought his mission to a successful issue. His royal father, the Atneer, had often showed in the course of his career that he had an extremely rough way of marking his displeasure and even blood relatives had not always escaped chastisement. The Shahzada, had, therefore, very good reason folpreferring Western hospitality to the rugod reception;that be was likely to receive at Kabul. It is now rumoured that the worst fears will probably be realised. The Amer is stated to be in a state of "irritation" with the result that he has burnt alive a number of people while many others hate already escaped by crossing the fron- tier. One prominent member of the Shatizada's suite is to be tortured ein his arrival, and it is said the Shahzada himself will be lucky if he escapes with banishmeat. The Shahzada and his suit might

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 23rd, 1895.

THE Sultan of Turkey evidently Politics : gives Great Britain credit for being Foreign and Domestic, the leading partner in the concert of Europe. The speech which Lord SALISBURY, speaking as the Prime Minister and representative of this country, made at the Guild- hall a week or two ago and particularly the pointed references to what might happen in the event of continued misgovernment, have had an extraordinary effect upon his Imperial Highness. He has, therefore, taken the unusual course of writing directly to Lord SALISBURY, and Lord SALISBURY in the speech which he made at Brighton on Tuesday made public a part but not the whole of this unique missive. Tne letter is undoubtedly satisfactory as far as it goes. It r. seems to indicate either that the SULTAN is honestly determined to make the reforms in Armenia and elsewhere which he has promised, or that he has become really alarmed by the resolute front which the six combined European powers have now assumed. Referring to the reforms the SULTAN declares in his letter that he will execute them. "I have already told my ministers so," " he goes on to say. "The only reason why Lord '1 SALISBURY should thus throw doubts on my good intentions must be the intrigues of certain persons here, or else false statements have been made to , cause such an opinion. I repeat that I will execute the reforms. I will take the paper con- taining them, place it before them, and see my- self that every article is put in force. This is my - earnest determination and I give my word of honour. I wish Lord SALISBURY to know this,and k I beg and desire that his lordship, having con- p _

fidence in these declarations will make another , speech by virtue of the friendly feeling and dis- position he has for me and my country. I shall await the result of this with the greatest anxiety." Such are the contents of an extraordinary docu- ment which will be remembered as a startling variation on the usual routine of diplomatic pro- cedure. The SULTAN can not, at all events, com- plain that Lord SALISBURY has not complied with his request to "make another speech." though whether he will derive any satisfaction from the speech itself is another question. The
Paimic MINISTER still seems to be somewhat seep-

tical in regard to the promised reforms, and he makes a pointed reference to the need of unani- mity in action on the part of the combined powers. On the whole, the SULTAN has no just ground of complaint if his latest promise is not taken as final. He has made many promises in his time which have not been honourably kept, and even now it would probably be a bad day for the Armenians if the powers ceased to supervise the carrying out of the latest list of reforms. Lord SALISBURY'S speech on Tuesday, unlike that at the Guildhall, was mainly devoted to domestic affairs—which is equal to saying that

the second speech was much less interesting than the first. Our present PRIME MINISTER is not averse to contemplating change and move- ment in foreign affairs, but when ho comes to touch upon domestic questions his remarks are
bald and monotonous in the extreme. There is, first of all, the perennial taunt that the Liberal Party is not now what it was fifty or more years ago. Lo i d SALISBURY seems to be afflicted with

a constitutional incapacity to see that if the Libe- ral Party had made no changes during the last fifty years it would have ceased to be a Liberal Party, or, indeed, any party at all: Progression is one of the necessities of'its existence. Even the Tory party has been unable to stand still, and a "stalwart" of fifty years ago if recalled to life tvcruld probably be very much disposed to re- pudiate any connection with the hybrid coin-

bination which keeps the present Government in Power. After this allusion to the Liberal Party, Lord SALISBURY passes on ns usual to the oft- repeated gibes at the Irish party. He considers that Irishmen are now as in the days of STRONG- Bow, a quarrelsome lot, and his solution of Irish questions is to be found in the following words—

' whenrver the Irish trouble you with proposals Of disir.tegration, hold on for a few years, aud you will soon see them at each other's throats." That is the statesmanship of Lord SALISBURY as sp. died to Ireland. Such an open and insulting

CONCERT IN Sr. LUKE'S SCHOOLROOM. The members of Nelson-street School Subscription Band and concert pirty gave a vocal and instrumental concert in Sr. Luke's schoolroom on Monday evening. Mr. G. 13. Klrkham presided. Songs were contributed by Messrs. T. Shaw, J. Cliffs, G. Holt, W. Cooper, W. Price, Miss Shallcross and Miss Moores. The proceeds were in aid of the uniform fund. RuNconx PRIZE Cnotn. A meeting in connection with the Roncorn Prize Choir —or better known as the Tonic Soffit Choir—Was on Monday evening, when it was decided that staff notation readers should bo allowed to join the choir on passing a test, equivalent to an elementary pass in the Tonic-Sulfa system. • JUVENILE MISSIONARY, MEETING. Tinder tne presidency of Mr. E. Taylor, a jervenila missionary meeting was held on Thursday evening in Brunswica-st. schools, and was largely attended. Mr. Robinson threw on the screen a number of pictures Ulu.- trating missionary work in Ceylon, and the Rev. W. George gave the explanatoi y reading.

TME GRUESOME FIND AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday morning, Mr. Sutton,assistant overseer, applied for the reimbursement fr ,m the county of the sum expended on the burial of the headless woman recovered from the Bridgewater Canal at, Runcorn. The request was granted. MILL BROW SUNDAY SCHOOL .—INTERESTING PRESENTATION. On Wednesday evening the annual scholars' tea meet- ing at the above named school was held. The school room had been tastefully decorated under the superin- tendence of Miss Moore and Mr. Graham. Plant:: had been lent by Mr. Thomas Thomas. There was a good attendance. Tea was dispensed by the Misses Pope, Moore, M. Pilgrim, and Austin. After tea a programme of vocal and instrumental music was 'gone through. Mr. Frith plesided,and he was supported by Messrs. Pope, Graham, Ftndlow, and G W. Yates. Songs were given by Messrs. Henry Thomas and Edgar Johnson ;a violin solo by Mr. G. W. Yates ; piano solos by Mr. H. Pope and Miss Pope, and Mr. Robert Yates ; and qtiartet.e by Miss Pope, Miss Mayan, Mr. G. W. Yates, and Mr. T. Johnson. Miss Austim gave a reading. Advantage was taken of the occasion to present a testimonial to Mr. Frith on his re- linquishing. the position of superintendent of the Sunday school, alter 30 years' service. Mr. Pope made the pre- sentation which consisted of books. Mr. Frith,in acknov. - ledging the gift referred to Messrs. Rutter and Pope being the only persons connected with the school when he joined, and he spoke of the satisfaction it had been to labour in the school on behalf of the young people. Various games were afterwards engaged in. DEATH OF MRS. CROWLEY. Last week we recorded the death of Mr. John Crow- ley, ot 29, Church-st. To-day we regret to announco the death of his wife which took place on Thursday forenoon. The deceased lady had for the last two or three years been a great sufferer. She was 66 years of age, and had been married 47 years. Six sons and four daughters are left to mourn this double bereavement.

private, the first prize was wen by private Woodier of F Company ; and the second by Private Bradbury ef G Company. So that out of the prizes given there was only one that was not carried off by the Runcorn com- panies. (Applause.) Those were not the only honours gained by Runcorn. On the day of inspection, the In- specting Officer went down the ranks when in line, and he specially stopped before one of the Runcorn com- panies and highly commended them to the Colonel and the officer for the very smart and soldierly manner in which they acquitted themselves. He (Captain Ashten) did not think tney could have gained a greater honour than to have been thus specially mentioned,by a Colonel of the line. (Applause.) The prizes were then handed to the respective winners, and in iny of the recipients were loudly applauded, i especially Sergeant Harvey. Colonel Ashton afterwards said he was asked to ex- press the thanks of the Runcorn detachment to the donors who had contributed so very handsomely to the : pr;zes that had just been distributed. He did so with ; the greatest possible pleasure, and to the thanks of the , detachment he should like to add his own. He felt sure that demonstrations of that kind by the public were a great incentive to the well-being of the Volunteer move- ment. They found such demonstrations took place in I almost every corps throughout the country, and that shoved that the country had much sympathy with the movement. They had heard a very glowing account of the Runcorn detachment, and he could assure them that 1 he had the greatest pleasure in endorsing every word that had been said, At the present time he be- lieved there were not finer companies in the re- i giment than the Runcorn men. He felt proud that such a detachment formed part of his battalion. He might say that the remainder of the regiment were not jaalous they believed the Runcorn detachment deserved all that . they had gained. It might encourage others to put 11 themselves forward to gain some of the prizes which the Runcorn detachment had gained that year. The Rev. Dr. Preston in seconding the vote of thanks, I referred to the new commander-in-chief of the forces, and said Lord Wolseley had the cause of the Volunteer 4 forces most seriously at heart. FORTHCOMINO ENTERTAINMENT AT VIE PEBLIC HALL. Tableaux Vivants to be given by Miss Pierpoint and friends will be the chief attraction ni an entertainment at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening. There will also be recitations by Mr. Cyril Chantler. songs by Mr. Branch. and a selaction of music by a well-equipped orchestra. Scenery is to be lent for the occasion by Mr. Caddick. The proceeds are to be de- voted to local charitable objects.

div.head: FORTHCOMING SALE OF VVORIC AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FORTHCOMING SALE OF VVORIC AT RUNCORN.

As will be seen from a glance at our advertising columns, a sale of work, the proceeds of which are to be devoted to the building fund of St. John's Presbyterian Church, Runcorn will be held in the schoolroom on Wednesday and Thursday next. Mr. John Humphreys, of Nottingham, has consented to op-sn the sale on Wed- nesday. Numerous attractions will be provided each evening.

div.head: SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN:
div.p: SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN:

The weekly entertainment in connection with this Institute was held on Tuesday evening, and was pro- vided by friends from St. John's Presbyterian Church. Mr. Shaw, missionary, presided, and there was a g,Aod attendance. The Misses Warburten contributed mando- line and pianoforte duets, and songs were nicely rendered by Miss Hayes, Miss Pritchard, Mr. Charleston and Mr. Faulkner. Miss Hayes, Miss Pritchard and Mr. Cnarles- ton also sang in duets. Recitations were given by Master Howard and Miss A. Evans. A vote of thanks was accorded those who had taken part on the motion of Mr. Byfield, seconded by Mr. Evans.
REDUCTION OF SEASoN TICKETS FROM 'RUNCORN TO LIVERPOOL.

A short time ago a memorial was forwarded to the di- rectors of the Landon and North-Western Railway Com- pany by a number of persons travelling regularly be. tween Runcorn and Liverpool. and Mr. Harrison, the general manager, has intimated that the following re- duced rates have been adontoci :—First class : For 12 months, from £8 10s.to £l5 103. ; six months,from £l2 to £9 53. ; three mouths, from £7 to £5 10A. Second class : Twelve months, from £l4 103.t0 £ll ; six months from £lO to £7 ; three months, from -2.5 103. to £3 15s. Third class : Twelve months, from £ll 12i. to £8 184. ; six months, from £8 to £5 12s. ; three months, from £4 Bs. to £3. The concession has given general satisfac- tion. AN OLD OFFENDER COMAITTED TO THE QUMETER SESSIONS.

Enoch ItoHinson, a boatmen, well-known to the police who has served various terms of imprisonment, including one of seven years penal servitude, was charged at Run- corn Police Court on Friday morning, before Mr. E. Imi- son, with stealing' five pair of stockings, the goods of Anthony Bradley. of 75, Bridge-street, the previous day. —P.B. Lee deposed that on Thursday morning he was standing on the steps in front of the Police Station when he saw the prisoner go to the front of Bradley's shop The stockings were then hanging on a nail in front of the shop window, and the prisoner took them, put them under his coat, and proceeded up Bridge-street. Witness followed him and overtook him. The stockings were found under the prisoner's coat, and on being charged at the Police Station with stealing them, he replied' I didn't steal them, I bought them."—William Davies, raanager at the shop gave evidence as to hanging the bundle of stockings outside the shop. Ile identified them by the ticket.—The prisoner on being charged did not reply, and he was committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRLRY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRLRY.

A meeting of the Library Committee was held in the Council Chamber on Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. William Handley, and there were also present Messrs. H. J. Grice, W. Hank.nson, T. Riley, S. Pope, W. J. Cunningham and Mr. J. D. Jones (librarian). The monthly report of the librarian was submitted which showed that 2,050 books were issued in the lending department, and 28 in the reference department, during the month of October, showing an increase of 124 in the former department and a decrease of 26 in the latter.— Mr. William Handley stated that he had been approsched by students of the Naval Architecture Class at the Tech- nical Institute for the purpose of inducing him as Chair- man of the Library Committee, to introduce into the Library two works dealing with the subject they were studying. They were :—Thearle's "Theory and pra.tise of Shipbuilding." two volumns, 16e, and " Lloyd's rules of shipbuilding." Thearle's work had already been pur- chased by two or three of the students, and he (the chairman) thought a copy should be got for general use. —Mr. William Hankinson called attention to the state- ment made publicly that Sit John Brunner had offered to provide any books required for the Technical Institute students.—lt was decided to remind Sir John Brunner of his offer. The Book Selection Committee submitted a list of 126 volumes to cost £22 184. 2d. for confirmation by the committee. The last was approved of, and this concluded the business. THE TECIESICAL INSTITUTE.

There was a good attendance at the second of a series of entertainments to be given during the season to s students of the Technical Institute, held on Saturday evening. Mr. Wiswall, CE,, chairman of the committee presided, and in the course of a short address he urged the students to persevere in their respective studies and take full advantage of the advantages which were now placed at their disposal. An excellent programme of vocal and musical items was then gone through. A glee given by Misses A. Taylor and Simkin and Messrs. Crosby and Morris, was the first contribution. So!os were well rendered by Mr. Crosby, Miss Simkin, Mr. Morris, Miss Alice Taylor, and Mr. Scott, Several en- cores were demanded. Violin solos were most efficiently given by Miss Lena Flarris.m, the pianoforte being pre- sided at by her sister, Miss Kitty Harrison. Several duets were also contributed by the vocalists mentioned. Mr. W. B. Kay who acted as accompanist performed a pianoforte solo. At the close of what proved to be most ' enjoyable concert, Mr. Marshall, the secretary to the Institute, arrangements had been made for a conver- sazione to be held early in January.—P-, may he here mentioned that a lecture on " Whittier," the American poet is to be given the Technical Institute tonight (Friday). The lecture is the first of a serious to he given during the winter under the auspices of the Runcorn Free Library Committee.
BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.-MISHONARY ANNIVERSARY.

Anniversary sermons in connection with the Runcorn auxiliary of the London Missionary Society were held on Sunday. The Rev. W. E. Cousins, M.A.,preached at the morning service, and also delivered an address to the Sunday school children and friends on missionary work in Madagascar in the afternoon. The Rev.l.John Yonge, of Warrington, was the preacher at the evening service. The annual missionary meeting was held on Monday evening, when the chair was occupied by Mr .I.J Speak- man. He was supported by the W.VA. W. E. Cousins and W. Lawrence, missionary in the South Sea Wands. and Mr. W. H. Chadwick, the treasurer. Addresses on missionary work were delivered by the two rev, gentle- men named. odr. W. H. Chadwick read the report. This showed that the young men of Bethesda oche )1 had riven £$ 18s. 7d. and the girls £4 9s. lii., total £lO 7s. Std., as against £lO 19 id. last year. Then there had been subscrihed £2 74. 61., making for Bethesda £l2 15s. 4i. At St.Luk-'s the receipts were £3 163.21.. compared with £3 64. Mi. twelve momths ago. The meeting closed with the umual vote of thanks.

SHRMONS ON BEHALF OF A DAY SCHOOL AT RUNCORN. The annual sermons on behalf of ;Newtown Mission Day School were preached in St. Michael's Church, on Sunday. The Hey. W. Stanton Jones. of Widnes,preach-d at the morning service, and in the evening, the Rey. E Bullock, M.A.. vicar of St. Jude's, Liverpool. At the evening service, the preacher dwelt upon the education question, of which he said he was heartily sick. He re- ferred to the In inner in which the managers of the voluntary schools had been conmelled te expend large sums of money to meet the requirements of the Educe- tton Department under the late Government, and also remarked that present aciminstralions were apparently lukewarm with reference to denominational schools. He urged the people to ascertain exactly what was re- quired, and then having arrived at their decision to make it known with no uncertain sound. He warned them against being favourable to secular education,and pointed out the evils consequent upon it in towns and cities on the Continent. England's greatness depended to a very great extent on the religious education im- parted to the children, end it was imperative that this would he continued. They had noble examples f the assistance rendered to the Church of England schools by princely donalions from merchants, Stl.. hut the ques- tion arose did the rank and file, by their small contritm- ions, do as much RA they ought ? Be urged them to give a more loyal and hearty support to their schools in order that they might be carried on successfully and efficiestly. The choir was under the eolductorsbip of Mr. Chas. Pascual!, and Mr. Timmins, jun., presided at the organ.

div.head: TRADE AT RUNCORN. SHORT TIME ON THE BRIDGEW&TER
div.p: TRADE AT RUNCORN. SHORT TIME ON THE BRIDGEW&TER
UNDERTAKING.

No official intimation had been received in Runcorn up to this (Friday) morning, of the decision of the Castner- Kellner Alkali Compatstv respecting their selection of a site for their new chemical works. Representatives of the Company have been in the district during the week, and it is rumoured that Weston has been fixed upon by the directors of the Company as the scene of operations, but no official confirmation of this has yet been made. A disquieting piece of news was made known in Runcorn on Saturday to the effect that the managers of the vari- ous departments of the Bridgewater Undertaking at Runcorn received notification that the men under them should be placed on short time, i.e., that they should only be emuloyed every alternate week. The notices will take effect next week, and for the present it is understood that it will remain in operation until Christmas. This has reference to the permanent staff, and will affect several hundred artizans in this locality. It includes the engineeriug department at the Sprinch Works, where a large number of men are engaged. So far as concerns shipping, the hours to be worked will greatly depend Joon the traffic. It is believed that the order for the curtailment of b.urs on this portion of the waterway belonging to the Ship Canal Company, will not simply be nontinefil to Runcorn, but will affect the whole length of the undertaking. Under these circum- stances, combined with the keen depression that has so long prevailed in the chemical trade, the outlook for the winter is certainly not of a roseate character.

div.p: VOLUNTEER -CONCERT AT RUNCORN.
DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES.

The Volunteer concert and distribution of prizes has for some time now, been one of the chief events of the year in Runcorn; and this year it proved no exception to the rule. There was a large and fash- ionable audience in the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening when this annual event again took place. Special artistes had been engaged for the occasion, and the promoters are to be congratulated upon their admirable selection. The vocalista were Madam Dews, Madame Jennie Sadler, Mr. Charles Chilley and Mr. Reginald Mountfield. As an intro- duction both to the first and second parts. the Volunteer Band, under the conductorship of Band- master Outhwaite, played selections. In their first essay they performed selections from " The Bohemian Girl," in which solos were Played by Sergeant Gittins, Privates J. Thornhill,F. smith. G. lianth, A. Hnmphries, and W. Outhwaite. Selections from "A Gaiety Girl" comprised their second contribution, and inrreduced the popular song "Tommy Atkins." Madam Dews is a name well-knnYrn in the musical world, and her singing on Wednesday was a , treat to listen to. Her rich contralto voice was heard to I great advantage in the old and familiar song " The Better Land," and in response to a most marked dsmon• stratirm of approval by the audience she bowed her an- knnwledements. The applause,however, continuel.and she complied with an encore. singing with great eff-ct "She wore a wreath of roses." "Jeanette and Jeanot " mnst appropriate song, and "The Forge and the Bell" (Stephen Adam!) further evidenced Madam Dews' ability as a vocalist, and the applause which greeted her efforts attested that they were ap- preciated by the audience. "Britannia" was capitany sung as an encore. "My Land of Spain" was Madam Jeanie Sadler's first rffltt, but she was more successful in the song " A Dream of Para- dise." For this she was deservedly encored, and TPS- praidod with "Killarney" which was rendered with Such I point and finish as to still further delight the nudience. She also gave an excellent interpretation of " Vainka's Song." Mr. Charles Chilley was a vocalist at the last annual Volunteer concert, and his singing was then much appreciated. In the first part of the programme he sane twice, his first contribution being the old Eng- lish song arranged by F. H. Cowen, "There is a garden in her face," and his second, "The Is/filler's Daughter " from words by Lord Tennyson, and arranged bv Ellen Wright. Both !rings were finely rendered, and he was further successful in his singing of An encore was demanded,.and he complied with" Sally in our Alley." Mr. Reginald Mountfield infused a little humour Into the proceedings by his refined humor-up; aongs,which were entirely free from the coarseness wiaich is often too apparent in songs of this diameter. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS —The Foreign Mission- ary anniversary was held in Preston Prook Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday, when the preacher WEVI the Rey. W. Geirge,of Runcorn. On Tuesday evening a well attended missionary, meeting was hold, presided over by Mr. Bis- hrown.of Runcorn,who delivered an interesting address. The annual report was read by the Rev. W.George.which showed that the school children had done good and earnest work. Mr. G. Robinson, of Runcorn, by means of a lantern showed a number of pictures illustrative of mission work in Ceylon. The Rev. C.De Putron Oliddon gave the connective readings.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

FOREIGN MISSIONARY SERIKONS.—The Rev. C. De Patron Glidden preached at the missionary services in connec- tion with the Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday morning,and Mr. Crosby preached in the evening. The annual mis- sionary meeting was held on Wodnesdav evening, when the chair was occupied by Mr. Dodd. The annual report, which WPI4 a most satisfactory one. was read by the Rev. W. George. ApPropriaie addresses were delivered by the Rev. T. Brackenhury and Sister Annie. Mr. Robinson showed a number of lime-light views, and the Rev. W. George gave the connective readings, Col- lections on behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society were taken. . _
