PRIMITIVE METHODIST SALE OF

A sale of work with the onject of raising funds for the , renovation and decoration of the Primitive Methodist I Chapel, Greenwav-road, was held in the schoolroom on Wednesday and Thursday. Tne room had been taste- fully decorated for the occasion by Mr. T. Leach. There were three stalls containing useful and ornamental arti- cles. The married ladies was in charge of Mesdames Booth, Wilson, James Stubbs and Jab-z Stubbs ; young ladies stall, Mrs. Richardson, Misses R. Stubbs, Myles, Sayle, Withington, Davies, P. Hillidige, Fleet, Coombs, A. Davies and Moore. 13.ehive, or children's stall was in charge of Misses Shingler, Lunt, Catterall, and about thirty young girls of the Sunday school. The refresh- ment dep utment was in charge of Mesdames Collier, Reynolds, Jackson, Broadhurst, Thompson, Withington, Dowdle, and Miss Vernon. A cream and sweet stall was provided by Mr. George Shingler. There were in addition, a museum of curiosities, in charge of Mr. Holt and Mr. Hayes, a waxwork exhibition by Mr. James and Mr. Jibez Stubbs, and Mr. Shaw, of Top Locks, kindly provided a musical box. Concerts were given at night, and these were arranged by Miss Wilson and Mr.

At the opening ceremony on Wednesday amongst those present were the Revs. T. Braman, W. Moores, Messrs. Wilson, Reynolds, Bro-tdhurst, Stubbs, and others. Mr. John Wilson in introducing Dr. Mdienzie to the large assembly present stated that he Lis(' known him for some time, being associated with him in public work. He had found this, that if anyone was doing their best to help themselves and not getting on very well, the doc,or was always willing to come forward and render a help- ing hand. He had warm-heartedly and generously come to their assistance that day and they were all pleased to see him. (Applause.)—Dr. McKenzie, who was received with applause, said he was very pleased to be amongst thorn that afternoon. He was not accustomed to take an official part in those kind of things, but when he was asked by Mr. Broadhurst to come and help them at Greenway-road he gladly consented. He did so for two reasons. He wag a member of a self-supporting church in Scotland—the Free Church of Scotland—and secondly because he had a deep sympithy with the. work of the Primitive Methodi,t body. From the commence- ment of Primitive Methodism, which was less than 100 years ago, that body had done most excellent work, and he felt satisfied that they would do still greater work in the future. He wa; personally acquainted with their labours in Runcorn, and he could bear testimony to its usefulness and worth. The handsome building in which they wee met and the chapel adjoining were a nasnument of the sturdy charac- ter and indomitable saint of Primitive Methodism in Runcorn, and it was his wish and the wish of all present that they might continue to flourish side by side with the other religious institutions of the town. (Applause.) —Mr. Reynolds proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. McKenzie, and in doing so spoke of him in highly com- plimentary terms. The Rev. William Moore seconded, and it was carried with acclamation. _

The sale then commenced and the takings amounted to £63 4s. 241 exclusive of subscriptions. The sale was again opened on Thursday afternoon. The Rev. T. Bramall conducted the proceedings and ex- plained that Miss Salt, of Preston Brook, was unable to be present to open the sale of work in consequence of the inclemency of the weather, but she had sent a good sub- stitute in the person of Mr. Spruce.—Mr. Spruce said he appeared there in the place of Miss Salt, who was unable to be present on ac- count of her advanced age and the weather. She took a deep interest in any work that had for its object the promotion of that which was good, and she I had given him a donation to present to the treasurer, and he took it that that was one of the chief parts of the business of the individual who performed the Opening ceremony. Knowing something of the character of the workers connected with the church, he felt sure that when the subject of a sale of work was first mooted,suc- cess was ascured. Be was very pleased to hear that they had succeeded so well the previous day, and expressed his earnest hope that the objects they desired might be realised.—A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Spruce for his attendance, en the motion of Mr. Thomas Both, seconded by Mr. W. Gittens.
The total amount realized was just within £llO. FRODSHAM.

I BREAKING INTO A Raga CKLIAR Frodsham police I Court en Wednirs lay F.fternoon. Ernest Ainsworth, Booth-qt.. Was charserl with breaking and entering the cellar of Elizabeth You& Cheshire Cheese publicause Main-street, on the 16is inst., and also with breaking and entering the same cellar and stealing 14 bottles ef stout ,m October 27,1-I.—Mr. Linaker, solicitor,defeaded. The evidence showed that the prisoner Was seen crouch- ing behind the garden hedge, and shortly afterwards was observed by George Yowl, to poll off his boots, and nnen the cellar door. On searching for him they found him hiding behind the door. Information having been given to the police, Sergeant Clstys apprehended the prisoner. He acknowledged that on October 27th another man went into the cellar and he kept watch. He received a portion of the goods stolen. Toe charge was ultimately reduced to one of being on enclosed premises for an unlawful purpose, and he Ails sent to gaol for two months. ASSAULTING HIS NEWLY-MARRIED WlFSL—Obadiah Duncalf, of Frodsham Bridge, was charge under a warrant+ at Frodsham Police Court, on Wed- nesday with assaulting his wife. Beatrice Dun- calf, on the 16th inst. Mr. F. Turner appeared for the complainant and Mr. Linaker defended. Mr. Turner, in opening the case, stated that the parties were married quite recently and in that case marriage had Proved a failure. On Saturday night, between 8 and 9 o'clock, on Mrs. Duncalf returning hems her hus- band threatened her and struck her with his fist, and she went away. Later he came to her brother-in-law's house and on the promise that he would give her some clothing,she accompanied him to the house. On entering he locked the doer and she ran upstairs. She tried to get out of the window. He came, pulled her back, and then pushed her, the result being that her hand went through the glass and a severe wound was caused. He then seized her, knocked her down, knelt upon her, kicked her, ani struck her about the face and body. In conse- , quence sif her screams her sister,brother-in-law, and the I prisoner's sister came upon the scene. Ultimately she escaped from the house, and went ta Dr. Selby, who dressed her wounds. It had been a deplorable mareage for she had been constantly assaulted. He asked for a separation order. After complainant had given evidence in support of this statement, Mr. Linaker expressed wil- lingness to plead guilty to a common assault.—Mr. Turner pressed for a separation order, and the Bench granted one of ss. per week. They also imposed a fine of ss. and costs, and characterised the behaviour of the prisoner as that of a coward.

On Thursday night a meeting of the Emergency Com- mittee of this Union was held at the George Hotel, Huilderafield.—Mr. H. H. Waller, Brighouse Rangers, presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Platt (Old. ham). A. Fattorini (Manningham(, H. Sewell (Leeds), J. Clifford (Huddersfield), and J. M. Mills (Stockport).— Fred Wood, Brighouse Rangers, and W. Robinson, Broughton Rangers, were reported for wrestling in the match Brighouse Rangers v. Broughton Rangers on Novemher 16, and the committee decided to suspend both players up to and including November 30.—A.Ray, Leeds, was reported by the referee for striking a player in the Leeds Av. Halifax A match. The committee con- sidered that Ray had been sufficiently punished already, and gave him permission to play from date. —The ap- pointments for December were made, and will he given to the press the first meeting in December, at the Spread Eagle, Manchester.—The Yorkshire v. Cheshire match is fixed for next Monday at Headingley, and the Lan- cashire v. Yorkshire match will he played at Oldham on December?, and the details will be arranged at the meeting to he held at the Spread Eagle. Manchester, next Wednesday.—The Liveraedge v Oldham match was fixed originally to he played at Oldham on the 7th Decensher.but the Venue has been changed to Liveraeige on the 10th December, and the Oldham Clob hag given the Liversedge Club a subscription of £l5 towards their , expenses.
THE DROWNING OF RUNCORN MEN
IN THE GALE.

Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquiry at the George Hotel, Soutoport, on Wednesday touching the death of William Eloxworth, aged 19 scars, whose body was found on the shore at Marshside at 130 on. Monday morning. The father a the deceased gave evidence of identification, and said that his son had lived with him at 39, Lowlands-road, Runcorn. The deceased was mate of the flat William Henry, of which witness's brother was the. captain. He loft home on the 18th of October to join his flat, which was to sail from Widnes to Llandillos. He arrived there on the Monday follow- ing, on which day the flat began the return journey. Witness afterwards saw a report in the papers that the flat had been wrecked off Ethyl and that all hands were missing. The body of another of the crew had been found a day or two ago off Kirkham. The night of Monday, the 21st o.tober, the day on which the flat was last seen, was very stormy. Evictsnce as to the finding of the body having been given by John Wright, fisher- man, Marshside, and Police-constable Falconer, the jury returned a verdict ,st " Found drowned." THE FUNERAL,

The funeral took place in Runcorn Cemetery on Thurs- day afternoon in the presence of a large concourse of people. A procession was form-d in front of the de- ceased's home in Lowland's-road ,a nd walked to the ceme- tery. In the forefront there were the Rev. T. Braman, and Mr. William Shaw (missionary), followed by Capts. Millingtain,Corker, Betley,Toren,s Burrows,Waterworth, Messrs. A. Riley (on bihalf of Messrs. P. Speakman and Sons), William Byfield, U Cooke. Alexander Hammond, Peter and William Darlington, H. E imonds, Webster. Lloyd, and J. W. remperley. Ton followed the hearse at the side of which walked the following bearers : Messrs. Thomas Shaw, William Shaw, John D miel Shaw, John Jones, and Joseph Carter. The mourners included Mr. William Hoxworth (father). Jolin Roxworth and Joseph Hoxworth (brothers), John arid Joseph Hox worth and William Rands (nephews), George Rands (brother-in- law), Samuel ffoxworth, George Shaw, Owen Jones. Thomas Mousedale (Liverpool), William Hughes, (Liverpool) William Carter (Widnes). E. Aston, Charles Kirkham, John Hayes, William Astbury, and William Cooper. The service at the grave- side was conducted by the Rev. T. Braman, and at the close, the hymn " God be with you till we meet again" was sung. Wreaths had been sent by the following : Nephews (Jonnie, Joe, and Richard), brothers and sis- ters (Sarah Ann, John, Alice. George), Father and Mother : sisters and brother (Mary, Thum, and Joe). Uucle George, Aunt Jane, arid cousins ; brother and sis- ter (John and Mary), nephews (Willie and Georgie),aunt (E. Hoxworth) and cousins, Mr. and Mrs. Dowdle, Mrs. Benson, Mrs. Woodcock, Mrs. C. H. Kirkham, Aston, Mr. and Mrs. Redmond, Widnes, Mr. and Mrs. T. J. Kirkham and Mrs. &rape. _ . _ . _ .

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

SOUR SAUSAGES FOR SALE.—A WARRINGTON BUTCHER FINF.D. On Monday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before the Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough), Aldermen Harrison, Francomn and Wright, and Mr. Samuel Wright,a butcher named Frederick T. Lashford, 59, Chorley.st., was charged with having exposed for sale, on the 11th November, 3'bs. of sausages which were unsound and unfit for human food.—Defendant admitted the offence. Nuisance Inspector Norman said that on the previous M nday afternoon he was passing along Chorley-st., when he noticed some sausages on a large dish in the defendant's shop window. The appear- ance of them struck him as not being fresh, and he en- tered the shop and examined the sausages. They were wet and unfit for food, and he accordingly had them conveyed to the fown Hall. Dr. Gornall, medical officer, examined them, and havin2 certified them them to be unfit for food of man they were destroyed on the authority of a justice of the peace. Witness, when he seized the sausages, asked for the defendant, but was told that he was in Liverpool on business. Subsequently witness called again at the shop, and seeing the defen dant asked him for some account of the matter. He replied that before he went away that day he had put the sausages aside, but after he had gone someone in charge had inadvertently placed them in the window again. When asked why he did not at once destroy them he answered that he was saving them for an old person, who would have given them to her fowls. Wit- ness told him that the fowls would be much better with- out them, seeing the condition they were in.—Dr. Gor- nail, medical officer for the borough, deposed to having examined the sausages. He found them slimy, sour, and wet ; and on cutting them open discovered that the bread was decomposing, as well an the meat. In his opinion they had been made the greater part of a week, and he attributed the early decomposition to the ex- ceedingly moist wea. her. They were totally unfit for food. As this was the defendant's first offence, the Bench fined him only 10s, including costs,

div.head: WARRINGTON HORSE SLAUGHTERER AT THE LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.
div.p: A WARRINGTON HORSE SLAUGHTERER AT THE LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.
SLANDERING AN EARLEi fOWN BUTCHEI.

On Saturday, in the Nisi Prius Court of the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Kennedy arida common jerv, the cause of Allen v. Robinson came on for heerine. Henry Allen, bircher, Esrlestown, sought to reeover from Peter Robinsen,horse slaughterer and cattle dealer, Warrington, damages for sander alleged to have been uttered against plaintiff, to the injury of his business. ' The defence was a justifieetinn of the statement which had been made. Mr. A. G. Steel (instructed by Mr. U. J. Longton, of Warrington) was counsel for the plaintiff and Mr. Cellinewood flips (instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw) for the defendant. In the end cf July last the plaintiff had b-en asked hr Mn. Marsh. a farmer, to look at a mulch cow. Plaintiff found the animal to be evidently suffering from sore throat, and to be in poor condition, and he would not give any offer for it. A little later Me was asked by the farmer to kill the animal, the carcase of which was taken to Lord Gerard's dog kennels, plaintiff paying 104. for the hide, and taking the heart, liver, and kidneys to his own house to boil dewn tor the fowls. The first slander complained of was uttered on the 30thluly,in the 0 Id. fellows' Arms public-house,Earlestownen presence of Dr. Patterson and several others, the defendant telling them that.havin,g heard of a diseased cow for sale at Newton- le-Willows, he went over. but found that it had been se- cured by a butcher who h-id a wooden shop or hut at the corner of the market in Eerlestown. In explanation of the eerious nature of the libel, counsel said that the plaintiff was the only bucher answering to the deserip- tion. Defendant added, in presence of the others, "The cow is not fit for kuman food,and is now in Allen's 'Mop in Fairclough-st. ; I think it is very dangerous to sell moat diseased with tuberculosis. Dies anyone know the name of the sanitary inspector ?'' Later on the same day the defendant repeated the slander to Polica-inspec- tor John Morgan. Again, on the 1311 August, the de- fendant repeated the slander to John Gregory, inspector of nuisances, saying that the heart and liver were in plaintiff's shop, and that he was prepared to swear to it if the officer would take proceedings. As a result of those slanders plaintiff's business had fallen off very consider- ably.one customer who had been in the habit of buying regularly and extensively from him,saying that she did not want diseased meat. Evidence in supped of the allegations was given by the plaintiff, by Dr. Patterson, Police-inspector Morgan, and John Gre- gory, inspector of nuisances, the last-named stating that the defendant came to him after he (witness) had satis- fied himself that the carcase had been sent to Lord Gerrard's kannels.—The defendant, in giving evidence on his own behalf, said plaintiff was a total stranger to him, and the first he heard of the affair was in the Odd. fellows' Arms, where, in answer to a question, he said he had been to Newton to look after the carcase of a cow, part, of which, he found, had gone to an E irles- town butcher. Mr. Lythgoe, the landlord, then said to him, " It has gone to Harry Allen's ; nobody but him would buy such dirty stuff." Dr. Patterson added, ' " It's him and nobody else ; he sells some cruel stuff,and ought to be punished." Defendant afterwards went to plaintiff's shop,where be saw banging up the cliacoloured heart of a cow and a portion of a liver,which was black. Both might have been taken from a" groped" or a con- sumptive cow. Of this he informed the police inspector and afterwards the nuisance inspector, from a sense of public duty, and not from malice in any way.—His Lordship, in summing up, said that the charges must be substantially proved bet ire they could find for the dr- fendant. In assessing damages, they should take into consideration the defendant's persistence in pleading justification, and also prohably the unwi.dom of the plaintiff, as a butcher, in buying diseased meat for his fowls.—The jury found for the plaintiff, damages £65. and his Lordship gave judgment for the amount with eosts.

WARRINGTON "A " v. Sr. MARY'S, WARRINGTON.— These two teams met on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday in very unpropitious weather. There was an attendance of about 1,000 at the start considerable in- terest being evinced in the game as the teams,each with a good record, had not met before. Owing to the high wind four quarters were played in the match. St. Mary's kicked off hut Warrington returned and imme- diately pressed. The visiting forwards broke away but the rush was stopped almost on the Warrington line by Scott. Hampson immediately alter made a dashing run alone touch, but was pulled over on the line by Clarke and Lawb-ss, ray then rested for awhile on the War- rington line and Foden gave relief with a good run and kick. A neat passing movement between the whole of the " A" team threequarters reached the St. Mary's line, but a pass forward spoiled an otherwise good opening. Half-time then arrived with the score nil on either side. The second half was commenced by St. Mary's taking a vigorous initiative and Foden got away from a scrim- mage on the line, but nothing ensued and play—if it could be called play—was pretty even. The steam thscri came down with blinding fury, the players being scarcely visible, while the hall was so wet that the men could not hold it, must less make a run. Under these adverse conditions the genie could not be contested with any success, and at the call of time there was still no score and the match ended in a pointless draw.

THE NORTHERN RUGBY UNION. WARRINGTON v. BATLEY.

At Batley on Saturday last. Teams :—Warrington: Heesom ; Moores, Forster, Cross, Burton ; Nevins, Houghton; Thorniley, Andrews, Higham, Fairhurst, Hill, Wilcock, Thornton, Barrett. Batley : Joseph Naylor ; Goodall, White, Mllnes,Shaw; James Naylor, Oaklands ; Lowrie, Shackleton, Shibly, Littlewood. Welsh, Wilby, Munn!, Spur. Referee, T. E-igland, Huddersfield. From the above it will be seen that Warrington made the journey to Batley with a team greatly altered and i•ertainly not strengthened from the team as originally chosen, Moores, Fester, Houghton, Thorniley, being called from the reserve to take the places of Barber, Broady, Foden and Burrows. When Mount Pleasant vras reached nothing could be more of a contrast than that happy name and the unhappy condition of things that prevailed, for there was a regular storm of wind and rain. This lasted for half-an-hour, and it seemed then that the match could not possibly come off. Things cleared a little but it was by no means inviting when the players came on the fiela before a mockery of an attendance. It was almost as much an act of necessity as it was of mercy to curtail the game to two thirties.

..... Batley started. The reply was feeble and things might have opened badly for Warrington, had not the defence been live to the occasion, and by their advoitly getting the hall away the first scrum was formed well tnto Bat- ley quarters. From this, amidst much slipping and slushing, the home team kicked clear. It was next to impossible to hold the slippery leather and before the Warrington back division had steadied themselves,Good- all was upon them, and was first in real possession. Ile made a random kick which had the good fortune to strike the upright and the better fortune to be veered over the cross bar by the strong wind. No one was more surprised with his success than Was Goodall himself,but everything mints in love, football and war; and as it turned out this lucky shot was the only count of the game. Little damped by this early reverse, Warrington resumed their tussle with the elements with Batley- with a bit keener relish. But it was a scrambling affair at best, and only one ar two efforts in the open relieved the tedium of the quarter of an hours' scrimmages and lines out for the wind even more than the players was continually finding touch. These scrimmages, which it , must not be forgotten were always back ' and fore about Batley quarter flag and rarely reached half-way, showed even under the then prevailing conditions that our forwards were on a par with their opponents. Whr never there was a ' dead set to scrimmage Batley generally worked it better bit then Warrington eight was much quicker on and more certain in their use of the ball. The wind and rain subsiding the game opened out more freely where Oak- land and Shockleton had a run to themselves but long before they had covered half the distance towards War- rington goal Foster, Moores an I fleetly Heesom frus- trated any further progress. Two features of the re- mainder of this half were fine attempts for goal made he Nevins from free kicks at nalf way, the one going a trifle wide and the other dropping just under instead of just , over the cross bar. Once again Batley were almost let ' in, Fleesom was passed but Burton got before the Batley men and saved with a ponderous kick. This was well followed up and scrimmages close in were being worked to Warrington's advantage vr!.:ose Forwards were act- ually all on a heap on their . opponents lines when the half time whistle sounded. Half time Batley 1 goal (dropped) Warringteo nil The wind and rain had now considerably abated and the second half therefore opened much faster than the first., although the ball hovered mostly at halfway. A penalty to Batley did not avail tt em much for when they got in the open Forster was very clever with a run. Be did not use his advan- tage to the full for he retained possession too long. AS it was Nevins and Burton were in close attendance but nothing came of their fine display as at parting kick was too strong and Batley breathed more freely. They pressed in turn and for Thorniley too eagerly tackling his opponent the ball was brought back. Exchanges all in Warrington quarters, between Miles and Cross, gained ground for Warrington which was supplemented by Burton smartly making his mark. A scrimmage was formed, from which a flying kick was well attended to by Heesotn who gathered the slippery ball and got in his kick very smartly indeed. The pres- sure was kept up and a seeming br-akaway by Batley was more than counterbalance by Nevins. This player pluckily forced his way from one quarter flag to the other. Joe N iylor proved safe. Another visit was soon paid to Heesom where Oakl.nd almost dropped a goal, this bill Fist missing the post. Warrington were back again in a trice and although play continued OR the verge of the Batley lines no score was forthcoming. Nevins, however, scored what was apparently a try, but it was disallowed. Cross was well to the fore with a dodgy run. A series of exchanges ended in a minor for Batley. The drop out was well followed up, the War- riagton forwards again proving themselves a smart a lot, in, fact, trifle smarter than their opposing eight. Warringtnn towards the close made strong efforts to score. Wilcock and Fairhurst came within an ace of doing so but though pressing at the finish and after hav- ing had the best of the play but the worst of the luck, Warringtnn had to retire beaten by a dropped goal (and that a very lucky one) to nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v. TYLDESLEY.
div.p: RUNCORN v. TYLDESLEY.

For this match on Saturday the Tyldeslev committee had endeavoured to improve their team. Runcorn on the other hand had several of the regular hands off. Abrams, it is feared, will not be able to assist the club again, though matters may not turn out 34 serious as is thought. Taylor. Farmer and Johnson were also absent, hut in Liglithiet. Willieme and W. Pendlehury, the com- mittee have good reliable reserve men. Rain feil heavily all the day, completely rendering the ground unfit for play, and spoiling any chance of the increased gate to , which the committee had looked forward to meet the additional expenses the new union had incurred. The teams faced each other as follows :—Runnorn : J. Jolley. hack; T. Warder, G. Robinson, R. Myers. W, tiayter, three-quarter hacks ; Pend`ebury and J. Faulkner, half back:: W. Faulkner, J. Langley, F. Gavter, S. Walker, W. Lightfoot, R. illiams, R. Reece, and G. Moores. forwards. Tt Ideeley :A. Trow, hack; J. Lawton, J. Wilson, Miller. and Cameron. threequar- ter. backs: J. Berry and W. Berry. half backs; G. Wood- ward, It. Berry, J. Worthington, J. Roberts, W. Wood- ward, J. Tinker, J. Harris, and W. Roberts, forwards. Woodward started fully half an hour late, owing to Tyldesley's late arrival, and Warder responded, and at the same time followed up his kick. Cameron missed picking up, and Warder dribbled on, going gaily for the line. Lawton, however, raced across the ground and got up in time to kick dead, just as Ward sr was ground- ing,a very near thing. This piece of play quite enlivened the proceedings, an no sooner had the ball been re- started than the home forwards, with a grand piece of combination, went right to the Tyldesley half. From the scrimmage J. Faulkner threw to Robinson, who, by a smart tricky run, cleared several men, then throwing to Myers a really fine effort was rewarded with a try, the kick at goal missing its mark. This success completely , roused the enthusiasm of the spectators. Rain now fell in torrents, greatly interfering with the play. Resuming, the Tyldesley forwards, for the first time, got into the home half, but a concerted move- ment was started by Myers, and after a bout of passing W. Gayter was pushed into touch by Lawton when dangerously near the line. Buff Berry gave short relief. hut Jolley with good judgment played the ball hack to touch, gaining considerable ground. For some- time Runcorn peppered the Tyldesley lines until Pendle- bury got his chance and dashed over in fine style, scot-- ing.the second try. The kick at goal again failed. Ttre score was not increased up to the interval. The teams immediately changed ends, and the game proceeded in a rain storm. A heavy mist also came across the ground, ' which made it difficult at times to follow play. Faulkner started the ball, and it seemed almost impossible to keep the home team from scoring, Tyldesley having a warm time. Afterwards the Runeorn team seemed to slacken, and the game became more even, though back play was Out of the question. Through this nalf Lawton was prominent by a single-handei effort to break through the home, defence, but this was nipped by W. Faulkner, who made a very smart collar. Towards the close Run- corn looked like scoring,and it was only by a most deter- mined defence that 'Tyldesley kept their line from being crossed. Final score : Runcorn, two tries ; Tyldesley nothing. ROCHDALE HORNETS v. WIDNES. At Rochdale, on Saturday, in miserable weather, the cround being in wretched condition. Widnes made their first appearance on the Hornets' 'ground. Play was even at the start, hut grand play be Mideley caused Widnes to defend. Mt ley scored. The visitors paid a visit to the Rochdale quarters, and were almost successful in scoring. Even play followed at centre. Half-time score, Hornets, one tly ; Widnes, nil. Resuming operations Rochdale showed grand combination,and Keowles even- tually scored after much pressing. The Hornets kept up the pressure for a time, and were near scoring on two occasions. vVidnee broke away and invaded, but Rig e cleared in magnificent style when surrounded. Rochdale coetinued to have the best of mstters, their forwards playing a grand game. Widnes pressed towards thn finish, but could not score. Final result, Rochdale Hornets, two tries', Widnes, nil.

div.head: ASSOC I ATI ON. WARRING TON CUP COUPRTITION. FIRST ROUND.
div.p: ASSOC I ATI ON. WARRING TON CUP COUPRTITION. FIRST ROUND.

RUNCORN ASSOCIATION V. PRNIERTH.—The above tie was played off at Huncarn on Saturday. Both organisa- tions were thoroughly represented,and when Mr. Cathall commanded the line up. the Runcorn team appeared as follows :—Goal, Bough; full hacks, Carter and Bloor ; half-backs, Pyo, Paton, Rorrows ; forwards, Walker. Jones. Baylie, Walker, Peacock. Penketh won the toss but elected to play against the wind. Baylie kicked off and Walker and Peacock were soon in evidence, the latter having hard lines with a grod shot. Play settled in Penketh quarters for some time, and Bayne at last shot through. Penketh soon equalized through Smith, who sent in a Mow low shot, which the home custodian allowed to Mile through his legs. Peacock soon put on another for the home team, after some hard play by Payton and Pye. Bowyer got down the rig,tittand passed back to his partner. %Vila shot quite a couple of yards over the bar, but the referee.pointed to the centre, not- withstanding the strong appeals of the home team Nothing further was scored in the first half, and the interval arrived about the same time as a drenching downpour of rain which damped the players in a very few minutes. The rain did not, however, slacken the pace, and Pye and Walker added goals for the Blues about ten minutes from time. Final result: Runcorn, 4 goals; Penketh, 2 goals. ST.ELPRIN'S V. CHESTER RESERVE.—At Wilderspool. Causeway on Saturnay. Scientific football was out of the question, and ten minutes after half-titne the match had to be abandoned. The "'scramble in the mud " resulted in Chester netting the ball once in the first half and again on re-crossirg after the interval. Of course the match will be considered a draw.

LYlll2it v. KNUTSFORD.—At Lymm, in miserable weather. The visitors were fully represented, but Lymm were without Holt and Sidley. The visitors won the toss and played with the wind and rain behind them. In the first half the game was even, the homesters showing the best combination, and had hard lise in not scoring on more than one occasion. On changing ends Lymm were soon pressing and scored after ten minutes' play. The weather was now so bod that correct play was out of the question, and no further scoring took place, Final result : Lvmm one goal, Knutsford none, FAEMWORTH V. WAR RINGTOIP.—ThCiIIi two dubs met on Saturday on the Widnes Parish ground Moro 500 spectators. The elements were directly against football. and altbmigh rain kept off in the first half the second half saw i falling througnout the game. Farn worth were without G. Randle, The visitors started ,and were the first to press but good play by Hirst and Bell trans- ferred operations to the other end, and for some time Warrington had all their wok cut out. Webster saved several shots, and then Shone was put on his mettle. He threw out a volley,and Giles Randle passing to Miry that player got down well, but the ball went outside. The h Alves and forwards during the last half- hour played badly, and had it not been for the backs the score would have been augmented. Randle got the first goal for Farnworth, Warrington replying with a couple In the second half Farn worth played up grandly, and although the visitors showed better form in the first half they pressed their opponents throughout in the second half. Wareing and Tilley were both conspicuous, the former getting a couple of goals in fine style. A few minutes before the end Warrington ran off the field owing to the rain, F trnworth scoring. Result—Farn- worth, four; Warrington, two.

div.head: DAMAGES FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT. THE WHI FECROSS COMPANY. LIMITED, v. ALEXANDER AND DUNCAN.
div.p: DAMAGES FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT. THE WHI FECROSS COMPANY. LIMITED, v. ALEXANDER AND DUNCAN.

The plaintiff company in this case which was heard at the Liverpool Assiz,s on Wednesday are steel and iron wire workers at Wsrring,tnn, and the defendants are agricultural er gineers and proprietors of iron work' at Leominster. The action Was brought by the plaintiffs, who were represented by Mr. flerridge (instructed by Messrs. Alsop, Stevens, and Co.), to recover £l5O dam- ages for breach of contract from the defendants, for whom Mr. Cnllinewood Hope appeared (instructed by Mr. W. J. Yeoman for Mr. H. J. Southall,of Leominster. The plaintiffs' case was that in November last year the defendants cave to plaintiffs' traveller an order for 150 tens of galvanised strand wire, which being used chiefly in the hop districts, was only marketable during certain months. When the order wag Oven, the traveller, with the consent of his principals, allowed 2i per cent. dis- count on a quarterly account. The order was given in writing. and read. "at the undermentioned prices please enter order for about 150 tots" of the wire described. The plaintiffs in February wrote asking the defeudanta about the carrying out of the order, and, after two or three letters had been sent, the defendants replied repudiating the order, stating that no contract was entered into, and that the memorandum given to plaintiff's traveller was simply a statement of the terms on which defendants might give an order, subject to the confirma- tion of both rarties. The claim of plaintiffs of £l5O was based nn a loss of profit of £1 a ton on 150 tons.— Mr. Collinew.,od Hope contended on behalf of the de- fendants that no contract was entered into, and there• fore they were not liable.—Mr. Duncan said that he was Ithis year Mayor of Leominster, and partner in the firm lof defendants. He had the interview with plaintiffs' traveller about the wire, and,as the latter seemed not be in a position to definitely agree to terms at 41. per cent, discount, witness got his clerk to write out the memorandum of the terms on which an order could be carried out if agreed upon by both sides. This traveller stated that he would submit the memorandum, which ne could not accept as an order, and which was not signed by witness, to his principals. As witness received no reply from plaintiffs within a f n•tnieht, 11. bought else- where.—The jury found for the plaintiffs, awarding them £ll2 10. damages. Hie lordship gave judgment in accordance with the finding.

div.head: RECEPTION OF THE NEW
div.p: RECEPTION OF THE NEW
CHIEF CONSTABLE AT THE POLICE Ci 1111i.T. INTRODUCTIoN TO TRE POLICE FORCE,

On Monday morning, Mr. Luke Talbot assumed command of the Warrington Borough Poliee Force, and previous to the holding of the court, he was introduced by the Mayor to the members of the force in the parade room. The men paraded at 930 a.m., the duties of drill instructer being taken by P.C. Phillips. Mr. Talbot WAS accompanied by the Mayor (Councillor Faire lough), the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyoe Whittle), the retirir"n, chief constable (Mr. S. Hunt), the magistrates' clerk (Mr. Hi). White), the deputy magistrates' clerk (Mr. G. F. F. White), the borough treasurer (Mr. J. Fairhurst), Alder- men Francomb, J.P., Harrison, J.P., and Wiight, J.P., Councillors Pierpoint, J.P., Heaton, Cannell and Woods, ' Dr. Gornall, .I'. (borough medical officer) and Messrs. I C. JaAkson Holmes, P. Davies, and A. Browne. The MAYOI2, addressing the police force, said that he Was there that morning, for the purpose or introducing to them their new chief constable. He hoped they would obey his instructions willingly. He had been for a considerable time in Kendal, and he had had under his ,command, a number of men of whAm lie was proud. His regret was that he could not bring those men to Warrinuton. Their late chief constable had been proud of the Warrington fcrce, and he (the Mayor) hoped they would show their new chief constable that they had as good policemen in Lancashire, as in Cumberland. Mr. Talbot M'AA quite a stranger in the town but he was perfectly cPrtain that the men would do all they could to assist him in his duties and in other ways,and that be would reciprocate their kindne3s in the future. Mr. TatnoT, in reply, thanked the Mayor for intro- ducing him tl the members of the police force. To the (nen ti.emselves, he would say that he was proud to find himself in command of a body of men who looked so dean, well-set,and soldierly. He hoped they would get on very well together, and he did not see any reason why they should not do so. Their retiring chief con- stable, their venerable and good friend, Mr. Hunt, gave them a first-rate character. He therefore thought that they would eet along very well, and in order that they mi,4lit start fair, as it was said, he would give them some idea of his likes and dislikes. In the first place, be liked a clean, smart policeman, who was proud of his uniform and kept it all snick and span. A man who was that, was efficient in other branches of duty as well as that. In the second place,he liked a sober policeman, not necessarily a teetotaler,but a man who did not make 4 habit of drinking on duty. He was sorry to say that in many police forces, there were men who could be ,quared, but he hoped that there were no men of that ,lort before him. Next,he liked a man who did his duty without fear or favour; a man who did not care what people thought about him so long as his conscience told him he was doing what was right. It was a very easy matter for policemen—as they all knew especially old officers—to be called a "nice man." All he had got to . .

-1() was to shut his eyes to everything he saw, and a certain section of the public would tell him " he was a nice man." There was another, and a better class of the public, however, who would despise that man and say he was dishonest, and he (Mr. Talbot) would say the same. He did not mean that he liked a man always pushing for cases and trying to make them. Better let three Cases go.if they were doubtful, if they get a fourth which was a right one. That brought him to the neces- •=ity of truthfulness among policemen. That was the primary and greatest virtue a policeman could have. It was necessary for police officers over all others, to have the soul of horn.ur, and the tongue of truth. A man who WAS found ta, be wilfully guilty of falsehood should b's hunted from the police force as a public danger. He was more a menace to the public, than 12, aye than 50 professional thieves in the town. Again, he liked a man who was straightforward and above board in all his actions, a man who respected himself, who was loyal to liiin.elf and was loyal to his superior officer, and the public whom he served. If they wanted anything, let them come to him for it, and frankly state what they wished, and if it was something he could give them he would do it. If they had a grievance, he asked them not to get together in twos and threes and have hole and corner discuesions, but let them state it fairly in writing to him, through their inspectors,and if it was something he could PersonalLY remedy, it should have his attention. If is was something which required the interference of the Watch Committee he would fairly represent it to that committee on their behalf, and it would have fair consideration. They were losing a chief constable whom he was sure , they must reverence and respect very deeply. But they were getting a new chief constable, who besides being their chief, wanted to be their friend, and who would be their friend, if they worked hand in hand with him to serve the people of Warrington. (Applause.) . . . .

dd • Mr. HUNT then said, a ressing r. Talbot, that in handing over to him the command of the police force of the ancient borough of Warrington, in the first place he shsuld like to say how pleased he was, and he was sure the men with him to welcome him to Warrington and to the responsible post he was called upon to occupy. From what they had all heard,he was sure that the Warrington Town Council could not have made a better selection than they had done, and while he held office he (Mr. Hunt) trusted and believed that he wnuld find the men under him loyal, faithful, and willing, as he had invari- ably done during the many years he had held the proud position of Head Constable of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) In introducing the men to their new Chief, he could only thank them for the loyalty and kindness they had shown to him and he hoped and believed that their relations with their new Chief would always be as cor- dial and as respectful as they had been to him. He thought the Warrington force was a force anyone might be proud to command, and they one and all would do their utmost to keep up its best traditions. (Applause.) He now bade them farewell as their Chief.

div.head: PROCEEDINGS AT THE POLICE COURT.
div.p: PROCEEDINGS AT THE POLICE COURT.

On Monday morning previous to the business of the Warrington Borough Police Court being commenced, the Mayor formally introduced Mr. L. Talbot, the Chief Constable of Warringten. to his brother magistrates on the bench, Aldermen Francomb, Harrison and Wright, Couneillor Pierpoint, and Mr. S. Wright. Ile (the MAYOR) then said Mr. Hunt and Mr. Talbot reminded him very much of gladiators,—Mr. Hunt com- ing out of the arena without a scratch, to enjoy well- earned rest, and Mr. Talbot just corning in, with his battle to fieht,iand the speaker hoped he would corae out with credit to himself and all connected with him. Ceuncillor DAVIM naid he thought it was a remark none the worse for repetition,that Mr.Flunt had done his duty well and nobly for the town. (Hear, hear.) He had worked hard, and the speaker was sure Mr. Talbot would have a difficult example to follow. The speaker had had almost constant communication with Mr. Hunt for le or 17 years and he had always noticed that when he was prosecutor he had done his best fairly and hon- ourably, and if he could say anything in the favour of a person charged with an offence he always did so, and endeavoured to g't the bench to be lenient in first, , second, or third offences. If he believed there was a chance for a moment of a man retrieving himself, Mr. Hunt - ould try and give him another trial. That was the character of a gentleman and also of a man of honour. (Hear, hear.) He congratulated Mr. Hunt upon his success in the way he had carried out his duties as Chief Conatahle of the Borough of Warrington. No one had had more respect and he hoped sincerely that the new Chief Constable, Mr. Talbot, would simply walk in Mr. Hunt's footsteps and he respected just the same. It would be a pleasure to Mr. Talbot to know that he would be welcomed by the body he (Mr. Davies) represented, and he congratulated him upon taking the position be Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE said Mr. Hunt had taken a kindly interest in him on a great number of occasions, advised him to do what he thought fit and best, and he was clad to say he had followed that advice. Mr. Hunt had been there something like 28 years, and as Judge Iffoulkes had said that the County Court did not seem like a court without a Nicholson neither did the town or police force seem the same without the name of Hunt connected with them. He only hoped that during his well-earned rest, Mr. Hunt would remain in Warrington and continue the friend of the people. With regard to Mr. Talbot, the speaker wished him every success in his office. He suggested to the magistrates that they should follow a precedent set in Liverpool, and petition the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster to raise Mr. Hunt to the bench. Mr. H. B. WRITE, thE magistrates' clerk, said he could not allow an ocensinn like that to pass without saying a few words. He had known Mr. Hunt an a friend and chief constable tor nearly 30 years and they had always w•rkod together most harmoniously. He had great esteem, respect, and friendship for Mr. Hunt and it was a satisfaction to feel th it though he lost him as chief constable he could still look unon him as a friend. The Town Clerk, Mr. .1. L. Wurrrus, wished Mr.Flunt all happiness in his retirement, and would liko to add a word of welcome to the new chief in his new office. alderman FlssursoN said he could not resist the terffp- tation to say a word or two. It was his privilege to be bete sufficiently early to hear Mr. Talbot's address to the police officers. It was a great treat to hear what he said, displaying his practical knowledg,s and giving friendly advice to them. That OCCEVIIOII reminded him of the saying tt Welceme the coming, speed the parting guest." Thry had both the coming and parting guests present, for when they spoke of the latter they wars speaking of Mr. Runt's retirement to that honourable ra- 'lns. which a long life of earnest and sincere devotion to bin duties moat fairly entitled him to, and the speaker hoped he would be spared many years to enjoy the fruits a it. With reference to Mr. 'Met, he had heard

good deal of him before he came, and it was his privi- ledge to assist in putting him in the position he Low held. There was in him something they had to 1, ok forward to and he expected, not in vain. He was qu te sure that Mr. Talbot's life and antecedents gave promise of an earnest devotion to his duties which would do much to atneliorate crime and would also entitle him to the sympathies and love of those with whom he had to deal.

Mr. HUNT thanked all the previous speakers most s,ncerely for their kind and complimentary expressions of approval of his past service. He also thanked the tnagistrat s' clerk, Mr. H. B. White, and the deputy magistrates' clerk, Mr. G. F. F. White, for their great assistance in intricate cases where their legal knowledge and advice had been at his command. Mr. Hunt wished also most respectfully to thank the professional gentle- men whose business had brought them there, for their ready forbearance with him when he occasionally found it necessary to differ from them in matters of evidence, Ste. During his long service in that Court he had always striven to do his duty without fear or favour, erring rather on the side of mercy than otherwise. H 9 also expressed his thanks to the force, which had become very dear to him, for the zealous assistance they had rendered him in difficult circumstances. Referring to the bench, Mr. Hunt said he had nothing but feelings of lively gratitude to them for their kindly approval of his duties. It had been his one desire to obey their instruc- tions, and he hoped to remain in Warrington all his days. His succe‘sor was coining to live amongst a loyal and good-hearted people who he was sure would use him well. He coacludecd by saying that he had put in about 45t years at police work. Mr. TALBOT thankrd the Bench, their learned Clerk, an i the gentlemen of the Bar for the words of welcome which had fallen from their lips that morni-g. Be could not say he was a stranger to police work, as he had had more than 16 years of it. For many years he had been conducting prosecutions before various be-ches, and he had always found the members of the magistracy, their clerks,and the members of the Bar most kind,considerate and helpful, and lie was deeply indebted to them. He trusted, in fact, knew, that he would find in Warrington no divergence from the general experience. To the Bench he looked with all c.oufidence. A police force without the hearty and cordial support of the magistrates was a use- less and ineffectual organisation. He hoped and knew that he would have their hearty co-operation and sup- port in looking after the best welfare of this ancient and honourable borough. (Applause.)

div.head: FURTHER PRESENTATION TO MR. TALBOT.
div.p: A FURTHER PRESENTATION TO MR. TALBOT.

The Kendal licensed victuallers made a presentation to Mr. Talbot in the form of a handsome set of chimney- piece ornaments, at the Rainbow Hotel, on Friday after- noon. The Chairman (Mr. Alderman Robinson) after expressing the feeling of the licensed victuallers towards Mr. Talbot for his general urbanity, and his desire to assist them in the management of their houses, said he ' had known Mr. Talbot's conduct before the Watch Com- mittee, and had always appreciated it, for he never sup- ported any prosecution unless it were for some great infraction of the law, and after the landlord had been warned. He trusted that the gentleman who was com- ing to fill Mr. Talbot's place would act as the latter gentleman had done. The publicans asked no favour; all they desired was to be treated honestly and fairly, and in conclusion he asked Mr. Talbot to accept the three vases to adorn his mantelshelf at Warrington, and expressed a hope that Mrs. Talbot and himself might experience good health and like the place. Mr. Talbot suitably responded, and said the vases should have a place of honour in one of his living rooms, and they would remind him of many kind and familiar faces in Kendal.—A complimentary dinner to certain Kendal aldermen who are retiring was given the other day at the Rainbow Hotel, when CouncillorLittlewood proposed the health of the retiring Flead•Constable, Mr. Talbot. The speaker, as a member of the Watch Committee, re- ferred to Mr. Talbot's smartness, intellectual ability,and experience in police work, his undoubted fairness in lay- ing cases before the magistrates, his solicitude for the comfort of the men under him in the fire brigade, and for their better equipment, and said that the favour he had gained with the Watch -.3ommittee had never been purchased at the expense of his subardinates. His duties as inspector of weights and measures had been discharged fairly and well, and he now left the town with the good wishes of all that he might long be spared to be an ornament to the profession he adorned. Mr. Talbot feelingly responded in a neat speech.

div.head: EPIDEMIC SPREADING.
div.p: THE EPIDEMIC SPREADING.

There are to-day more than a hundred developed cases of this dread malady, Bright's Disease, in London; and, in spite of the untiring efforts of physicians. this scourge is spreading with alarming rapidity, threaten- ing every home in Great Britain. With many, the first system of alarm is that dreadful " swelling," which comes unannounced in the feet, hands, under the eye- lids, or in the throat. Others suffer with dull, inde- finite pains in various parts of the body, and feel un- accountably weary, feverish, have loss of appetite, and general feelings of melancholy. These simple symptoms are the first indications of Bright's Disease of the Kid- neys,which, unless promptly checked, are certain to result in serious illness or death. A short time ago, IN ST. THOMAS' HOSPITAL.

a young man lay rapidly sinking, struggling in the toils of this dread monster—Bright's Disease. In spite of the best treatment they could suggest,the dropsical swelling was rapidly iscreasing. With the usual profound shak- ing of the head, the deprecatory shrug of the shoulder, the uplifting of the eye-brows, which to the poor patient means a sentence of death, they discharged him as incurable. What a dismal return to the parental roof ! Could nothing be done to save ? Is there no help for victims of Kidney Disease? Must he give up ? No ! He remembered that Warner's Safe Cure had cured others ; why not him ? He immediately commenced using it, and the result is given below in his own words _

"Early in January this year," writes Mr. A. Under- I wood, " I took a slight cold, which, however, only seemed confined to the head, and not sufficient to cause any anxiety on the part of a young man in the prime of life, as I was. Two or three days alter I noticed a little swelling in one of my feet. I went to a doctor, who seemed to think little of it, but advised application of hot water. The next week the other foot commenced to swell, and I noticed my back seemed weak, and I was suffering from a dull, heavy pain in the small of the back. The water was darker than usually passed, and the quantity seemed very.small. Suddenly my eye-lids and face showed signs of swelling, and then my throat also became swollen. I had no idea what the trouble was, but was so frightened I determined to get the best advice possible, and immediately went under treatment in the London St. Thomas' Hospital. They prescribed medicines to reduce the dropsical swelling; but falling in their efforts, they resorted to hot vapour baths three times a week, in addition to the medical treatmen". By this time my eyesight had become affected, and I was subject to severe headaches, general enervation, and increasing pains over the region of the kidneys, and the dropsical swelling was daily increasing. The 017 si- clan in charge said I had Bright's Disease of the Kidneys, and after lying in the hospital twenty-one weeks I was discharged as incurable. I then returned home, and for- tunately heard of, and determined to try, Warner's Safe Cure. I took it faithfully for a month before I notieed any improvement ; then there seemed to be a lessening of the dropsical swelling; the water passed more freely and naturally. Then the dropsical swelling commenced to rapidly decrease; my strength began to return, and my convalescence from this time was uninterrupted. I had not tried, as many seemed to have done, all other known remedies, nor had I been under a multitude of doctors for treatment; but as soon as! found physicians of a leading hospital, could do me no good, I lost no time in commencing Warner's Safe Cure. The health which I now enjoy, after such a tedious and serious illness, is quite sufficient te make me very grateful, and for that and no other reason I called upon the vendors of this medicine to give them this letter. If any doubt my wonderful rescue, the facts can be verified by calling upon my relations at 94, Wells Street, Camberwell, Lon- don, where I can he seen at any time."

div.head: WARRIORS (5N WHEELS.
div.p: WARRIORS (5N WHEELS.

Military authorities have come to the conclusion that the bicycle will play an indispensable part in the wars of the future. Its sphere, at least in its early military stages, will be that of the uhlan of the 1870 war. The cyclist,in preliminary operations, will act as an impene- trable advance cloud or screen for the army,pushing far ahead into the enemy's theatre of operations, making his power felt long beim'', the enemies have a chance to come together, paralysing the enemy's communications, making descents now here, now there, often rashly and often making mistakes. In spite of this, he will always be able to obtain infor- mation for headquarters better than any ether form of scouting, feeling the enemy retiring before him when outnumbered .but contesting the ground whenever there is a chance of contest. Be will, in fact, pursue exactly the course followed by the Prus:ian cavalry in the early days of the Franco-Prussian war ; always acting in company with light horse artillery, with the gunners mounted on bicycles, and not according to the present oubof-date system, )n caissons. With these and the flying cyclists, it is believed the modern army has an offensive combination such as has never been equalled. The cyclist will be a crack shot with the rifie,and that will he his only weapen. Be has one decided advantage over the cavalryman, in that he is not bothered by the question of forage. On poor roads and in poor weather, the cavalryman has everything in his favour, and this will make the conservative soldier view the bicycle with suspicion. Against the radical disadvantage is placed the fact that under moderately fair conditions the cyclist can outmareh the cavalryman two to one,or 100 per cent.,and under almost the worst conditions he can do the same with infantry. Another important duty the cyclist may have to per- form in the next war is to act as the anvil for the main army to hammer the enemy against, to reach the enemy's rear, to get on his communications, take up a defensive position and wait for his attack. This could only be practicable with a heavy force of artillery. The value of the rce,liqt aq a messenger or in guarding trains and supplies is obvious.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING OF MEMBERS.
ELECITION OF OFFICERS, &c.

The annual meeting ol the members ot the Liberal Club was held in the billiard-room of the club on Wednesday week. There was a good muster of members, and the chair was taken by the President, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who was supported by Mr. J.H. Fleming, J.P., vice-president, Councillors Pierpoint, elhaw-Green, Furness, Wilkinson, and Tinnion, Messrs. C. J. Holmes, G. Clay, W. ROberts, F. R. Roberts, M.A., Tr Pemberton (hon. sec.), • &C.

THE BALANCE SHEET. The balance sheet, which was submitted by Mr. Pemberton, showed that the profit of the club on the year was £l2 Ils. 7d.—Mr. J. H. FLEMING, in moving the adoption of the balance sheet, congra- tulated the club upon its President during the past Year. He had behaved handsomely to the club,and had given a handsome present fur the billiard han- dicap. It was inspiriting to see their young men Coming amongst them. They wanted them to take the places of old fogies like himself. (Laughter.) He was glad that the balance of the club was on the right side,and it showed that the club could be kept going. (Applause.) They had plenty to be thankful for lately to judge from the municipal elections.—Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS seconded the adoption of the balance sheet, and said that a great deal a credit was due to the excellent manager of the club,Mr.Mitchell. (Load applause.) He believed that it was largely due to his energy that the club had been so succe,sful. (Applause.)—The motion
Was carried unanimously. MESSAGES OF REGRET FROM MR. SCOTT, AND COTINCILLOR

ROBERTS. Mr. CEOSFIELD then read a telegram from Mr. Scott in which he said that he regretted that he was unable to be present with the members of the club and at the same time sending his kindest regards to them. Mr. Crosfield said that they were exceedingly sorry not to see Mr. Scott with them that evening. (Hear, hear,) He had also to announce that Councillor H. Roberts was unable to be present, owing to a business engagement in Wales.

ELECTION Or PRESIDENT. Mr. J. Et. FLEMING proposed the re-election of Mr. A. H. Crosfield as president for the coming year. (Ap- Diause.) He said that they could not have a better man for the post. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PIIIRPOINT seconded the motion. He en- dorsed every word that Mr Fleming had said with reter- ence to the desirability of young men becoming members of that club, and he was sure that they could Dot do better than again appoint their young president. (Ap- plause.) The president's year of office had markea to some extent the progress of the balance sheet which had Just been passed. He was glad to find that the Liberals had another success besides being able to show a credit balance sheet. They had a vary great credit balance on the first of November—(applanse)—and they did exceed- ingly well at the Parliamentary election. (Applause.) He was aura that the Tories would not be overpleased at the satisfactory condition of things at the Liberal Club. (Laughter.) The club had shown a vitality which was _

not the result of increased subsidies from the pockets of a few rich men—(bear, hear)—and he was proud that the Liberal party in Warrington had realized that it did not depend upon the individual exertions of a few rich men. There was no need to refer to the municipal generosity of Mr. •Crosfield in giyine the handsome present for the billiard handicap. (Applause.) That pi esent not Gnly gave pleasure to the members of the club, but it enabled the committee to devote the whole of the proceeds of that handicap to extend the heating apparatus of the club so as to make the place more cnlnfnrt-thIP., (Applause.) Lieutenant MCGARTY heartily endorsed everything Which had been said about Mr. Crosfield and hoped that he would do in the future as he had done in the past. Mr. F. R. ROBERTS also supported the re-election of Mr.Crosfield and expressed his gratification at the active Part he had taken in the work of the Liberal Associa- ..

tion of Warrington. His own conviction was that a rich Man who did nothing was a acurce of weakness to a party. but a rich man who helped them was a blessing !Indeed. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfield's family had been Identified with Liberalism in Warrinron for a long period and he was delighted that Mr. •Crosfield was following In their footsteps. (Applause.) The motion was carried with acclamation.

Mr. CROSFIELD. in reply, thanked the members for their vote, and said that he could not but think that there were other gentlemen who had a much better Claim and who would much more gracefully and effici- ently fill the position than himself. (Cries of No, -No.) He did not like making individual referencea,but he had hoped that they would have had their friend,Mr. Scott, with them that evening. Had he been so, he would cer- tainly have proposed an amendment to apnevint Mr. Scott the president of the club. In Mr. Scott's absence and as they had most kindly received his (Mr.Crotfield's) name, he could do nothing, but take the position. (Ap- Alause.) He did so in the hope that as time went oo,he raight improve upon his record of the last 12 months, lie was delighted at the improvement of the club. Be thought that their admirable secretary, Mr. Pemberton, ought to have some credit for that. (Applause.) He had the pleasure of looking through the figures for the last few years,t'and taking the whole period from the commencement of Mr. Pemberton's tenure of office in 1838—taking the whole of that period and contrasting the first few years with the result of last Year, he thought it only confirmed what Mr. Pierpoint had just n w said that they were getting fairly overwhelmed with he triumphs of the Liberal party in Warrington, and he only hoped that they would keep their heads steady and not let them - get turned with success. (Laughter.) The previous night, they had a very interesting discussion at the De- bating Society. and perhaps some members present had the pleasure of listening to Mr. Scott's able address in which he dealt with the reasons for that reverse which, throughout the country the Liberal party had suffered. He thought it was s very small reverse they had suffered in Warrington. (Applause.) De thought they had done Uncommonly well, and he knew that those responsible for the conduct of affairs on the other side thought the %Me. (Applause.) With regard to the club, Mr. Gros- field paid a tribute to Mr. Mitchell, the manager, and said that he was a very efficient manager of the club. He thought that the club ought to have a larger member- thin, for at the last general election, Mr. Scott registered 55,300 votes. He therefore thought that there was plenty Of scope to add to the membership. (Applause.) This Vas not the season for bowls, but it was the season for billiards, and he thought that it was most gratifying that the returns from the billiards were so satisfactory. It was not long since that lots cf good people looked with hoi horror at the idea of the billiard table. Be con- fessed that personally he had wasted a good deal of time With billiards, and he hoped to waste a good deal more. It was exceedingly satisfactory that the returns from billiards showed such a sul.stantial increase for the past twelve months, and he hoped that they would have a Satisfactory tournament at Christmas. He thanked them heartily for his re-election. (Loud applause.)

ELECTIOV OF' VICE-PRE,IDENTS. ETC. The following offilals were also appointed the vice- -o..tesidents :—Messrs. P. B. Scott, Councillor Piernoinr, and J. H. Fleming. J.P. ; hon. treasurer, Mr. J. Croafield. J.P. ; hon. secretary, Mr. T. Pemberton ; auditors, Messrs. J. Harrison, and W. Ford ; committee, Al.essrs. 1. Hayward, W. Harnes,James Thomas, William J. Robinson, T. Critchley, J. Critchley, S. Dun. u.obbin.W. Cross, G. Clay, and W. Roberts : represents- byes on tho executive committee, Messrs. Robinson, Critchlev ; epresentatives on the genera! council, messrs. Robinson, Gleave, Warren, J. Critchley, and T. Critchley.

VOTES or Trtaxxs. On the motion of Mr. C. JACKSON HoL3trs, seconded bp Mr. M. KNowiss, a vote of thanks was passed to the cfEcers, committee, and manager, for their services to the club during the nest year. Councillor Slimy Gnaws prono7ed a vote lf thanks to H. Hro4,-Id for presiding that night.—Mr. T. LLOOD in seconding, said that Mr. Crosfield's family had D'en identified with Liberalism in Warrington since 1815. He hoped that Mr.Creafield would long be spared tq support the principles of the pArty of reform in War- rington.—Tho vote was carried unanimously and Mr. ,CaOSFIELD in reply said that he appreciated the kindly ;Otte of the last speaker and said that he did net need to De reminded of the privilege as well as the obligation IThich he felt it to be t follow in a small way the much Rreater records established in the old days by his grand- father and father. (Applause.) He hoped that he ItoUld be instrumental in a small way in helping to keep ! healthy political feeling in the town extant and Uollrialling. (Applause.) The meeting afterwards terminated.
A "RUNNING DOWN" CASE.

div.head: STRONG REMARKS BY JUDGE FFOULKES.
div.p: STRONG REMARKS BY JUDGE FFOULKES.

Gearge Chelvers,cabproprietor,Manchester,was sued at the Warrington County Court on Thursday week, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, by Henry Leather Lymm for £l5 damages sustained, owing to injuries received by a collision between his trap and a bust belanging to the defendant. in Lyrnm on October 10th. A further claim of £3 3s. was made for the damage of the trap. Ms. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, represented the awd Mr. Woodburne, barrister, Manchester, iwstructed by Mr. A. T. Spencer, represented the defendant.

Mr. Browne said that the plaintiff was Henry Leather, an undergardener at High Legh Hall, and resided with his parents at Broom Edge in Lymm. He was 17 years. of age. On October 10th, at about 8 p.m., he was sent with a pony and cart to meet his mother at Lymm station. At the time it was just getting dusk. After going about a quarter of a mile, he picked up three friends, and drove with them towards Lymm. On get- ting near to Lymm church, they saw a bus drawn by four horses approaching from Lymm, on the wrong side of the road. Although they shouted, the driver took no notice, and Leather took his trap nearer to his own side of the road, se that it was partly on the footpath. The driver did not go to his own side of the road,aod Leather in his anxiety so avoid a collision, drove right on to the footpath, nearly running into Dr. Lunt. In spite of what the boy did, the bus' collided with the trap, the wheels interlocking. The boys were thrown out, and Dr. Lunt considered that it was a miracle that Leather was not killed, as he was thrown under the hind wheel of the bus. It was alleged that the driver of the bus' was under the influence of drink if not drunk. When he drove into the trap, he refused to stop,but tried to get through the trap, the consequence being that the leaders were pulled down on their knees. The driver got off his seat and tried to prevent some witnesses from getting ' the name of the owner. Soon afterwards the driver rode away, with the whole of the party. When plaintiff's , solicitor sent a letter with reference to the accident, defendant's solicitor denied that the driver was drunk, and said that there was negligence on the part of the boys owing to there being no lamps in the trap. Henry Leather gave corroborative evidence to Mr. Browne's statement, and denied that he was under the influence of drink. After the accident he did not go to work for ten weeks, and then an abscess forming in his leg he had to be away for another fortnight. Flis wages I were 12s. per week, and had received nothing for eleven weeks. There was also a new hat valued 7.5. CL, and his boots, whic.h were spelled. The boots, which he did not wear again,cost 125.61 Dr. Wright's bill was £115q., and Dr. Lunt's 73.6d.—1n cross-examination the witness admitted that there were no lamps to his trap, but that. there were to the 'bus.—A large number of witnecses were also called, who all exculpated the plaintiff from all blame in the matter. Mr.Woodburee said that there were no cases in which there was more passibility of mistake than a running down case, He han several witnesses to call who would tell his Hoeour that the fault was that of the boys in the reap. The driver would say that it was the trap which ran into the 'bus. The driver also denied that he was drunk, and this was proved by the fact that when he was stopped by the police in Altrincham, because of the accident,they allowed him to go on. Had be been incapable, they would not have done so. James Farrington,the driver, was then called,and said that !the boys were in the middle of the road, and did not slacken speed when they saw the 'hug, but ran into it. He also averred that the plaintiff was under the influence of drink.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Browne the defendant said that neither Dr. Lunt nor any other Lunt was present at the time of the accident.—His Honour: You need say no more.—The next witness called was Austin Booth, Mr. Woodburn° aeked him whether he had any interest in that case on behalf of the defendant, to which he promptly replied, amid the loud laughter of the Court,"Yee, Sir."—Mr. Woadburne : Then you can sit down.—Other witnesses were called who denied that the driver was drunk, and said that the blame of the accident lay upon the occupants of the trap.

Ms Honour said that this was a sad thing—a shocking case—to think that a number of people should be banded together to misstee the truth in order to support the driver, who was alleged to be drunk. The less said the better. It was a sad exhibition, and he should give judgment for the plaintiff on both claims, as his wit- nesses he mild not doubt were witnesses of truth.

div.head: IVARRINGTON CEMETERY HOTEL SUBSCRIPTION BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: IVARRINGTON CEMETERY HOTEL SUBSCRIPTION BOWLING CLUB.
PRESENTATION TO THE PRESIDENT.

The tea in connection with the closing main of the above club which was played on Saturday,October 12th, took place on Thursday week at the Cemetery Ho'-el, about 50 members and friends being present. The season just closed has been the most successful since the formation of the club, as in addition to securing premier honours in the Warrington and District League, the club won the second prize in the Association Division of the Lancashire and Cheshire Competition,and further are in the proud position of having the gold medalist (Mr. J. D. Brimelow) and the amateur champion (Mr. J. Allison) for season 1895 of Lancashire and Cheshire, in the club and in addition Mr. A. J.Jones secured third prize, andlidr. William Wood fifth prize in the Amateur Championship Competition of Lancashire and Cheshire. After tea the chair was taken by the President, and the evening's entertainment was commenced by an overture on the piano by Mr. George Anderton, whicu was followed by the toast of the "Queen and Royal Family," ably proposed by the Chairman and suitably acknowledged. Mr. R.Anderton favoured the company with a trombone solo, "Pilgrim of Love," which was rendered in capital style. After this the President dis- tributed the prizes to the successful competitors in the closing handicap, each of the 35 players taking part in the competition obtaining a prize. The following is'a list of the chief prize winners :-1, Mr. J. Ellison, fancy lamp, &c. ; 2, Mr. J. T. Whittle, cruet ; 3, Mr. B. Ander- ton, lady's satchel ; 4, Mr.J. Allison, bowls and j4ck ; 5, Mr. W. Gleave, hat, do. ; 6, Mr. A. Ball, set of vases ; 7' Mr. F. Berry,copper kettle ; 8, Mr. W. Barton,coal box ; 9, Mr. J. Sankey, butter cooler ; 10, Mr. J. Farrington, carver and fork. Consolation ;-1, Mr. A. J. Jones. umbrella ; 2, Mr.W.Flaigh, foot stools ; 3,Mr.W.Hughes, pipe and pouch; 4, Mr. W. Kerfoot, flower vase. Extra handicap :-1, Mr. T. Healing, cruet : 2, Mr. G. Lea, dozen cut glasses. Mr. Young afterwards favoured the company with a capital ren,lering of "The Big Fat Man " which was well received. The Chairman proposed the health of the captain of the club (Mr. J. D. Brimelow) and com- mented on the way in which the team had been managed during the season and his capabilities as a bowler, and, in honour of his securing the gold medal, presented him on behalf of the members with a gold albert upon which to append the medal.—Mr. Brimelow suitably acknowledged the gift and thanked the mem- bers for the manner in which his name had been re- ceived.

Mr. T. Healing finely sang "The Anchoris Weighed," after which the toast of the evening was proposed "The President, A. H. Cro;field,Esq." by Mr. J. D. Brime- low, who reviewed the progress the club had made since he (Mr. Crosfield) had been connected with it and hoped that Mr. Crosfield would go in for bowls instead of the game of golf which had been characterised as an awfully slow game and on behalf of the members presented him with a beautifully carved oak writing cabinet with clock and aneroid barometer affixed mounted in silver. Attached to same was a silver plate bearing tin- following inscription :--`• Pre- sented to A. H. Crosfield, Esq., by the members of the Warrington Cemetery Hotel Bowling Club in recognition of his valuable services as President. November, 1895.' Mr. WILLETT supported the proposition. ' The PRESIDENT, who was taken aback at the presenta- tion, said he was obliged for the hearty manner in which his health had been received but could not under- stand why such a handsome present had been given to him. Had he been president about 15 years instead of three years he could have better understood it. He , added he should have liked to defend his game of gr.lf but would overlook it on this occasion as it would take him some time. He stated that he was prepared to do all in his power to help healthy recreation, and he hoped the bowline club and kindred associations would prosper. , (Applause.) I The rest of the evening was spent in a convivial manner, Messrs. T. Mather, J. Allison. Brimelow, It. Anderton contributing songs which were much appreci- ated whilst the following-toasts were duly honoured : " Officers and Committee" was proposed by Mr. :'etford ; " The Visitors" lw Mr. W. Haigh; and the "Cemetery Bowling Club" by Mr. Willett. The pro- ceedings terminated with the singing of "Auld Lang Sync."

Sir,—l shall esteem it a favour, if you will give me space in your next issue, to inform at concerned in the above that my absence therefrom was unavoidable, and due to causes over which I had no control. Also that I was not able to wire, or send word, that night. As soon as I possibly could, I sent a full explanation of the whole matter, to the Secretary (dr. Harrison).
