div.head: WARR i NGTON rARISH CHURCH BAZAA R.
div.p: THE WARR i NGTON rARISH CHURCH BAZAA R.

Sir,—ln your last issue of the "Examiner" a •state- meat is made by which a model of the Old Parish Church shown at the Parish Church bazaar, held at Parr Hall, is credited to having been made by a Mr. J. Mounfield, of Warrington, and represented six months' work during leisure hours with a penknife. I trust you will be so good as to allow me to c.mtradict this statement. I made the model of Warrington Parish Church, and, al- though tl e penknife was my chief tool, many others were used, and the time taken to comp •te this model was five months. I lent the model to the tr.z. ar, and how Mr. Mounfield should receive the credit I am at a loss to understand. Trusting you will afford me a brief space in your next issue.—l ,m, yours faithfully. ARTHUR EDWARD DOBDINSON. 47, Price-st., Warrington, Nov. 1901,1895.

div.head: TEE WALTON LEA GARDENS.
div.p: TEE WALTON LEA GARDENS.

Sir,—Being one of a large number of people who took advantage ot Mr. Crosfi. ld's generosity in throwing open big grounds to the public on Sunday and Monday last, in order to view the fine show of chrysanthf-mums, it oc- curred to my mind whilst there, what a fn- opportunity presented itself to help the Infirmary. If Mr. Crosfield could be induced to allow collecting boxes to be placed in various parts of the grounds, I feel sure that the visi- tors would respond generously to so good a cause. The Infirmary is in want of money, and advantage should be , taken of opportunities like these to collect it. I think i: would not be out of place if Mr. Crosfield was approached on this subject and asked if he would allow boxes to be placed the next time the grounds are thrown open, or , make a small charge for admittance. The Duke of West- ! minster handed over £6OO to the Chester Infirmary a few weeks ago. This money was collected from visi- tors by charging one shilling each for admittance to his hall and grounds. I think this a good example and one which coull be followed by our local gentry. I feel auto it would be appreciated by everyone who has the in- terest of the Infirmary at heart.—Yourt faithfully, J. GRIFFITHS. 177,1Iewsey-road.

div.head: INTOXICATING DRINKS AT PARR HALL.
div.p: INTOXICATING DRINKS AT PARR HALL.

Sir,—On Monday last an occasional license was granted by the magistrates for the sale of intoxicating drinks in the new Parr Ball on Wednesday last, on the occasion of the bazaar held there this week. As this is the first time I have Noticed any reference to the grant- ing of a license, occasional or otherwise, to sell intoxi- cants in the new Parr flail, I shall feel obliged if you will kindly give me the opportunity, through your columns, of uttering my most emphatic protest as a rate- payer, a citizen, and a minister of Christ against the in- troduction of the baneful influences of intoxicating drink into the commodious, and most useful public hall so recently presented to the town by Mr. Parr. A public hall is a great educational institution, and may be abun- dantly useful to the whole community in a great many ways; but, surely, the tendency of everything permitted In the hall should be in the direction of the moral and social .uplifting of the people, and I hope the members a the Town Council who have the moral well-being of the people at heart will not be satisfied until a resolution is passed to the effect that any person or persons taking the hall shall do so on the clear understanding that no license to sell intoxicants on the premises shall be ap- plied for.—l am, dear sir, faithfully yours, EDWARD T. REED. 17, Museum-st., Warrington, November 15th, 1895.

WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND MESSRS. BISHOP AND CO. Sir,—We beg to etiMotie copy of the letter addressed by us to the Rivera' Committee, which, we shall be glad if you can see your way to insert in your Saturday's paper.—Yours faithfully, W. A. BIE:HOP AND CO.

The Rivers' Committee,Town Rail, Warrington. Gentlemen,—At the recent municipal elections in War- rington, the action of the Rivers Committee in agreeing to allow us P. wharf, but whose decision was reversed by the Corporation, was brought prominently before the electors of Warrington. So much interest was taken in the subject that a manifesto was issued signed by twelve members of the Corporation upholding the decision of the Council. Three of these gentlemen were retiring
- - councillors, namely, Councillors R. T. Fairclough, J. Hill-, and J. Cannel'. Dr. Carmen's seat was not contested, but in St. John's Ward and Fairfield Ward. both noun-

cillors were replaced by candidates strongly in favour of the wharf being granted to us and the minutes of the Rivers Committee confirmed. This being so and having regard to the fact that nearly three out of every five of the burgesses of Warrington are of tbe same opinion as the R vers Commit Ase, we should be glad if you would again bring the matter before the Council with the following observations from us. We should like to have the wharf as arranged because .sve have already obtained the necessary permission of the Manchester Ship Canal Company and the Mersey Conservancy. If the Corporation will consent to this course, we are quite open to enter into an arrangement whereby a tcnspor- ary wharf can be put down immediately whilst the

, other work of a more permanent nature wag proceeded with at leisure. We take this opportunity of asking you to represent the urgent necessity for a wharf at the en- trance to the Warrington Docks on the Manchester Ship Canal.where steamers up and down to Manchester could ti.ke on a parcel of goods without entailing ana- great iss of time.—Yours faithfully, (Signed) W. A. i3isitor AND CO.

Tax WESLEY Gmtn.—The first monthly social meet- ing was held on Monday evening, when 51 persons were present. The president,Rev.C.P.Glidden took the chair. Miss By& read the roll, and Mr. John Hassall was ap- pointed to the office of librarian. Conversation was en- gaged in between the items of the following well- arranged programme : Organ solo," March by Farmer," Mrs. Gliddon ; solo, " The river of years," Miss Boys ; reading, " The seli-disparager," Mr. W. Rowe ; duet, "The pilot brave," Miss A. Locker and Mr. C. P. Brad- bury ; reading, •• An affair of oysters," Mr. W. Moors ; solo." The pilot," Mr. T. W. Barrow ; reading, " The cynics end," Rev. C. P. Glidden ; duet, " The morning land," Rev. C. P. and Mrs. Gliddoci. Daring the short time this guild has been estatlished, it has done good work, and bids fair to become a very valuable source of belp to the church. Jtritime SALE.—On Friday, a jumble sale was held in the Girls' school...As the result of the energetic effort.

Of the Vicar and his helpers, there was a large collection of sucharticles as are seldom seen together in ole room. There were: ducks, poultry, rabbits, crockery, veget- ables,carcase of a sheep, water-cans, books, fa3cy goods, old clothes, &n. The sale was opened at 3 o'clock by Mrs. Hervey Talbot. of Dutton Lodge. She said it gave her great pleasure to open the sale, as she took as great interest in the services of the church as any parishioner preseat. They were most fortunate in having such a vicar, who with the help of his wife, did PR much to brighten their homes and lives. The Vicar, Rev. G. D. Wray, thanked Mrs. Talbut 1. r coming so far in such inelemAnt weather to open the sale, and said it was very pleasing to have such an interest taken in the parish and church by one at such a distance. He explained the object of the sale, which was to raise money for the church and the mission ehurch. A great deal bad been done, during the last 12 months, to beautify the church and to improve the services. He spoke in grateful terms of thehelp he triceived in his labors, from all sorts of people. He said the Church of England was sometimes called the church of the classes: ia Halton, it certainly was the church of the workira.: classes, who gave it their hearty and generous support. The attendance in the afternoon was very large, and at night the room was crowded. Those who preferrod speculation to open pur- erase. could ent rin a raffk or dlp into a bran-pie. Much Inn was caused b^ a mock auction conducted by Mr. Job Hancock. Every article was sold; and the SUM realized was £36 16s. 3d. SHIP CANAL LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC. The sea-going traffic on the Ship Canal last week was somewhat below the avert.ge,the total number of vessels arriving and sailing during the seven days ending Fri- day, November 15, being 98, with an aggregate net re- gistered tonnage of 29,215 toms, as 4g4inst 150 vessels of 38,408 tons during the preceding sever days. Coastwise traffic was less by 46 ships and 2,954 registered tons, whilst in the foreign trade there was a decrease of ships ' and 6,239 regiseered tons. Amongst the cargoes im- ported were 18 of general merchandise, 14 of stone and slate, five of china clay, five of pig iron, two of timber, two of vreen fruit.and one of logsvood. Twenty-three general cargoes were exported, four of coal, and one of pitch, a large cpiantity of wiiiriii is now being shipped ti Aotwerp by the regular weekly boats,.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOO [TALL.

Warrington are still dogged with ill-luck, and it is quite time that they should have a few smiles of the tickle jade, for they certainly have had frowns enough. The game on Saturday was one in which Warrington were especially unfortunate, for they were attacking the greater portion of the time, and actually got over the line, but the try was not allowed. Two penalty kicks also only just missed going over the goal posts. On the other hand, from a kick by a Batley player, the hall was carried cvQr the goal posts by the strong wind,and this, which was as much a surprise to the kicker as to any- one else, was the only score of the game. •

Dropped goals have been very frequent in matches in which Warrington have taken part, but unfortunately, only one has been on the right side. Batley, Bradford, Hull, and Hunslet have each dropped a goal, against Warrington, and in each case, with the exception of Hunslet, have the droppers won. The Yorkshire clubs appear to be greater adepts at the art of dropping goals than Lancashire clubs, for not a single dropped goal has been scored against Warrington by a club tor the latter county. The weather on Saturday was about the most miser- able there has been this season, and at Batley there was some doubt at first whether the match could be Played, as the wind and rain were so fearful. As it was, play only lasted an hour. Good form was utterly out of the question, but the Warrington team showed themselves the smarter of the two, despite the accidental dropped goal scored against them. The forwards were much quicker, though they were not quite as heavy as their vis-a-vis. Nevins and Houghton also played a good game, while the remaining backs defended well. Pas- sing was of course, out of the question. Warring ton were very much weakened by the absence of Barber, Broady, Foden, Burrows, and Saunders.

The cguninittee of Batley were anything but courteous in their treatment of the Warrington players, and if they treat everyone like they treated Warrington, visiting teams will not be very anxious to go there. No convey- ance cr anything else was provided and the players had to find their way to the field themselves. The day, as everyone knows, was a most miserable one, and after the game was over, the players were pitiable sights, owing to the rain and sludge. Notwithstanding this fact, no water was pr vided for the Warringtonisns,who had either to pay for water, or else to rub themselves down as best they can. How would Batlay like to come to Warrington under such conditions?

To-day is the" Derby " day of Warrington, and it is to be hoped that fine weather will favour the match with Oldham. Should it do so, there will no doubt be a record gate at Wilderspocl, for the Oldham team are great favourites at Warrington. If every team played the aame attractive game as Oldhatn, there would be no need to fear any decadence of Rugby football. There is also another thing which makes the visit of the Old- hamers very acceptable to the club they visit, and that is, they always bring a large army of followers, and thus help to swell up the receipts.

Oldham are playing very erratically this season, and it is a very difficult matter to reckon up their form. They have thus far played 12 matches, won 7, and lost 5. Notwithstanding the fact that they have dropped 10 points in the comry.tition, they have made a larger aggregate score than any team in the Northern League with the single exception of Bradford, as they have scored 99 points. Should they, therefore, score to-day they will pass their century. They came a cropper last Saturday week at Leigh, and Warrington will endeavour to emulate the latter's example to-day;

To do this, the following team has been select.d to represent Warrington: Heesom, full back; Barber,Cross, Burton and Broady, threequarters ; Nevins and Foden, half backs; Burrows, Fairhurst, Houghton, 11111,Barrett, Thornton,andrews.and Thorniley, forwards.

All the games in the Northern Union on Saturday were spoiled by the rain, and consequently the scores were in most cases, but small. Wigan will establish a record, if they continue in their present course. They have played twelve games, and exaetly half of them have been draws, and in five of those half dozen, there has not been a single score. They have a marvellous defence, but they are lamentably dr ficient in scoring power. St. Helens who played a pointless draw with them on Satur- day, come next in number of draws, with them.

Runcorn continue in fine form, and on 83turf3ay, de- feated TyWesley for the second time this season. This victory which was by two tries to nil,has landed them in the second place in the League, and a single slip of Brig- house Rangers wIl let them in to tbe top,as they are only a point behind. It is a very surprising fact that Run- corn, who have lost such a good man as Houghton, and have, not a great supply of reserves to draw upon have shown such form in the competition. They are only a light team, but they. are so well balanced all round that they make up by combination what they tackle weight.

Widner. have had a far .differenf experience from therr near neighb-wra, for whereas the latter are second from the top. Widnes are second from the bottom. They had to suffer the humiliation af being beaten by two tries to nil by Rochdale Hornets on Saturday,a team which pre- viously had only won ane match and that only by a try to nil. They have not justified their early promie, and will be fortunate if they escape the " wooden spoon."

The rival Rangers of Broughton and Broughton met for the fir t time in their history on Saturday, and the result was the most decisive of the afternoon, for the Yorkshire club were victorious by 11 points to 3. Hull also went down at home to Flunstet by 12 points to 5.

-- There were four games in which the victors only won by a try to nil. the winners being Oldham, Wakefield Trinity, Manningham, and Liversedge, and the losers, Stockport, Leigh. Leeds. and Huddersfield, Bradford have now dropp.d to the third place in the League owing to the defeat thus suffered at the hands of Palifix on Saturday. It is singular how badly they fare against clubs of their own country. Although they rank so high in the united competition,they have only won one match ,1 with a Yorkshire club this being Wakefield Trinity, and have lost four, On the other hand, they are as yet un- beaten by a Lancashire club, and have won eight And drawn one. This is a matter for wonder, and especially when we consider the care of Batley, who previrius to Saturday, had not won a single match with a Lanea. shireclub, but had been'fairlylauccessful with Yorkshire clubs. Football is a very peculiar game,

THE LOCK-OUT OF SHIPBUILDERS. MEETING OF EMPLOYERS. Representatives of the master shipbuilders of the Clyde, Tyne, Wear, and Tees and at Belfast met at Carlisle on Wednesday to consider the situation in the shipbuilding trade. The proceedings were private, but at the cross of the conference it was officially announced that the meeting had been unanimously in favour of the federation a the enr;ineer employers" for defensive purposes," and that a reptcsentativs committee had been formed to carry out the necessary arrangements.

THE LIBERATOR TRIALS. The trial of the Liberator Building Society case con- cluded on Wednesday evening. Jabez Balfour and two of his co-defendants, Brock and Theobald, were found guilty. The iury could not agree as to Di.,ley. S-ntence on the convicted defendants was postponed, and Sir R. Webster asked for time to consider what course he ehould take in regard to Dibley.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 23, 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 23, 1895.
SAD SCALDING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

Hilda Riley, daughter of Mr. William Arthur Riley, died on Sunday morning from the effects of scalds,wbich were sustained under most distressing circumstances on the 7th inst. Mr. J. E. Worley, coroner, conducted an inquiry at Wilson's Botel,on Tuesday.—William Arthur Riley, 6, Albert-terrace, Runcorn, was the first witness called, and identified the deceased as that of his daugh- ter, who was three years of age. He did not know the circumstances which led to the child's death.—Edith Jones, servant for Mrs. Riley, Bridge-st.: grandmother to the deceased, dep..:seti that the child was at Mrs. Riley's on the 7th inst. Witness had been into the kit- chen and bad drawn a bucket of scalding water from the boiler for the purpose of washing up the tea things. When reaching the doorway of the scullery the child ran against the buaret with its chest and was splashed by the water. Mrs. Riley was in the kitchen at the time, and she took off the child's clothing. A doctor was afterwards sent for. —Dr. McDougall stated that he Witi called in on the evening of he 7th lest, immediately after the accident, to see the child. He attanded it .until the time of its death, and saw it the night before it lied. The child was badly scalded on the upper portion of the body. The war. r seemed to have splashed pretty well all over the chest. Every- thing possible was done for the child. It was a singularly nice and entertaining child. It died on Sunday morn- ing at five o'clock from shock to the system the effect of the scalds, and exhaustion.— Che Coroner said it was a sad case, and there could he no question that death was due to an accident. He was sure he expressed his own opinion and that of the jury in sympathising with the parents in the loss they had sustained by the death of such a promising child. A verdict of " Accidental I death" was returned.

div.head: INTERESTING CASE AT RUNCORN
div.p: INTERESTING CASE AT RUNCORN
COUNTY COURT. '
A DISPU'rE ABOUT PIGEONS.

Before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes at Runcorn I County Court on Tuesday, a claim of £29 183. id. was made by Peter Coyle, licensee of the Weaver Hotel, Weston, against William Orme, quarry proprietor, Higher Runcorn. The items in the account included £l6 16s. for four pairs of prize pigeons; £3 3s. for an English concertina; inhabited heuse duty £1 13s. 2d ; club money £1 is. ; harness and traces £2 5.3. 8.1. ; arid an amount for corn, oats, &c. Mr. Orme made a counter-claim against the plaintiff for £3B. £2B ofl this amount was for converting to his own use fourteen horn- ing pigeons, bred at Rose Cottage, Weetou-rcad, and left at the Weaver Hotel by agreement with the plaintiff who was to keep and look after them. The other item of £lO was for the plaintiff converting to his own use one horn- ing pigeon. Mr. Grier, of Liverpool, instructed by Mr. Burton, of Runcorn, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. , Trevor Lloyd, of the North \Vales circuit instructed by Mr. A. Linker, appeared on behalf of the defendant. In opening the case, Mr. Grier said the defendant Orme diseuted the sum of £3 33. for the concertina and £l6 163. for the pigeons. The rest of the items were admitted. In the year 1893 the defendant was landlord of the Weaver Hotel, and he told plaintiff that he was desirous of leaving and selling his interest in it and the furniture aud fittings. The plaintiff was one of those lucky people who happened to have made some money out of the Manchester Ship Canal. He was a foreman fitter and seemed to have taken contracts and to have made censiderable sums.—His Honour: Not a share- holder? (Laughter.)—Mr. Grier: No. The plaintiff bought the business, &c. for £2,000 on the 12th July. 1893. That sum iecluded everything inside and outside the house, but exception was now taken to a number of valuable pigeons. The plaintiff contended that they were part and parcel of the purchase. Counsel referred , to the fact that nothing was said respecting them until' the action was instituted, and therefore it was impos- sible ler Mr. Orme to recever his action for detention as he must first make same demand which should be re- fused. Ha would call the auctioneer who would show that the defendant left the house, saying that he had taken everything belonging to him. When the inven- tory was drawn up he made no objections to it. Peter Coyle, landlord of the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, stated that at the end of June 1893, the defendant sugaested to witness that he might buy it, and on July 12, 1893, he went to the hotelf saw the defendant there, and he again asked him to purchase it. He mentioned that the lowest price was £2,000 for everything inside and out as it stood on that data. Witness went through the house with him and then outside. He was taken to both pigeon cotes, and Orme told him that those in the lower cote were very valuable birds. Witness asked him the value and Orme said they were worth £lO 103. per pair. He agreed to pay the money asked for if it could be arranged. He paid £l,OOO down and the other in in- stahnents. Mr. Orme sent for Mr. Hickman, auctioneer, and he came. Defendant told him the terms arranged, that witness was to have everything for £2,000 with the exception of the things in the nursery. Mr. Hick- man went through the place and was pointed out the different things 'inside and outside the house. A roueh draft of an agreement was drawn up by Mr. Hickman and signed and he came back on the following Saturday. Mr.Flickmas asked Orme if he had removed everything belonging to him, and he stated that he had with the exception ot his own clothing. Nothing wes said about the pigeons. The agreement was then signed. An inventory was afterwards made by Mr. Hickman, and it included 81 pigeons. He had seen the defendant several times since the inventory was made, and Orme had never suggested to him that he should give up to him some pigeons. Shortly before Christmas, 1891, witness met defendant when he asked him if he had parted with all the pigeons, and he ultimately agreed to sell him four pairs at £4 43. per pair. Ha also agreed to give witness £3 33.f0r a concertina.—Cross-examined by Mr. Lloyd witness acknowledged that it was agreed the remaining £l,OOO should be paid by instalments. He admitted that one sof his bills of exchange had heen dis- honoured. He gave two of the best pigeons to his wife's brother, but he denied that Urmson, a man in his em- , ploy, remonstrated with him, stating that they belonged no Orme. It was not originally agreed that witness should keep sixteen of the best pigeons fir Orme. He ' swore he had not told Urmsnn that the sixteen birds in the lower cote belonged to Orme, or that he had told Orme that he wished him to fetch his pigeons. William Hickman, Arpley-street,Warringtoreauctioner and valuer, stated that in response to a telegram he went to the Weaver Hotel in July, 3893. lie saw the pleintiff and defendant there. fie was told by the ! parties that they wished him to manage the business for I them as Mr. Orme was about to sell the business to Mr. Coyle. Witness asked them on what terms. The terms were that Mr. Orme was to sell the licence. possession, , tenancy, furnitures stock-in-trade, outdoor effects, pigeons, poultry, pigs, at the sum of £2,000, Two exceptions were made, one with regard to the r oetents of the nursery, and the other, two oil paintings of himself and son, which were to be kept by Mr.Orme. He drew up a memoran• dum,and it was signed by both of them. The purchase was completed on the 15'11 July, 1893, three days after he visited the premises. He received instructions to pre- pare an inventory. On his second visit Orme teld him that he had removed all his things, and said he was pre- . pared to walk out of the house with his hat and coat on, Beth Orme and Coyle seemed satisfied. The result of the inventory taken by him was that he valued the total worth of the effects at £1,889 11. e. His valuation included all the pigeons on the place. The concertina,which was ! damaged and out of tune, he valued at £l.

Samuel Clarke, hay and straw dealer, Frodsham, said he visited th heaver Hotel at the time the agreement was made. He flaked Mr. Orme to make him a present of a couple of pigeons,but he told him that they now be- longed to Mr. Loyde.
Peter Hughes, liconsed victualler. Dunham-rith-Fliii, confirmed this statement.

George Coyle,son of the plaintiff, spoke to making out an account to the defendant. William Turner,Weston Point,deposed that he saw Mr. Orme leave the pigeon cote at th., Weaver Hotel with a hasl<et containing pigeons. He heard him ask Mr. Coyle : to sell him seine. Mr.Llovd,on behalf of the defendant,said there would be a good deal of contrary testimony, and he should call witnesses to show conclusively that a bargain was made between the defendant and plaintiff that the siveen valuable pigeons were to remain the property of Mr. Orme, and to be kept by Mr. Coyle. That arrangement ' was come to for a good reason. Mr. Orme was going to live with his mother, and she did not wish to have the birds about her house. It would he further stated that when Coyle was about to present a relative from Chester with a pair of the best pigeons, Urmson remonstrated with Coyle, telling him that they were Mr.Orme's, and he answered, "It is all right. I have made it right with the late landlord." His (counsel's) case was that plain- tiff had got the pigeons and paid nothing for them. He thought the claim was a false one,and was made because Coyle had got "his back up" through the defendant is- suing an execution for his money which was owing on the purchase. The valuable pigeons in question were never put in the valuation. They claimed that they were theirs, and as they had been sold by the plaintiff they claimed for the doss.

William Edward Orme give evidence as to selling the Weaver Hotel. There were two cotes of pigeons, one containing 61 common birds, and the other 16 valuable ones. The latter birds were locked up and were not seen by the auctioneer. He valued the 16 pigeons at £BO. The arrangement made was that tney should remain with Mr. Coyle until witness had convenience for them. He did not receive a bill for pigeons he had taken from Mr. Coyle's place until after an execution had been ishued against him On a visit to witness's mother's house, Coyle said" I wish you wisuld fetch your pigeons away," aad witpess replied" I will come on Saturday." He went to the Weaver Hotel for that purpose and brought away six. On Sunday morning he examingd the birds and five of thNn were common ones. He went to Coyle who told him that the valuable birds had been sent to Chester,and on being returned they should be sent to his house.—ln cross-examination witnesa ad- mitted that he had nothing in writing to show that the pigeons were to be excepted from the inventory. Be had not paid a penny for the keep of the pigeons. He would have brought an action for the recovery of the birds,but for the advice of his mother. He had also never received from the plaintiff any interest ; it had taken him all his time to get the principal. On being questioned respecting the evidence of Mr. Turner, witness stated that lots of people were bought over for 2+. 61. His Honour : How do you know lots of people can be bought for 2s. 61. ?—Witness : Because Mr. Tur- ner never heard such a thing mentioned as he had stated. —His Honour : That is not an answer tl ray q.iestian.— Witness : They would not say such things as they do without it.—His Honour: Why not £6 instead of 2.. 6a? —Witness: They would take £5 sooner than 2s. 6.1. His Honour: Do you mean to tell us that you can hire witnesses for 2s. .6d. ? You are making a strong asser- tion against your neighbourhood. He careful what you say.—Witness : 'fhere is DO truth in Mr. Turner's state- ment.
Henry Urmaon, 86. Shaw-street, Runcorn, Richard Marshall, Regent-strtet, Runcorn, and Mrs. Ormelso gave evidence for the defence, bearing out the barrister's statement.

Plaintiff was recalled and stated that defendant did not come to him the day after receiving the pigeons, and ask for :t certain valuabio bird. He did come however, sometime after, and witness told him that it was in Chester.

- His!! nour in summing up, said in the written and signed agreement there were no exceptions whatever made, and no exception made E 1.4 to the pigeons. H the pigeons were worth £3O one would have though that the defendant would have said that there should have been something stated in the document concerning them. It was not denied that the inventory was correct. He pre- ferred to rely on the written document. and he must give judgment for the plaintiff on the claim stir] counter ( laim. He would reduce the claim to £27 153. id, in consequence of the value of the concertina.

div.head: FUNERAL OF A: OE LITE MR. ROBERT ROYLE, RUNCORN.
div.p: FUNERAL OF A: OE LITE MR. ROBERT ROYLE, RUNCORN.

The remains of the late Mr. Robert Royle, of 9, Co-ot,erative Terrace, Halt me-road, Runcorn. were interred in the Nonconformist portion of the Runcorn Cemetery. on Monday afternoon. The deceased gentle- man prominently identified himself with the Co-operative movement, and was one of the founders of the Society which has now become a very flourishing organisation in Runcorn, Widnes and district. The various establish- ments of the Society were closed on Monday afternoon, from 32 to 4 o'clock, in order to give the employees an opportunity of manifesting their respect and esteem to the memory of the departed. The funeral corteee formed outside Mr. Royle's late residence, and shortly before two started en its way to the place of burial. In advance walked Mr. M. Timperlev, representing the United Methodist Free Church, Runcorn, and Mr. J. Betney, of Widnes. The came the following members of the Management Committee of the Society, Messrs. Dudley, Rhodos and Aston, Mr. J. Evans, cashier, Mr. W. Upton, secretary, Mr. W. M. Morris, assistant manager, and Mr. J. J Shaw, assistant secretary. After thee came Messrs. Brodwick and Bates, represent- ing the holesale Society and Mr. Minns. of Chester, who represented the Cheshire and North Wales District Conference Aseeciatiore Immediately behind them came about 80 of the emplrec tiee inconnection with the various shops at Rtincorn and Widnes. Behind these were gen- tlemen representine the general public.and among them were Messrs. A. Hough, J. Sefton, W. Powell, W. Crop- per, sea., W. Nickson, of Runcorn, and Messrs.. J. Fitz- patrick, and T. Igerbury, of Widnes. On either side of the hearse walked the bearers, Messrs. S. Johnson, R. Richardson, J. Leach, and W. Blinston, and following were the two carriaees containing the mourners. In the first rode Charles and Robert Royle, sons ; Albvn, grandson, and T. Hoyle and J. Went, nenhews. The second contained R. Royle, J. Percival, J. Yates, and T. Walker, nephews, and the Rev. J. Stafford.

The service was conducted by the Rev. J. Stafford, who, in the coarse of an address, said that the large con- course of people was indeed a glowing tribute to the memory of the late Mr. Royle and manifested their sym- pathy with his family. Their departed friend and brother was no ordinary man,he had served his day and generation well. They called to mind the good services which had teen rendered by him in political reform, for Mr. Hoyle was was one of those who were in the van guard of political freedom, and advancement. Besides this he had rendered imporunt service to a great commercial enterprise in Runcorn and Widnes. They were clad to know that Mr. Royle was one of the patrlarcs of Co-operation, and they were pleased to see present one of those who at- tended the first meeting held at which their departed brother was also present. From that time onward he was in heart and sympathy with everything to elevate• man, to bring aboat 'sobriety, and the spread of the Gospel. For some years past their friend took a great interear in the Sunday School and Church work carried on in Ellesmere-street, and they were pleased to testify that he had endeavoured to make a good finish and that he had lived a consistent life, in accordance with his teachings. He hoped that all present would live for God 80 that when their bodies came to be laid in the silent grave their friends might have the fullest assurance that they had gone to Christ. On the coffin was a number of beautiful floral emblems, cnntributed by, .wife and family, A. Mathews, Mr. and Mrs. Ackerley, Mr. and Mrs. W. Powell, Mr. and Mrs. Lacy, Miss Flesmondalge, Mr. and Mrs. R. Morris, and A. Douglas. The employees of the Co-operative Society also placed on the grave a beautiful artificial wreath. The arrangements were cirried out under the s.pervision of Measrs.lVV. Lacy and W. M. Morris. Mr. W. Nixon supplied the coffin, and Messrs. Booth and Sons furnished the mourming coaches. Letters of condolence have been received from the Whole. sate Society, the Cheshire and North Wales District Co- operative Association, and from the Runcorn Co-opera- tive Society.

div.head: EARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
DRIJNICENNIISS.
James Carlin and Jot,n Fristoll, colliers, of Athol- st., Newton, were charged with being drunk and fiz,lating in Earlestown, on Saturday night, and were fined 23. 61. and co,ts. . .

John Gill, a collier, of charged with being drunk and disorderly in Earle-st., on Satur- day night, he was further charged with assaulting P.C.'s Tiveney and Burns, and with damaging the uniforms ot the officers. On the application of Sergeant Clarke the prisoner was remanded to the Warrington Petty Sessions on Wednesday. LO.G.T. (EBENEZER LODGE). The usual weekly session of the Earlestown Ebenezer Lodge No. 752 was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Tuesday evening, and was presided over by Bro. W. Hatton, C.T. The roll al officers was called and responded to. and minutes of last session were read and adopted, after which the digest of T.W. District Lodge was then read. One candidate was proposed for membership and initi- ated same time. The programme of the evening was then proceeded with, as follows :—Bro. A. Morris, reading Bro. J. Dickson, song ; Sister Mrs. Taylor, reading; Bro. J. Taylor, song; Bro. W. J. Taylor, reading ; Bro. J. Jones, song; and others. Lodge closed in due form at 9.30, the members hay- lug spent a very pleasant evening. TRAP ACCIDENT AT NEWTON.

On Wednesday afternoon 31; ;..-Ber-r-y-,..0f the Leah Arms Hotel, Newton, with her son, were driving to Warrington, and when passing through Winwick they met a traction engine on the road. At a nar- row point in the road when attempting to pass, the trap came in contact with a telegraph pole erected at the roadside, and was overturned, the occupants being thrown to the ground. Mrs. Berry, besides being injured,suffered a severe shock to the system and was medically attended on her arrival home. Her eon escaped unhurt. PURSBITTATIoNS AT EARLESTOWN.

There was a very pleasant gathering at the Mis- sion Earlestown, on Wednesday evening in connection with the choir of St. John's Church, for the purpose of presenting marks of esteem and congratulation to Mrs. Squires nee Lewis, and Mr. G. E. Jackson, botn members of the church choir. The Rev. T. R. Matthews presided, and besides the Rev. E. W. Kaye there were about 30 members of the choir present. The chairmaa made the pre- sentations, which consisted of a silver-plated tea pot and jam spoon to each of the parties named, and referred in graceful terms to their connection with the choir. Mr. Latimer replied for Itirs. Squires, and Mr. Jackson also thanked the members for their beautiful gifts. Those present afterwards partook of a coffee supper, and the remainder of the evening was spent in games of various kinds.

div.head: G 00 D"TEMPLAIIS.
div.p: G 00 D"TEMPLAIIS.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templara was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, on Monday evening. Bro. J. Hatton,C.T., presided over a large muiter of members and visi- tors. One candidate was admitted to membership and several others were proposed. The digest of business for the District Lodge quarterly session to be held at Prescot on Saturday was read by Bro. Newman,L.D.,and representatives were introduced. Arrangements were made for a monthly public en- tertainment on Saturday, November 30th. The pro- gramme of the evening was " entertainment and coffee supper." Bro. W. 11. Crowther and G. Clarke gave musical items and Bro. W. Wilson a recitation. tiro. W. Willis presided at the piano. A coffee supper followed, to which a large number was present. • FOUND DROWNED AT EARLBSTOWN. Shortly before eight o'clock on Tuesday morning a man named James Prince, engaged to look after the mschinery of the canal locks, found the body of a man limiting in the S3nkey Canal near the St. Helens Road bridge, Newton Common. He hauled the body to the side with a rake, and lifted it on to the towing path, and afterwards sent for the police who removed it to a stable behind the lock-keeper's house, inquiry showed that, the body was that of Edward Hughes, a collier, who resided with John Williamson, of Railway Vievr,Collins Green. Hughes left home on Monday nigt t saying he was going by the 6.30 train to Earlestown. This he appears to have done, and on his way home again, called at the Ship Inn near the canal, where he stayed until 9.30. lie then left for home, being at the time quite sober, and after crossing the canal walked along the towing path towards St. Helens Road. Nothing more was seen or heard of him until his dead body was found as stated, and it is not known how he came to be in the water.—The inquest was held at the Ship Inn, Earlestown, on Thursday morning by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner. Evidence bearing out the foregoing facts was given, and a verdict of " Found drowned "was returned.

div.head: EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The 140th quarterly meeting of this society was held in the Ce-operative nil on Monday evening. Mr. J. Moss presided and there was a large attend- ance of members. The report and balance sheet stated that toe cash receipts for goods sold over the counters amounted to £3,939 14s. The nett. amount available for dividend was £515 Sc. 93. which would pay a dividend to members of 28. 6d. in the .£ on their purchases, absorbing £513 12s. 6d. and Is. 3d. to non-members which Would require 3s. 91, leav- ing a balance of £1 12s. 6d. to be added to the con- tingent fund. During the quarter 17 new members had been admitted and 45 struck off, thus leaving 963 on the books of whom 668 had brought in cheques. The average purchases of these amounted -to £6 per member per quarter, or about 9s. per week. The average tor the whole number on the books was about £4 per quarter or 6s. per weak After a lengthy discussion the balance sheet was adopted. Messrs. Parr and Mullins were re-elected to serve on the Committee of Management. The Chairman said he had received a circular from the Medical Aid Society appealing for support, and it wbs decided to give a donation of ..C2 2s. to the Society. The question of the annual tea partywas brought up,but it was thought that November being the best mouth in which to ,hold the festival, and the month being so far advanced that it would be better to hold it over for another year. The meet- ing was then dissolved, A special general meeting was afterwards held to consider a revision of cer- tain rules, but owing to the lateness of theevening, it was decided to call another meeting in a fortnight to specially consider the revision. MASONIC INSTAVATION A NNWTON. On Tuesday the • brethren of the Makerfield lodge No. 2155 of Freemasons held an installation cerenaony at the Masonic rooms, Pied Bull Hotel, Newton. The ptoceedings were presided over by the W.M. Bro. T. Ormand, and amongst the visitors present were Bros. W. Goodacre, P.G.5.8.,Pr0. 0.8., G. McClelland, P.M.,P.P.0.D. (Unanimity 287), W. Bowden, Pro. G.R. (Worslev 1814), E. Burchall, P.M. (Prince of Wales 1035), T. Yarwood, P.M. (Marquis of Lorne 1354), K. E. Fairclough, I.P.M. (Clapton 1365), J. W. Travers, W.M. (Marquis of Lorne 1334). R. H. Pearsou, S.W. (Lights 148), W. Gilbert, S.W. (Faith 484), 11. T. Arnott, J.D. (Alex- andra Palace 1541). T. J. Lloyd, I.G. (Light SI 148), S. W. Smith, S.S. (Bootle-Wilbraham 2463), W. Burgess (Merchants 241). G. Goff (Faith 484), W. J. Fairclough (Merchants 211). Amongst the mem- bers of the Lodge present were Bro. W. H. Arnott, I P.M., Prov. I.G. VV. ; P. Garton, P. NI., W. Tongs, T. Graham, W. Travers, FL Houghton, W. Storrer, J. Ferguson, J. 11. Lane, T. Barnes, James Prescott, B. Corlett, T. Southern, F. J. Emmett, O. Maktn, R. J. Berry and J. Williamoou. The instating master WAS Bro. T. °tumid, who gave the charge in an ex- ceptionally able and impressive manner, Bro. H. Btone, P.M., Pro. AG.'. officiating as director of ceremonies. Bro. Ormand then proceeded to invest the officers as follows Fairclough. W.M. ; T. Ormand, I.P.M. ; C. E. Arnott, S.W. ; C. H. Bodmer, J.W. ; J. Singleton, Pleas. ; J. Gooding, Sec. ; C. S. Bennie, S.D. ; J. Sankey, J.D. ; 11. Stones, P.M.D C.; W. F. Aruott, organist ; J.G.' C. Starkie ; LG., J. DM, A. W. Anderton, B. Corlett, T. Graham (stewards), J. H. Galloway, I'. M. Tyler. A P.M.'s jewel was afterwards presented to the I.P. M., Bro. Ormand on behalf of the Lodge by the W. 61., and a treasurer's jewel was presented to Bro. S. Hewitt,on behalf of the Lodge by Bro. H. Stonee,P.M.,in recog- nition of their services to the Lodge. The members at the close adjourned, and the festival of St. John was celebrated by a banquet, which was served in first class style by Mr. J. Dorman. The feast was much enjoyed and during the after proceedings a number of Masonic toasts vrece presented, and honoured. Songs were contributed by Bro. S. W. Smith and B. Corlett, and a recitation by Bro. J. H. Lane. Bro. W. F. Arnott presided at the organ,and Bro. J. Prescott at the piano.

div.head: CAIRO-STREET LECTURES.
div.p: THE CAIRO-STREET LECTURES.
"ART IN LARGE TOWNS."

The Cairo-st. schoolroom was again crowded on Mon- day evening when the fifth lecture of the season, " Art in Large Towns," was given by Mr. T. S. Handal!, of Manchester. Lantern slides were exhibited by Conu- cillor Monks with his usual skill.

Mr. Jouta CROSFIELD:J.P.:Zia he had great pleasure in taking the chair that night, and introducing to them his old friend, Mr. T. C. Horsfall, of Manchester. He called him old —(laughter)—not because he was very old but because their friendship dated back for 45 years. (Applause.) He dare sav that a good many present there that night would know that Mr. flonfall:f had exerted himself in Manchester to improve the condition and elevate the taste of the working classes.fle had been influential in establishing an art museum in Ancoats, in Manchester, the lowest part of the town, thus enabling the working classes to see pictures which were calculated to cultivate their minds and elevate their taste. He was one of the law gentlemen who lived out of himself and lived to improve the people around him.(Applause.) He had done his utmost in Manchester to abate the smoke nuisance, and he wrote to the speaker some years ago to ask him to use his influence in Warrington to abate the smoke here because smoke was a hindrance to the enjoyment of human life. He (Mr. Crosfield) had to write to him to say that he was sorry he was helpless because the principal smoke in Warrington came from the iron works, and there was a clause in the act which exempted iron works, so that they could turn out as much smoke as they liked. (Laughter.) He was proud to say that they had made such improvements in their works at Bank Quay that they had smokeless chimneys,and he believed the same thing obtained in several other works in the town. (Applause.) They had not done much for art cultivation in Warrington,but still they had got a fair museum and library and also a good school Of Art, which, he was proud to say,had turned our some of the finest artists of the day. (Applause.) He might mention Mr. Luke R.A.—(applause)—Mr. Woods—(applause)—and that eminent sculptor John Warrington Wood. (Ap- plause.) Those were things that they might well no proud of,but yet there was a great deal more to do. He was also glad that in Warrington they had during the summer months a band of music in the park—(ap- plause)—which provided splendid recreation for the people every Sunday.afternoon. The speaker was pleased to see that the Manchester Museum last week was open on Sunday afternoon for the people. (Loud applause.) He intended to try if he could not get some influence to bear upon the Corporation of Warrington to open our Museum on Sunday afternoon. (Applause.) They (the Crosfields) opened the gardens at Walton Lea twice a year to let the people see camellias, azaleas, chrysanthe- mums, etc. (Applause.) He supposed that they had on an average an attendance of about 6,000 people. (Ap- plause.) There was perhaps one man in 50,000 tha; be- lieved it was wrong to open such places on a Sunday. He was not of that opinion. (Hear, hear.) He thought all of them ought to open ou Sunday. (Applause.) The working class required recreation and they ought to have it. (Applause.) They were told that there were sermons in stones, and he thought there were sermons in flowers. (Hear, hear.) .

Mr. HORSPALL, after a few preliminary remarks upon the importance of indulging in healthful pursuits as a means of avoiding temptation, cited art as a pursuit which was helpful to all persons who wished to live rightly. Cricket, football, tennis,and other such games were health-giving exercises, and did much to counter- act the attractions of pursuits of evil ; the study of literature and the discussion of great political questions were also means to this and ; but the study or art— more particularly of the branch known as pic- ture-making or painting—was perhaps the most beauti- ful and most powerful of all. The world in which we lived was most beautiful and wonderful in the t yes of those who had a knowledge of art, and the study of it was wonderful and beautiful also. It was necessary for them to come,under the influepce of persons who had acquired knowledge in this respect ; someone who would point out to them the beauties which this and that object possessed so as to create within them the love of observing those beauties of Nature for themselves. If the history of art were examined it would be found that picture-making had been the language that had been especially observed for the communication of the thought and the feeling by which one human being could be influenced by another human being. Suppose a man left smoky Warrington, went on a visit to the Welsh coast, and saw, while alone, the rising of the BUD under more striking conditions than ever before. He might be very much impressed by it, and when he returned to his home he might want to tell his wife of it. He would feel very probably at a loss for words to adequately describe the beauty of the scene, he would want his wife to understand and picture to herself the sight, but he could not help her to do so. What, then, would be his fint desire after his failure to paint the scene in words? It would be to paint it in reality in colours, so that she might gather some sound idea of the grandeur of the sight. This genie feeling had had a great deal to do with the origin of picture-making, and to-day it was still proved that the picture-making art was the language of admiration, love, and strong emo- tions. (Applause ) Therefore, if we wanted to give our fellow creatures the power to share in the intense delight of the beautiful things in this world, it was necessary for us to have recourse to painting pictures. Every parent should remember that if he wished to give his boys and girls a chance of enjoyment and recreation,and to prevent them falling into the temptations to fellow ev.l ways, he must have recourse te art. How could this be done ? The lecturer looked at the question trom the paint of view of those persons -who lived in large towns such as Warrington. In the first place ever) parent who wished to influence the tastes of his children should take them as much as possible into the presence of really beautiful things It was a most invaluable place of education to take a child into the green fields and woods, and let it see its parent enjoy tho beautiful things. Parents should make as full use Of the town parks as possible, and point out to their children ,the many things of beauty. They had a beautiful part' in Warrington—(applause)—and he adviaed all parents to use it for the purpose he bad named. Then again they could not better use their time of leisure than by visiting the Museum And Art Gallery, in Bold st. (Applause.) He (Mr. Horsfall) hid some idea of the contents of that building, for he had been in it that afternoon, and he knew that in the collection of beautiful pictures hanging there, was the requisite medium for forming the tastes of the children for art. (Applause.) If he could per- suade some workingmen to go into the picture gallery and find enjoyment there, he was sure they would after. wards admit that it was valuable advice. (Hear, hear.) They neeeed, of course, as he had said already, the influence of someone else who knew the beauties of the pictures. If they knew anyone, therefore, he advised them to ask that person if he would go with them and I tell them a little hit about some of the pictures. (Hear, ' hear.) lie advised them in this way because he knew, from personal experience, that they would get to like the visits. Lost winter he had himself persuaded several men to join him in a series of visits to the art galleries in Manchester on Saturday afternoons. The men wont with him for six Saturdays, 2e hours being spent on each occasion in steadily walking through the museum for the purpose of finding the beauties and of enjoying them. At the end of the sixth visit the men had actually asked him if he could seare them two more Saturday after- noons. (Hear, hear.) He, of course, acceded to their request, which plainly showed that his efforts had not been in vain. The slides were then shown, the lecturer explaining lucidly the beauty of each. At the conclusion of his remarks Mr. W. LONG pro- posed a vote of thanks to Mr. Hnrsfall, which was seconded by the Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND, both of whom spoke in complimentary terms of the lecturer's dealing with his subject. The last named gentleman expressed the hope that as a result of the lecture a keener interest would be taken in art henceforth. (Applause.) The motion was unanimously carried, after which Mr. Hersfell briefly responded. He mentioned that in the Education Code this year certain alterations had been made by which it had been possible for children in ele- mentary schools to be taken by their teachers to I Museums and Art Galleries, and that time thus used I should be accounted in the school attendance. He sug- gested that the teechers of Warringtcn should follow the exam lea the teachers of Ancoats in taking the children to the Museum and Art Gallery. Councillor MONKS explained that this had already be(n started in Warrington, Mr. floesirsee replied that he was pleased to hear that it had. lie went on to observe, however, that as one teaeher was only allowed to take charge of fifteen chil- dren, assistance was needed in order that all scholars might receive an opportunity of visiting. If qualified persons could only be induced to proffer to take charge of so many children, it would be very helpful. The more children attended these places the better they would be I able, whme in years of maturity, to appreciate art. (Ap- plause.) The proceedings than terminated.

Richard Wingrove, an army reserve man, was hanged in Newgate prison on Tuesday morning for the murder of a woman named Eagle. A disaster nf a peculiarly appalling description oc- curred in Cleveland, Ohio, on Saturday night. An electric tram line crosses a river at an elevation of a hundred feet. There is a swing bridge in the middle of the structure, and through the mistake of an official a tramcar full of people was driven through the gatvs— which were closed against its passage—and fell into the stream below. Several persons jumped if the car and were saved, but all who fell with it of course perished.
